Adding `argon2 = "0.5"` (RustCrypto family, MIT/Apache, MSRV 1.65) to `[workspace.dependencies]` is the only new external dep; `hkdf` was already present. **Net test delta:** +9 inline tests in `rustgate_core::encrypted::tests::kdf_and_rotation` covering Argon2id determinism, HKDF round-trip determinism (sibling to the existing RFC 5869 known-answer test), past-expiry admission rejection at the `active_key_expired_at` accessor level, no-expirations tracing-warn emission, rotation-due audit event with deterministic synthetic clock, raw-hex backward-compat happy path including writer round-trip, file-IKM equivalence with inline-hex IKM, missing-IKM-source rejection, and Argon2 short-salt rejection. The pre-existing 37 encrypted-module tests pass unchanged. **Out of scope (deferred to separate PRs that keep #883 open):** sub-item 2 (audit-chain sequence numbers), sub-item 3 (NATS infinite-redelivery on panic), sub-item 4 (per-tenant token bucket).
- **Federation JWKS URL fetching with periodic refresh (refs #952, sub-item 2)** — federation operators can now point at a remote JWKS endpoint (RFC 7517) and have ES256 / EdDSA verifier keys hot-reload into the running `rustgate_federation::jwt::JwtAuthority` without a binary restart. The new `rustgate_federation::jwks_client` module (gated behind a new `jwks` cargo feature so the reqwest compile cost is only paid by deployments that need it) spawns a `SubsystemHandle`-managed background task via `JwksClient::start(config, tls_config, authority)`. The task fetches `GET <url>` over HTTPS using the **same** `rustls::ClientConfig` the federation peer connector already builds — there is no separate JWKS-only trust bundle. Responses parse into `JsonWebKeySet { keys: Vec<JsonWebKey> }`; entries are filtered by `kty/crv/alg`: `kty=EC, crv=P-256, alg=ES256` register as ES256 verifiers, `kty=OKP, crv=Ed25519, alg=EdDSA` register as EdDSA verifiers, and `kty=oct, alg=HS256` are gated behind a `JwksConfig.allow_hs256: bool` flag (default `false`) because publishing a symmetric secret over HTTP defeats the asymmetric trust boundary JWKS exists to provide. The verifier set is stored on `JwtAuthority` behind a new `external_verifiers: ArcSwap<HashMap<String, VerificationKey>>` field — the same lock-free hot-reload discipline used by ACL / authz / CRL elsewhere in the workspace — and `decode()` consults it after the static `verifiers` map so an operator-provided inline kid still overrides a JWKS-supplied entry under the same name. The next refresh delay is taken from the response's `Cache-Control: max-age=<N>` header, clamped into `[refresh_min, refresh_max]` (the `MIN_REFRESH_INTERVAL` floor is 60s; the `MAX_REFRESH_INTERVAL` ceiling is 24h); a missing header falls back to `refresh_min`. **Fail-closed semantics**: on an HTTP 5xx or transport / DNS / TLS error, the cached keyset is preserved verbatim — no keys rotate out, validation continues to succeed against previously-trusted kids until the upstream returns a clean response. This protects against an attacker who can knock the JWKS server offline being able to silently un-trust a peer; the price is that a deliberately-removed kid only stops verifying once the upstream successfully publishes its absence. Audit emission lands under the `audit` tracing target with four new event types in `rustgate_core::audit`: `jwks_refresh_success(url, key_count)`, `jwks_refresh_failed(url, reason)`, `jwks_key_added(url, kid, alg)`, `jwks_key_removed(url, kid)` — SIEM rules can correlate refresh-rate dashboards against per-kid lifecycle transitions, and the same sanitisation discipline (`s()` boundary wrap) used elsewhere in `audit.rs` defends against an attacker-controlled `url` containing CR/LF bytes. The `JwksConfig` struct deserialises from TOML in kebab-case with `deny_unknown_fields` so operator typos surface at start-up rather than as silently-ignored fields, and rejects plain `http://` URLs with `JwksError::Config` before any network work. **Net test delta**: +10 in-file unit tests in `jwks_client::tests` covering config validation (HTTP rejection, refresh-min floor, refresh-max ceiling, inverted min/max), `clamp_refresh_delay` boundary cases, and JWK filter edge cases (HS256 rejected by default, HS256 admitted on opt-in, missing-kid skipped, unsupported `kty/alg` skipped); +7 integration tests in `crates/rustgate-federation/tests/jwks_client.rs` (gated behind the `jwks` feature) covering the full lifecycle: initial fetch populates ES256+EdDSA verifiers and JWTs verify end-to-end; refresh interval honours `Cache-Control: max-age` and clamps into the configured window; a kid dropped by the upstream stops verifying after the next refresh; a 503 response keeps the cached keyset valid (fail-closed regression pin); HS256 is rejected when `allow_hs256:false` and loaded when `true`; audit events fire for every lifecycle transition (success, failure, key-added, key-removed); and a hand-rolled `tokio-rustls` server validates that the JWKS client presents the federation client cert and verifies the server cert against the **same** `TestCa` the federation connector uses (so the trust-bundle-reuse contract is pinned end-to-end, not just by code reading). **Out of scope — deferred to a separate PR**: the kid rotation-window state machine (the `Active → VerifyOnly → Removed` lifecycle in `crate::jwks::KeyState`) is sub-item 3 of #952 and is **not** consumed here. This PR installs the current set of advertised keys verbatim; once the rotation-window work lands, callers will compose the two. The Ed25519 (RFC 8037 EdDSA) signing path itself shipped earlier via #1230 (sub-item 1).
- **X.509 stack scoping documentation (refs #803, F-91 only — partial close)** — adds `docs/x509-stack.md`, a contributor-facing scoping document that pins which of the workspace's three concurrent X.509 ecosystems is the right one to reach for in any given role. Pre-this-PR, contributors had to grep across crates to discover that `rcgen` is the cert-generation stack (used in `rustgate-test-utils::certs` and `rustgate-enrollment::signing`), `x509-parser` is the read-side parser on the mTLS hot path (used in `rustgate-transport::extract` and across the federation / http / diagnostics surface), and that `x509-cert` + `der` + `cms` together are the only stack permitted for CMS signature wrapping of EST RFC 7030 endpoints (`rustgate-enrollment::cms_bag` and `rustgate-enrollment::est` under the `est` feature) — leaving open the failure mode where a future PR pulls `rcgen` into a transport-side parser or reaches for `openssl` rather than the existing three. The new doc has a per-ecosystem scoping table (workspace dep, used-in crate list, role, explicit out-of-scope list), a "what crate do I reach for to do X" decision tree (parse fields, sign a CSR, build a PKCS#7 bag, validate a chain, etc.), an explicit contribution-gate rule that none of the three may be used outside its documented role and that no fourth X.509 ecosystem may be adopted without prior discussion, a clarification that `webpki` chain validation is a transport-layer choice not in scope for this document, and migration notes pointing at the `RustCrypto/formats` family as the first place to look if any of the three upstreams stalls. F-92 (replace anyhow in libs) shipped via #1210; F-93 (reqwest audit) and F-94 (dep isolation) remain in #803 for separate follow-up PRs. Pure documentation change — no public APIs, dependency versions, or wire formats are altered.
- **ES256 / EdDSA federation JWT + JWKS key-rotation state machine (closes #760)** — the federation V2 JWT layer (`rustgate-federation/src/jwt.rs`) already supported HS256, ES256 (ECDSA P-256), and EdDSA (Ed25519); this change closes #760 by wiring the asymmetric verifier registry through to a new `rustgate_federation::jwks` module and a `/.well-known/jwks.json` HTTP endpoint, and pinning the algorithm-confusion defense behind a focused regression test. **(1) JWKS serialization (RFC 7517).** The new module exposes `JwkSet` / `Jwk` types that match RFC 7517 §4 (kty / kid / alg / use / crv / x / y) plus a `build_jwk_set` helper that walks `JwtAuthority::verifier_views()` (newly added) and emits one entry per ES256 / EdDSA peer kid. ES256 keys serialize as `kty=EC, crv=P-256` with the SEC1 uncompressed point split into `x` / `y`; Ed25519 keys serialize as `kty=OKP, crv=Ed25519` with a single `x` field carrying the raw 32-byte public key per RFC 8037. HS256 secrets are explicitly filtered out of every JWKS — the symmetric secret never leaves the issuing host, even if an operator has registered HS256 verifiers via `with_hs256_verifier()` for legacy peers. Output ordering is alphabetical by `kid` so two servers serving the same key set produce byte-identical JWKS responses, simplifying caching and CI fixture pinning. **(2) Key-rotation state machine.** A new `KeyState` enum (`Active`, `VerifyOnly`, `Removed`) and a hot-reloadable `KeyStateRegistry` (backed by `arc_swap::ArcSwap<BTreeMap<String, KeyState>>`, the same lock-free hot-reload discipline used by ACL / authz / CRL elsewhere in the workspace) let operators stage a rotation in three steps: promote a fresh key as `Active` (signing flips, both old and new still verify), demote the previous key to `VerifyOnly` (in-flight tokens still verify, but the old key no longer signs), and finally mark `Removed` once the longest-lived issued token under the old kid has expired (JWKS no longer advertises the entry and the verifier rejects it with `JwtError::UnknownKid`). The transitions are deliberately one-way — `demote_to_verify_only()` only acts on `Active` entries and `remove()` is terminal — so a misconfigured rollback cannot silently restart signing on a demoted key. **(3) `/.well-known/jwks.json` endpoint.** The federation REST API (`crates/rustgate-federation/src/api`) gains a new `JwkSetFn` callback on `ApiState` and a `handle_jwks` handler. The route is matched separately from the `/api/federation/` prefix because RFC 8615 places discovery URIs under `/.well-known/`. Responses carry `content-type: application/jwk-set+json` per RFC 7517 §8.5 and `cache-control: public, max-age=300` so verifiers don't hammer the endpoint on every JWT validation. When `jwks_fn` returns `None` (the default — JWT auth is opt-in and not yet wired through `rustgate-server` orchestration) the endpoint responds `404 Not Found` so consumers can distinguish "JWKS not configured" from "empty key set". **(4) PEM key loading via `rustgate_core::secrets::read_secret_file`.** Four new loaders — `load_es256_pkcs8_pem`, `load_ed25519_pkcs8_pem`, `load_es256_public_pem`, `load_ed25519_public_pem` — funnel through the unified secret-file reader from #1188 so PEM private keys on disk inherit the same strict permission gate (`mode 0o077` rejected on Unix), size cap (16 KiB), and ownership-UID check that enrollment passwords and federation HMAC secrets already use. Private-key bytes are wrapped in `Zeroizing<Vec<u8>>`, wiped on drop. SPKI public keys are unwrapped to the raw form `JwtAuthority::with_es256_verifier` / `with_ed25519_verifier` expect (65-byte SEC1 / 32-byte Ed25519). **(5) Algorithm-confusion attack defense (regression-test pinned).** The classic JWT vulnerability — attacker takes a published ES256 public key, uses it as the HMAC secret, crafts a token with `alg=HS256` + `kid=peer-a`, and hopes the verifier picks the ES256 entry but feeds the public bytes through HMAC — is rejected with `JwtError::AlgorithmMismatch` before any signature work, because each entry in the verifier registry carries its `Algorithm` and `decode()` enforces `header.alg == verifier.algorithm()` first. The new `algorithm_confusion_attack_rejected` test in `jwks::tests` exercises exactly this attack shape against an HS256 issuer that registered a peer-a ES256 verifier, so a future refactor that drops the alg-mismatch check fails loudly here. **Net test delta: +28 inline tests in `rustgate_federation::jwks::tests` plus 3 JWKS endpoint tests in `api::tests` (jwks_endpoint_returns_404_when_unconfigured, jwks_endpoint_serves_jwk_set_with_rfc7517_envelope, jwks_endpoint_rejects_non_get_methods). The full ES256 / EdDSA round-trip, multi-key kid routing, alg-confusion rejection, JWKS HS256-secret exclusion, JWKS Removed-state exclusion, JWKS VerifyOnly-state inclusion, state machine three-step transition, PEM round-trip via `read_secret_file`, and Unix permission gate are all pinned. The endpoint is opt-in via the `api` feature on `rustgate-federation`; `rustgate-server` orchestration installs `Arc::new(|| None)` for now so the endpoint responds `404` until a follow-up patch plumbs through a configured `JwtAuthority`.
- **First-class Prometheus metrics for router/PEP/obligation paths (closes #768)** — the router's hot paths (`route_for_egress`, fan-out, dedup, position cache, replay, store-forward) and the PEP/obligation evaluation pipeline previously had ad-hoc `tracing` logs but no first-class Prometheus metrics, so operators could not dashboard or alert on those critical paths. This PR adds eight new metrics, each wired through the established OnCallback discipline (per #1183 / #1198 / #1202 / #1206 / #1222) so operators with `--features metrics` see the new exposition immediately, while builds without the feature observe identical pre-#768 behaviour because the callback slots stay `None`. **Router fan-out:** `rustgate_router_fanout_total{destination}` (counter labelled `direct`/`group`/`broadcast`/`multicast`, increments per `route_for_egress` call); `rustgate_router_fanout_subscribers` (histogram of recipient counts per fan-out, buckets `0,1,5,10,50,100,500,1000` so the no-subscribers bucket is distinct from the small-fan-out and the wide-fan-out shapes); `rustgate_router_dropped_total{reason}` (counter labelled `no_subscribers|backpressure|acl_denied|authz_denied|obligation_failed`, same vocabulary the audit log emits — Prometheus dashboards and SIEM pivots stay in lock-step). **PEP:** `rustgate_pep_send_decisions_total{decision}` and `rustgate_pep_receive_decisions_total{decision}` (siblings labelled `allow|deny|fail_open`, kept separate so dashboards can graph allow/deny ratios by direction without pivoting on a label); `rustgate_pep_evaluation_seconds{direction}` (histogram in canonical SI units, buckets `50ns…10s` matching the existing `rustgate_authz_eval_nanos` bucket family). **Obligation:** `rustgate_obligation_applied_total{kind}` (counter labelled `mask_point|mask_payload|tag_classified|audit_extended|unknown`, mirrors the `Obligation` enum with the `#[non_exhaustive]` arm bucketed under a single `unknown` label so a future authz upgrade cannot silently grow Prometheus cardinality); `rustgate_obligation_failures_total{reason}` (counter labelled with the same `mask_point_non_xml|mask_point_xml_error|mask_point_io_error|mask_point_attr_budget_exceeded|unknown_variant` vocabulary the [`rustgate_core::audit::authz_obligation_failed`] event emits, so a SIEM correlation rule can join the metric and audit streams on the same key). **Wiring:** four new callback type aliases on `Router` (`OnFanout`, `OnDropped`, `OnPepDecision`, `OnObligationApplied`) plus `OnObligationFailure` on `ObligationRateLimiter`, each `Arc<dyn Fn(...) + Send + Sync>` matching the workspace's existing callback shape; `Router::set_on_fanout` / `set_on_dropped` / `set_on_pep_decision` / `set_on_obligation_applied` setters are hot-reloadable via `ArcSwap` so the metrics layer can be installed and replaced after construction without any lock on the routing hot path. The four router callbacks fire from the existing fan-out, drop, PEP, and obligation-application sites — no new state mutation, just observation. The bridge factories `metrics::router_fanout_callback()` / `router_dropped_callback()` / `router_pep_decision_callback()` / `router_obligation_applied_callback()` produce the typed callback closures the server binary installs once at startup; the obligation-failure callback installs through `ObligationRateLimiter::with_on_failure` alongside the existing `with_on_unknown` from #769. **Net test delta**: +5 inline router callback tests in `rustgate-transport::router::tests` (`fanout_callback_fires_with_destination_and_subscriber_count`, `dropped_callback_fires_with_no_subscribers_for_unknown_direct_target`, `pep_decision_callback_fires_with_send_direction_on_route`, `obligation_applied_callback_fires_with_kind_label`, `obligation_kind_label_maps_known_variants`); +11 inline registration + callback-bridge tests in `rustgate-server::metrics::tests::router_pep_obligation_metrics`, including end-to-end tests that run the exact closure shape `main.rs` installs through the wire to confirm a single callback fire produces both the documented counter increment and the histogram observation. **Operationally additive**: every change is observation-only on the routing hot path. No state mutation, no early-returns, no new error paths; the callback emission is `if let Some(cb) = guard.as_ref() { cb(...); }` shaped per the workspace pattern, so the cost is one `ArcSwap::load()` per fan-out plus one virtual call when a callback is installed. Operators without the `metrics` feature compiled in see no behaviour change at all because the bridge factories and `set_on_*` calls in `main.rs` are gated behind `#[cfg(feature = "metrics")]`. The label vocabularies are all `&'static str` at the call site so cardinality cannot drift at runtime regardless of which obligations a particular policy returns.

- **DoD Zero Trust Seven Pillars alignment mapping (closes #872)** — adds `docs/zero-trust-alignment.md`, a customer-facing alignment document showing how rustgate's existing capabilities relate to the DoD Zero Trust Architecture v2.0 Seven Pillars (User, Device, Application, Data, Network, Automation, Visibility). The document has a per-pillar table covering Implemented controls, Gaps, and the relevant NIST 800-53 control families for each pillar; a NIST 800-53 control-mapping table cross-referencing the most operationally relevant AC / AU / IA / SC controls (AC-3, AC-4, AC-6, AU-2, AU-3, AU-9, AU-10, AU-11, IA-2, IA-3, IA-4, IA-5, SC-7, SC-8, SC-12, SC-13, SC-28) to the rustgate features that satisfy them; and a gap-remediation roadmap that links each named gap (hardware-rooted identity, classification tagging, W3C trace propagation, K8s operator, DLP, JWKS rotation, DevSecOps packaging) to its tracking issue (#856, #849, #852, #874, #857, #952, #871). The document explicitly states it is informational only — rustgate carries no formal compliance certification against DoD ZTA, FedRAMP, FISMA, CMMC, or any other framework, and formal accreditation requires an independent assessment. The code-side action items the issue mentioned (`Metadata.classification` ref #849, `Identity.device_attestation` ref #856, W3C trace propagation ref #852) remain open in their respective tracking issues — this entry captures the documentation phase only. Cross-links the existing `SECURITY.md`, `docs/threat-model.md`, `docs/authorization.md`, `docs/concurrency-model.md`, and `docs/runbooks/audit-chain-corruption.md` so customer evaluators and accreditation auditors can navigate from the alignment view into the matching technical depth.
- **Audit-chain CI verification + `policy_id` on receive-time PEP audits (closes #772)** — closes two #772 observability items in one focused PR. **(1) CI verification gate for the hash-chained audit log.** A new integration-test binary `crates/rustgate-core/tests/audit_chain_ci.rs` exercises the full `HashChainWriter` → `verify_audit_log()` cycle plus tamper detection on every CI run. The test writes 100 audit records, reopens the file, and asserts the verifier returns `records=100`, a non-genesis tip, and `tip_seq=100`; then a second test flips a byte mid-file (line 51, payload of record 50) and asserts `VerifyError::HashMismatch` lands on the tampered line; a third test deletes a record from the middle of the chain and asserts `VerifyError::Gap { expected: 50, found: 51 }` fires on the line where the deletion first manifests, exercising the monotonic-seq contiguity check extended by #1173 (runbook: #1191). Pre-this-PR the chain implementation had inline unit tests in `audit_chain::tests` but no integration-binary test that ran in CI — a regression in the writer or verifier would only surface in production, by which point the operator's forensic record is already corrupted and the chain cannot be re-verified retroactively. Integration-binary isolation matters because (a) CI now reports a dedicated `audit_chain_ci` test target so a red dot maps directly to "the audit chain itself broke" rather than to a generic `rustgate-core` failure, and (b) the test process is short-lived so any future addition that installs a global tracing subscriber for chain emissions cannot leak its callsite-`Interest` cache into other tests in the workspace (same rationale as `mask_point_recovery_audit.rs`, `obligation_static_reason_audit.rs`, and `position_replay_rate_limit_audit.rs` in the transport crate). **(2) `policy_id` field on receive-time PEP audit events.** `audit::authz_obligation_failed` and `audit::authz_obligation_unknown` are siblings of `audit::authz_denied` on the same receive-time PEP path: a deny blocks delivery, an obligation_failed signals that the policy hint was un-actuatable (e.g. `MaskPoint` on a non-XML payload), and an obligation_unknown signals that a `#[non_exhaustive]` `Obligation` variant the transport build cannot honour was returned by the engine. The two siblings did not carry the engine's `policy_id` despite already receiving it through `apply_obligations_with_limiter`'s rate-limiter plumbing (#769) — SIEM correlation across rolling policy reloads needs this for forensic clarity, because a `MaskPoint` failure under `vN` looks identical on the wire to one under `vN+1` but the remediation may differ when the policy file itself was the regression. Both helpers gain a `policy_id: &str` parameter (sanitized via `s()` at the audit boundary per #1197 + #1220, defending against a malicious operator who shipped a policy file with CR/LF bytes in its id), and the field flows through to the audit emission alongside the existing `subject_cn` / `obligation` / `reason` / `recovery` / `source_protocol` / `destination_kind` schema. `apply_mask_point` in `rustgate-transport::obligations` is updated to take and forward the policy_id, mirroring how `apply_obligations_with_limiter` already plumbed it through to the unknown-variant rate-limiter bucket key. `authz_denied` already carried `policy_id` (added at the same time as the receive-side PEP wiring in router.rs); a new `authz_denied_audit_includes_policy_id_field` regression test pins the wire shape so a future refactor that drops the field surfaces here. **Net test delta: +3 integration tests in the new `audit_chain_ci` binary; +5 inline tests in `rustgate_core::audit::tests::authz` (`authz_denied_audit_includes_policy_id_field`, `authz_denied_sanitizes_policy_id_at_audit_boundary`, `authz_obligation_failed_audit_includes_policy_id_field`, `authz_obligation_failed_sanitizes_policy_id_at_audit_boundary`, `authz_obligation_unknown_audit_includes_policy_id_field`); existing `test_authz_obligation_failed` and `test_authz_obligation_unknown` smoke tests now also exercise the new parameter, including the empty-string call site that callers without engine context use. Operationally additive: the new `policy_id` field is strict information gain and the existing `event_type` / `action` / `result` / `reason` / `recovery` tokens are unchanged, so SIEM dashboards keyed on the prior shape keep working.

- **Multicast oversize-drop and SA auto-upgrade Prometheus metrics (closes #741)** — closes two operational gaps that previously made capacity-exhaustion and fleet-upgrade-progress invisible at the metrics surface. **(1)** `rustgate_multicast_oversize_dropped_total` (bare `IntCounter`) increments once per multicast message dropped because the destination group list exceeded the router's `MAX_MULTICAST_GROUPS` cap. Before this counter, the only signal was a `tracing::warn` in `Router::route_inner` — operators could not dashboard or alert on the drop rate, so a misconfigured publisher fanning out to thousands of groups (amplification-DoS shape) or a federation peer that lost its group-membership view and fell back to a wildcard fanout was visible only via log aggregation. **(2)** `rustgate_sa_auto_upgraded_total{from_version}` (`IntCounterVec` labelled by `from_version`) increments once per SA payload whose `<event version=…>` attribute was rewritten by the new auto-upgrade path from a legacy form to the canonical `2.0` envelope. The two label values are `v1` (no `version` attribute on the `<event>` tag) and `v2-pre-2.0` (`version="…"` value below 2.0); finer cardinality (e.g. per-`1.x`-minor) was rejected because most pre-2.0 senders in the wild are `1.0` and label inflation would complicate dashboards without adding operational signal. The labelled counter lets fleet-upgrade-progress dashboards plot the share of senders still emitting legacy formats — a healthy roll-out trends both curves toward zero as legacy clients rotate to current ones. Both counters are wired via the existing `OnceLock` + `init()` + accessor + callback pattern from #1183 mavlink_heartbeat: the router exposes a new `OnMulticastOversizeDropped = Arc<dyn Fn() + Send + Sync>` callback installed via `Router::set_on_multicast_oversize_dropped`, and `rustgate_cot::MessageBuilder` exposes a new `OnSaAutoUpgraded = Arc<dyn Fn(&str) + Send + Sync>` callback installed via `MessageBuilder::with_on_sa_upgraded`. Server startup wires both under `#[cfg(feature = "metrics")]` so builds without the `metrics` feature see no behaviour change beyond the existing tracing-only path. The SA auto-upgrade itself is a byte-level rewrite (no second XML parse on the routing hot path) — the function `auto_upgrade_sa_version` scans the first 4 KiB for `<event` and splices over the existing `version="…"` value (or inserts one when absent), preserving original whitespace, attribute order, and namespace prefixes so downstream dedup/cache layers that key on byte identity stay consistent. The classification surface (`classify_legacy_sa_version`) is exposed for callers that want to observe without rewriting (e.g. SIEM correlation). All three transports that build a `MessageBuilder` — TLS sessions (`rustgate-server/src/session.rs`), WebSocket (`rustgate-websocket/src/server.rs` via a new `WsServerConfig.sa_upgrade_observer` field), and UDP (`rustgate-transport/src/udp.rs` via a new `UdpInputConfig::with_sa_upgrade_observer`) — funnel into the same `rustgate_sa_auto_upgraded_total` family, so the counter aggregates upgrades across every listener. Tests cover the registration surface (gather pattern asserting `MetricType::COUNTER` and the `from_version` label arity), label isolation (incrementing one label MUST NOT bleed into the other), router callback invocation on oversize multicast, and end-to-end `MessageBuilder` callback firing with the correct `from_version` label.

- **MSRV verification CI job (closes #783)** — adds a new `msrv` job to `.github/workflows/ci.yml` that pins the exact Minimum Supported Rust Version declared by `[workspace.package].rust-version = "1.94"` in the root `Cargo.toml` and runs `cargo check --locked --workspace --features nats,enrollment,est,proto,full-detail,metrics,federation,federation-ha,websocket,mqtt,otel,http` against that toolchain. Until this job landed, nothing in CI actually verified the published MSRV claim — every other job pins `1.94` exactly today, but that is brittle: a future bump of the workspace toolchain pin in `rust-toolchain.toml` to a newer compiler would silently mask MSRV regressions in the rest of CI, and a PR that introduced a feature, syntax form, or stdlib API requiring a newer toolchain would compile fine on the workspace toolchain while silently breaking the MSRV contract that downstream `rustgate-client` consumers and Linux distribution packagers rely on. The new job runs on every PR (`pull_request`) and `push` to `main`, gates on the same `lint, clippy` prerequisites as `check-features` so the toolchain install is not wasted on PRs with formatting or clippy issues, and uses the same shared-volume sccache + Swatinem/rust-cache fallback the rest of the workflow uses for cache-warm runs (typical wall time ~2-3 minutes on a warm cache, ~6-8 minutes cold). **Compilation only — no tests, no clippy.** Tests would ~3x the wall time without buying any additional MSRV coverage (test failures are caught by the existing `test` job on the workspace toolchain); clippy lints evolve between releases so a new clippy warning shipped in 1.94 vs 1.95 would be a false MSRV positive. The feature set is intentionally identical to the `clippy`, `check-features`, and `test` jobs so MSRV coverage matches what we actually ship — drift between the lists would create MSRV blind spots. A defensive `rustc --version | grep -F '1.94'` step fails the job loudly if `dtolnay/rust-toolchain` ever silently installs a different version (e.g. via a future action-side resolver change), so the gate cannot quietly stop verifying the MSRV.

### Changed

- **Property tests for obligation-dispatcher composition invariants + store-forward drain obligation reapply (closes #787)** — pre-this-PR the obligation actuator in `crates/rustgate-transport/src/obligations.rs` carried an `apply_obligations` docstring claim that "`MaskPayload over MaskPoint = empty body; either order works`" and a comment on the stable-sort step that "two permutations of the same obligation set produce byte-identical post-PEP output regardless of which code path or which engine emission sequence assembled the list" — both load-bearing for the per-recipient fan-out, the egress-bridge re-application, and the store-forward drain — but the existing per-variant unit tests covered only hand-picked pairs. A regression that broke composition equivalence (e.g. a future variant whose actuator was non-idempotent, or a non-stable sort substitution) would slip past the unit suite. **F-22 — proptest invariants.** New `crates/rustgate-transport/tests/proptest_obligation_idempotence.rs` pins four properties via `proptest`: (1) `applying_a_then_b_equals_applying_a_union_b` — applying two arbitrary obligation sets in sequence produces the same post-PEP payload AND `message_type` as applying their union in one shot, the canonical "stack Send-then-Receive obligations on a per-recipient copy" gate the router fan-out and the drain path both rely on; (2) `double_application_is_idempotent` — the same obligation set applied twice does not drift the payload, the gate that lets a transient delivery retry re-run obligation actuation without corrupting the stored copy; (3) `order_independence_for_known_obligations` — pairwise permutation of two obligations produces byte-identical output, the regression guard for the `Obligation::chain_sort_key` stable-sort discipline; (4) `permutation_independence_for_obligation_sets` — rotation of a length-up-to-4 obligation list produces identical output, covering the multi-element permutation cases the pairwise property cannot reach. The proptest's payload corpus exercises both arms of the `MaskPoint` dispatch fan-out — well-formed CoT with `<point>`, well-formed CoT without `<point>`, a binary frame for the non-XML pass-through path, and an empty payload for the post-`MaskPayload` terminal state — so a regression in either branch of the actuator surfaces here. The four known `Obligation` variants (`MaskPoint`, `MaskPayload`, `TagClassified`, `AuditExtended`) are covered; the enum is `#[non_exhaustive]` so a future variant landing in the authz crate without a corresponding strategy arm here simply does not get generated, leaving the same-property check valid post-upgrade. The unknown-variant audit-rate-limit contract is its own separate concern pinned by `obligation_static_reason_audit.rs` and is intentionally out of scope. **F-24 — drain obligation reapply.** Audit of the pre-PR drain test surface (`store_forward_authz.rs` plus the `filter_offline_messages` unit suite in `router.rs`) covered "policy unchanged → message passes" and "ACL/authz tightened to deny → message dropped", but not "policy was *augmented* with a new obligation while the recipient was offline → drained message must acquire the new obligation at delivery time". Without that path covered, a regression that bypassed the obligation re-application step on the drain (without affecting the allow/deny verdict) would silently leak stored payloads in their pre-tightening form to recipients whose live-stream form is now masked — invisible to the existing tightened-to-deny coverage. New `crates/rustgate-transport/tests/store_forward_obligation_after_offline.rs` adds two scenarios: `stored_message_acquires_receive_obligation_added_while_offline` routes a CoT position with raw coordinates to an offline recipient under an allow-all-no-obligations policy, swaps to a policy that attaches `MaskPoint` on `Receive` while the recipient is still offline, drains, asserts the raw drain still carries the pre-PEP payload (storage preserves the original bytes — the masking is produced by the drain-time PEP re-evaluation, not by any storage-time compute), filters via `filter_offline_messages`, and asserts the delivered envelope has `lat="0.0"`/`lon="0.0"`/`hae="0.0"` with no `38.8977` or `-77.0365` substring leak; `stored_message_acquires_mask_payload_obligation_added_while_offline` is the companion case for `MaskPayload` so the redactor pair (`MaskPoint`, `MaskPayload`) — the load-bearing leak-prevention surface — is pinned uniformly. Both fixtures use an in-memory `redb` queue under a `TempDir`, the workspace's `NativeEngine` for the allow-all baseline, and a custom `PolicyEngine` impl for the post-tightening state so the test does not require a Cedar policy file. Test-binary count delta on the `rustgate-transport` crate: +2 binaries, +6 tests (4 proptests + 2 drain scenarios). No production-code change — the dispatcher, drain path, and store-forward queue are all exercised through their existing public surfaces.
- **DashMap for the per-CN replay-bucket map; criterion contention bench added (closes #836)** — closes the issue's "evaluate first, swap if it wins" decision by adding `crates/rustgate-transport/benches/dedup_contention.rs` and using its data to make a single, scoped data-structure swap. **(1) The bench.** The pre-#836 criterion harness in `router_fanout.rs` exercises single-threaded routing latency only; it never touched the cross-thread contention pattern the issue called out ("Under 10k+ msg/s on 16-core production host, single mutex contends across all workers"). The new bench drives N concurrent workers (4, 8, 16) through a dedup-cache-shaped `lookup_or_insert` workload — a 50k-entry pre-populated map, half live-hits / half fresh inserts, raw `u64` keys so the measurement isolates *map* contention from SHA-256 / LRU-reposition cost — against two map shapes: `parking_lot::Mutex<HashMap<u64, Instant>>` (the workspace's existing convention) and `dashmap::DashMap<u64, Instant>` (sharded internal RwLocks). On the Apple M3 Max dev host (14 physical cores, 36 GiB), the 30-sample / 5-second-measurement run shows DashMap holds steady at 16–25 Melem/s across all worker counts while the parking_lot shape stalls between 7–8 Melem/s, with the parking_lot throughput visibly capped by the single global critical section: 4 workers at 7.0 Melem/s, 8 workers at 7.1 Melem/s, 16 workers at 8.4 Melem/s — no scaling from 4→8 cores. DashMap's deltas at 4 / 8 / 16 workers are +199% / +255% / +89% respectively (every point is well over the 15% threshold the issue gave for swapping). **(2) The swap is scoped to one map.** `Router.replay_buckets`, the per-CN `Mutex<HashMap<Arc<str>, Arc<TokenBucket>>>` consulted by `Router::replay_positions`, is the only contended map in the workspace whose data shape supports a clean DashMap drop-in: it is purely keyed by CN with no cross-key state (no LRU, no FIFO, no map-wide sweep) that would require a global lock to coordinate. The field becomes `DashMap<Arc<str>, Arc<TokenBucket>>`; `replay_bucket_for` now uses `DashMap::entry().or_insert_with(...)` so the lookup-then-insert runs under a single shard lock; `drop_replay_bucket` and the test-only `replay_bucket_map_len` collapse to direct DashMap calls. The 700 transport tests pass unchanged — including the prune-on-disconnect regression test (`replay_bucket_map_len` after `unregister`) that was the original reason this map exists (#724). **(3) Why the other candidates were NOT swapped.** `DedupCache.inner` (`Mutex<LruCache<Key, Instant>>`) has LRU semantics — `LruCache::get` mutates the entry's position, so DashMap's read-mostly sharded RwLock model is not a drop-in; a hypothetical swap would require giving up LRU eviction in favour of TTL-only or capacity-randomized eviction, which is a correctness-level refactor beyond #836's scope. `PositionCache.entries` (`tokio::sync::RwLock<HashMap<Arc<str>, RoutableMessage>>`) does O(N) iteration on capacity-driven eviction (find oldest by `received_at`) and broad-snapshot iteration in `get_all` — DashMap iteration is shard-by-shard and would not simplify either path. `DecisionCache.shards` is already a 16-way sharded `Mutex<{AHashMap, VecDeque}>` — the FIFO order queue is map-wide per shard and DashMap has no equivalent. `SlidingWindowLimiter.state` holds map-wide sweep bookkeeping (`last_sweep`) inside the same mutex — the sweep predicate cannot be split across DashMap shards without losing the "amortize cleanup under high churn" guarantee. `TenantQuotaTracker.counters` already uses `parking_lot::RwLock` with a read-only fast path on existing tenants and atomic counters on the hot path — tenants are bounded in cardinality (small N), so the contention surface is minimal. **(4) Operationally additive.** The wire format, audit log, metric labels, and external API surface are byte-identical to the pre-PR behaviour. The `replay_buckets` map is internal — no caller outside the router observes its shape. `dashmap = "6"` is added to `[workspace.dependencies]` and to `rustgate-transport`'s production deps; the bench-only consumer in `dedup_contention.rs` shares the workspace declaration so future swaps elsewhere reuse the same dependency line. The bench is registered as a third `[[bench]]` entry alongside `codec` and `router_fanout` and runs locally for tuning only — it is not gated in CI by an absolute-threshold guard because criterion's per-run noise floor on shared CI runners is too high to support a meaningful threshold without false positives, matching the discipline already documented for `router_fanout.rs`.

- **Per-crate READMEs across the workspace (refs #816, F-139 only — partial close)** — adds a contributor-facing `README.md` to every crate under `crates/` that previously did not have one, leaving the existing `rustgate-client` README untouched. Each new README follows a fixed six-section shape: a one-line title and purpose, a "Role in the workspace" paragraph that names which other crates depend on it and why it exists separately (with cross-links to the relevant sibling READMEs), a "Public API surface" bullet list of the most-important re-exported types / traits / functions taken from the crate's `lib.rs` re-export block, a feature-flags table sourced from the crate's `Cargo.toml` `[features]` section, an optional topology / deployment notes section for crates with non-obvious deployment shape (TLS listener position, federation peering, NATS broker requirement, CA-key handling, FIPS compatibility), and a "Where to look first" pointer at the one or two source files a new contributor should open to understand the crate. Pure documentation: no code, `Cargo.toml`, or wire-format effect. The workspace `README.md`'s architecture / crate-table now turns each crate name into a link to the per-crate file so the entry point from the repo landing page resolves to a concrete contributor doc rather than a bare identifier. The remaining sub-items of #816 — F-140 (ADR collection) and F-158 (CODEOWNERS path-specific rules) — ship in separate follow-up PRs that keep #816 open. F-141 (CONTRIBUTING checklist) already shipped in #1243.
- **CONTRIBUTING.md gains a step-by-step "Contributing a new feature" checklist (refs #816, F-141 only — partial close)** — extends `CONTRIBUTING.md` with an end-to-end checklist that walks a new contributor through the workflow visible across recently merged PRs: file a GitHub issue first (with explicit out-of-scope items, matching the multi-sub-item discipline of #803, #816, #882, #909); pick a branch name from the allowed prefixes (`feat/`, `fix/`, `docs/`, `ci/`, `refactor/`, `perf/`, `test/`, `chore/`) of the form `<type>/<issue-number>-<short-slug>`; write a Conventional-Commits-shaped message with a `Closes #N` or `Refs #N` trailer (the latter for sub-items of an umbrella issue); append a multi-paragraph CHANGELOG entry under `[Unreleased]` in the appropriate section (`Added`, `Changed`, `Fixed`, `Removed`, `Security`); run the local quality gates (`cargo +nightly fmt --all`; the workspace clippy command pinned to the eleven shipped features; `cargo test -p <crate>`; the `--test-threads=1` workspace pass for any change that touches global Prometheus state; `cargo deny check`); honour the F-156 `// justification:` rule on every production `#[allow(...)]`; open the PR with the matching title and a body that cross-links the relevant discipline docs (`SECURITY.md` for threat model, `docs/authorization.md` for authz boundaries, `docs/concurrency-model.md` for shared state, `docs/runbooks/audit-chain-corruption.md` for hash-chained audit log, and the gitignored `.claude/rules/shared-infrastructure.md` for workspace primitives); and merge under the repo's squash-only policy. Also pins the gotcha that "security" is not one of commit-lint's allowed Conventional Commits types — security-flavoured branches use `fix/` or `feat/` with the security framing in the PR title and body. The remaining sub-items of #816 — F-139 per-crate READMEs, F-140 ADR collection, F-158 CODEOWNERS — are scheduled as separate follow-up PRs that keep #816 open. Pure documentation change; no code, config, or wire-format effect.
- **Standardize config validation under `rustgate-core::config::validate` (refs #815, F-136 only — partial close)** — pre-this-PR the workspace had drifted on config-validation discipline: some operator-facing config structs carried `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` and others did not, and range / non-empty / file-existence checks were inlined per-field with subtle wording differences (`"must be at least 1"` here, `"must be > 0"` there, `if s.is_empty()` here vs `if s.trim().is_empty()` there). The drift made the workspace-wide validation discipline harder to audit and the operator-facing error messages inconsistent. **(1) New shared validators in `rustgate-core::config::validate`.** Four reusable, no-allocation validators — `validate_port(value, field_name)` (rejects port `0`, `u16` already enforces the upper bound), `validate_duration_secs_in_range(value, min, max, field_name)` (inclusive range, `min == max` permitted), `validate_path_exists(path, field_name)` (existence check, layered on top of permission/contents checks), `validate_non_empty(value, field_name)` (rejects empty *and* whitespace-only — guards against the env-var-rendered-as-spaces footgun). Each returns `Result<(), ConfigValidateError>` with one variant per kind so callers can pattern-match on failures, and each carries the caller-supplied field name verbatim so the operator-facing error points at the offending CLI flag, TOML key, or env var. **(2) `deny_unknown_fields` discipline applied to remaining operator-facing config structs.** Three structs that were missing the attribute now carry it: `rustgate_transport::quota::QuotaConfig` and `rustgate_transport::quota::TenantQuota` (per-tenant connection / byte limits loaded from JSON; without the attribute, a typo'd `"max_connectons"` was silently ignored, leaving the tenant unlimited — a security-relevant default), and `rustgate_enrollment::handlers::revoke::RevokeRequest` (the `POST /api/revoke` JSON body; without the attribute, a typo'd `"sereal"` would surface as the less actionable "missing serial" error instead of pointing at the actual mistake). **(3) `rustgate-server`'s `validate(&self)` migrates to the shared validators** for `--cert` / `--key` / `--ca` non-empty checks and TLS file-existence checks. The operator-facing message text is preserved verbatim ("`TLS cert file not found: <path>`", "`--cert (or [cert] in the config file) is required`") so existing operator runbooks and the regression tests that grep on those substrings (`validate_rejects_missing_cert_file`, `validate_rejects_missing_key_file`, `validate_rejects_missing_ca_file`) still pass — the shared validators run as yes/no probes inside the existing `anyhow::bail!` arms. **Backward compatibility:** every previously-valid TOML, JSON, and env-var configuration continues to parse and validate. The added strictness — `deny_unknown_fields` on three more structs — only surfaces existing typos that were already silently misconfiguring deployments. **Net test delta:** +17 inline tests in the new `rustgate_core::config::validate::tests` module pinning each validator's happy + sad paths and error-message shape, +5 doctests covering the public API examples, +1 inline test in `rustgate_transport::quota::tests` (`quota_config_rejects_unknown_top_level_field`, `tenant_quota_rejects_unknown_nested_field`), +1 inline test in `rustgate_enrollment::handlers::revoke::tests` (`revoke_request_rejects_unknown_field`), and +1 inline test in `rustgate_server::cli::tests` (`config_file_rejects_unknown_toml_key`) pinning that the existing `ConfigFile` macro continues to honour the discipline. The remaining #815 sub-items (F-137 JSON Schema export, F-138 config migration story) are separate follow-up PRs.
- **`Arc<str>` for CN/group on the router fan-out hot path (closes #784)** — the router's per-recipient envelope construction formerly cloned `Identity.cn: String` and `Destination::Group(String)` once per subscriber. For a 1000-subscriber group broadcast that was 1000 heap allocations per message just to copy the sender's CN bytes into each recipient's envelope. `Identity.cn` and `Destination::Group` / `Destination::Multicast` are now `Arc<str>`: per-recipient cloning is a refcount bump on a single underlying allocation rather than a fresh `String` heap copy. The wire format and external rendering are unchanged — `Arc<str>` formats identically to `String` via `Display`, derefs to `&str` for every consumer that previously took a borrow, and serializes identically across the audit log, NATS publisher, federation V2 protobuf bridge, and HTTP egress JSON envelope. Internal `HashMap<String, _>` indices keyed by CN (sessions, groups, cn-group-count, replay-buckets, position cache) were converted to `HashMap<Arc<str>, _>` so the same allocation flows from the sender's `Identity.cn` through the router's session / group / bucket maps without re-allocation; lookups by `&str` continue to work via `Arc<str>: Borrow<str>`. The criterion `router_fanout` benchmark from #1219 validates the architectural shift on the local development host (per-run noise on shared CI runners is too high for an absolute-threshold guard, but the per-recipient envelope path is now bounded by Arc-refcount work rather than `String` deep-copies). **Tracing guards on the per-recipient `debug!` sites** in `send_to_group`, `send_to_all`, and `send_to_group_excluding` now check `tracing::enabled!(tracing::Level::DEBUG)` before computing the `hash_cn(&handle.identity.cn)` field for the obligation-actuation-failure log line, so a 1000-subscriber broadcast with debug-level disabled pays zero hash work for those drop-path log lines. **Two new tests pin the contract**: `identity_cn_arc_str_clone_is_refcount_bump` in `rustgate-core::identity` asserts `Arc::ptr_eq` and `Arc::strong_count` increment on `Identity::clone` so a regression that switched `cn` back to `String` (or wrapped it in something that deep-copies on clone) trips here rather than at a perf-regression dashboard far downstream; `router_fanout_does_not_allocate_per_recipient_cn` in `rustgate-transport::router` registers 50 subscribers in a single group, routes one message, and asserts the sender's `cn` Arc strong-count stayed under `baseline + N` — a per-recipient `String` clone regression would push the count to `baseline + N` and fail the test. Operationally invisible: the audit log, access log, metric labels, NATS subjects, MQTT topics, federation FederatedEvent groups, and HTTP egress destination strings are byte-identical to the pre-PR behaviour. Pre-existing 689 inline transport tests, 500 core tests, and the integration test suites for authz routing, multicast egress, store-forward, position replay, websocket, MQTT, NATS bridge, federation, and HTTP egress all pass unchanged.
- **Documentation: reqwest HTTP client usage audit (refs #803, F-93 only — partial close)** — adds `docs/reqwest-usage.md`, a per-site decision matrix that documents every production use of `reqwest` across the workspace and explains why a leaner alternative was rejected at each one. Pre-this-PR, contributors reaching for an outbound HTTP client had no in-tree guidance on whether to extend `reqwest` (already used by `rustgate-http::publisher` and the optional `peer-discovery-consul` Consul backend in `rustgate-federation`) or open a new HTTP-client surface — leaving open the failure mode where a future PR adds a third async HTTP client (`surf`, `isahc`, `awc`) or pulls `reqwest` into a crate without justifying the dep cost. The new doc enumerates the workspace's `reqwest = { version = "0.12", default-features = false, features = ["json", "rustls-tls", "http2"] }` declaration with a per-feature rationale (rustls-only TLS posture, ALPN h2 multiplexing on long-lived publisher connections, JSON serialization integration with the rest of the workspace's `serde_json` use), a per-site table covering the `rustgate-http` egress publisher (custom `dns_resolver()` for SSRF-safe resolution, `use_preconfigured_tls()` for SHA-256 cert pinning, mTLS client identity, redirect policy, per-target timeouts) and the `rustgate-federation::discovery::consul` backend (one-shot async GET against the Consul catalog API, gated behind `peer-discovery-consul`), an explicit "what does NOT use reqwest" carve-out (etcd uses `etcd-client` gRPC, DNS-SD uses `mdns-sd` multicast DNS, federation V2 uses `tonic`, JWKS module is server-side only), a decision tree for new outbound HTTP work, and migration notes for a hypothetical hyper-direct future. The doc explicitly does NOT migrate any site off reqwest in this PR — the audit's deliverable is the per-site decision rationale and the contribution gate that no third async HTTP client may be introduced without prior discussion. F-91 (X.509 stack scoping) shipped via #1229; F-92 (replace `anyhow` in libs) shipped via #1210; F-94 (peer-discovery dep isolation) remains in #803 for a separate follow-up PR.
- **Eliminate `Bytes -> Vec<u8>` copies on the message path (closes #786)** — audited the message path (router fan-out, federation forward, HTTP egress, NATS publish, MQTT publish, WebSocket egress) for the `Bytes -> Vec<u8>` round-trips that allocate a fresh heap buffer plus `memcpy` the payload on every conversion. Three call sites converted to stay on `Bytes` end-to-end: (1) `rustgate_http::payload::serialize` now returns `(Bytes, &'static str)` rather than `(Vec<u8>, &'static str)`; the `RawXml` branch returns `msg.payload.clone()` (refcount bump, zero-copy) where it previously did `msg.payload.to_vec()` then immediately wrapped the result in `Bytes::from(...)` at the publisher hot loop. The `Json` and `Protobuf` branches still allocate fresh buffers (the underlying serializers — `serde_json::to_vec`, `prost::Message::encode_to_vec` — return `Vec<u8>`) but wrap into `Bytes` once at the boundary so retries and auth signing share a single allocation. The publisher hot loop and DLQ replay path were updated to consume the `Bytes` result directly, dropping the `let body = bytes::Bytes::from(body_vec);` round-trip wrapper. (2) `rustgate_websocket::server` outbound write loop replaced `Message::Binary(encoded.to_vec().into())` with `Message::Binary(encoded)` — tungstenite 0.29's `Message::Binary` carries `Bytes`, so the previous `Bytes -> Vec -> Bytes` round trip allocated and copied the encoded payload on every WebSocket frame written to every subscribed client. (3) `rustgate_federation::v2::convert::add_flow_tag` now takes `&Bytes` and returns `Bytes` rather than `&[u8] -> Vec<u8>`; the no-op fast paths (input is not valid UTF-8, or contains neither `</detail>` nor `</event>` marker) now return `data.clone()` (refcount bump) instead of `data.to_vec()`, so the common case of a federated payload that doesn't need flow-tag injection no longer allocates. The marker-found paths still build a fresh `String` via `with_capacity` and convert to `Bytes` once at the return; this is the unavoidable allocation since we are inserting bytes into the middle of the payload. The `manager::forward_inner` call site was simplified to drop the matching `Bytes::from(tagged)` wrapper. **A new `docs/bytes-discipline.md` documents the workspace's preference for `Bytes` end-to-end on the message path** with an anti-pattern grep table, the `Vec<u8>` allowed-zone (serialization boundaries, crypto APIs), and a "when in doubt, change the signature" rule for moving callers from `&[u8] -> Vec<u8>` to `&Bytes -> Bytes`. Operationally invisible: the wire format, content-type strings, and external API surface are byte-identical to the pre-PR behaviour because the conversions removed are transparent — `Bytes::from(vec).as_ref() == vec.as_slice()` holds by construction, and tungstenite's `Message::Binary(Bytes)` and `Message::Binary(Vec<u8>.into())` produce the same on-the-wire frame. The criterion `router_fanout` benchmark from #1219 was used to validate the perf delta on the local development host (the bench is intentionally not gated in CI by an absolute-threshold guard — criterion's per-run noise floor on shared CI runners is too high to support a sub-microsecond latency budget without false positives). Net test delta: existing `rustgate_http::payload::tests` raw-XML passthrough tests were updated to assert via `body.as_ref()` against the source bytes (the `Bytes` type does not impl `PartialEq<[u8; N]>` directly); existing `rustgate_federation::v2::convert::cot_to_event::tests` flow-tag tests were updated to construct `Bytes::from_static(...)` inputs and assert via `std::str::from_utf8(&result)` rather than `String::from_utf8(result)`. The dedup-after-flow-tag tests in `rustgate_federation::dedup::tests` were updated identically. No production-test coverage was lost — the assertions still pin the same byte-for-byte properties.
- **Split `Router::authz_evaluate` into direction-anchored Send / Receive variants (closes #730)** — the router's PEP-evaluation helper formerly took a runtime `AuthzAction` parameter and dispatched to either the Send or Receive PEP based on the supplied value. A refactor that dropped or relabelled an `Action` enum variant could silently route a sender-side decision through the Receive PEP path, or vice-versa, with no compile-time guard — the type system permitted the bug. This PR splits the helper into two private direction-anchored entry points: `authz_evaluate_send(engine, subject, resource)` for sender-side checks and `authz_evaluate_receive(engine, subject, resource)` for per-recipient delivery checks. Neither takes an `AuthzAction`; the direction is implicit in the function name and verified at the call site by the type system. Both delegate into a shared `authz_evaluate_inner(...)` helper so the observer dispatch, `rustgate_pep_*_decisions_total{decision}` and `rustgate_pep_evaluation_seconds{direction}` metric emissions, and latency instrumentation introduced for #768 remain identical between directions — only the public/internal entry points fan out. The split aligns with the direction-specific `pep_send_decisions_total` / `pep_receive_decisions_total` counters added in #1231 (closes #768) and pins the same separation a layer deeper. **Twelve call sites updated:** the `route_inner` Send PEP for direct/group/broadcast (line ~2005), the multicast egress per-group Send pass (line ~2235), the offline-message filter Send and Receive checks (lines ~2417 / ~2428), the position-replay Send and Receive checks (lines ~2651 / ~2681), the direct unicast Receive PEP (line ~2871), the per-recipient group Receive PEP inside `send_to_group` (line ~3108), the broadcast Receive PEP (line ~3245), the multicast Send PEP per-group (line ~3398), and the per-recipient Receive PEP inside multicast fan-out (line ~3477). Each call site now selects its PEP by *function name* — a future refactor that retires or renames an `Action` variant cannot silently reroute a PEP because the call sites no longer reference the action enum. **Operationally additive**: the wire behaviour, audit emissions, observer events, and metric labels are byte-identical to the pre-PR behaviour because the split is structural, not semantic. Net test delta: **+3 integration tests** in the new `crates/rustgate-transport/tests/authz_evaluate_split.rs` binary (`authz_evaluate_send_path_only_emits_send_action`, `authz_evaluate_receive_path_only_emits_receive_action`, `direction_swap_is_observable_on_full_route`); the third test pins the *order* invariant — Send PEP runs before Receive PEP for the same routing pass — by snapshotting the Send-event count at the moment each Receive event lands, so a regression that swapped the two call sites would produce a `0`-snapshot witness and fail loudly. The pre-existing 522 inline router tests and the integration test suites for authz routing, multicast egress PEP, store-forward authz, position replay, and access logging all pass unchanged.
- **Document and pin the workspace's sanitization helper matrix (closes #801)** — four sanitization helpers across the workspace had drifted into divergent docstrings and untested edge cases: `rustgate_core::sanitize::sanitize_for_log` (replace control chars / CSI bodies with `U+FFFD`, preserve non-ASCII, no NFC), `rustgate_nats::publisher::sanitize_nats_token` (NFC then strip non-ASCII / control / whitespace / wildcards, replace `.` with `_`, cap at 256 bytes, `Option<Cow<str>>` return), `rustgate_federation::trust_store::sanitize_filename` (replace anything outside `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` with `_`, no NFC, no length cap, `String` return), and the MQTT topic validators in `rustgate_mqtt::topic::{validate_publish_topic, validate_subscribe_filter, validate_topic_prefix}` (reject malformed input rather than transform). Each helper had legitimate reasons to differ — different destinations, different threat models, different output-character constraints — but the divergences were not documented, so a future change to one helper carried risk of accidentally drifting away from the workspace's overall sanitization contract. This PR adds a complete **Sanitization Helper Matrix** to the `rustgate_core::sanitize` module docs covering destination, control-char handling (replace vs strip vs reject), non-ASCII handling (preserve vs strip vs reject), NFC normalization, length cap, return type, and trust model for every helper. Each helper's own docstring now cross-references the matrix, so a contributor working in `sanitize_nats_token` is one click away from the comparison with `sanitize_filename` and the explanation of why the rules differ. **Operationally additive**: zero changes to the output bytes of any helper, pinned by new `*_byte_stable_for_known_inputs` regression tests in each home crate that capture the exact pre-PR output for a corpus spanning every documented behavior class. The matrix-axis invariants are also pinned by tests — `sanitize_for_log` does not NFC-normalize, `sanitize_nats_token` does; `sanitize_for_log` preserves non-ASCII, `sanitize_nats_token` strips it; `sanitize_filename` uses `_` (not `U+FFFD`); MQTT validators reject (not transform) — so a future change that breaks the matrix's claims fails CI loudly. Net test delta: +10 tests (+3 in `rustgate-core::sanitize::tests`, +3 in `rustgate-nats::publisher::tests`, +2 in `rustgate-federation::trust_store::tests`, +2 in `rustgate-mqtt::topic::tests`). Decision recorded inline in the matrix: the helpers cannot be cleanly consolidated into a shared core because their replacement strategies (replace with `U+FFFD` vs strip vs replace with `_` vs reject) and their non-ASCII policies (preserve vs strip vs preserve-as-alphanumeric vs reject) are mutually incompatible — the matrix table IS the consolidation outcome, making the divergences explicit so they cannot drift silently.
- **Consolidate federation circuit breaker onto `rustgate-resilience::circuit::CircuitBreaker` (closes #795)** — completes the workspace-wide consolidation of the three-state circuit breaker primitive. Pre-this-PR `rustgate-federation::peer::PeerHandle` carried its own circuit-breaker state machine implemented on top of `AtomicU8` + `AtomicU32` + a `Mutex<Option<Instant>>` for the cooldown timer, parallel to `rustgate_resilience::circuit::CircuitBreaker` already used by `rustgate-http::publisher::TargetState`. Two parallel implementations meant operational fixes (the `with_on_state_change` callback used by the HTTP DLQ auto-drain hook in #881; the success-threshold floor that prevents flapping recovery; the half-open probe cap that prevents thundering-herd against a recovering target) had to be ported twice or risk diverging — and #1198 already cited the federation-circuit-breaker as the reference duplicate to migrate. This PR replaces the federation crate's per-handle state machine with a `CircuitBreaker` field; the public `CircuitState` enum, `circuit_state()` / `is_available()` / `record_success()` / `record_failure()` / `circuit_trip_count()` methods, and the JSON-stable `PeerStatus.circuit_state` serialization remain byte-identical so the federation REST API and management UI see no wire-format change. The lifetime trip counter is now driven by the shared breaker's `on_state_change` callback (`OnStateChange = Arc<dyn Fn(u8, u8) + Send + Sync>`) — every transition into `STATE_OPEN` (Closed → Open AND HalfOpen probe-fail → Open) increments `circuit_trips` exactly once, fixing a subtle pre-#795 race where a fast-cycling peer could double-count the same trip via the two separate `record_failure` arms. **Behavioural differences worth pinning down for operators:** (1) `circuit_state()` is now an observation-only read — it returns the current state without driving Open → HalfOpen transitions on its own. The transition is driven by the shared breaker's `allow_request()` admission gate (which `is_available()` calls before every send), matching the canonical resilience4j / Polly contract. The federation manager's send loop calls `is_available()` before every dispatch, so the live forwarding path is unchanged; only test code or status-snapshot readers that polled `circuit_state()` waiting for the lazy auto-transition need to call `is_available()` first to drive it. (2) The shared breaker exposes a `success_threshold` parameter (number of consecutive HalfOpen successes required to close); the federation handle pins this at 1 to preserve the pre-#795 contract where a single successful send after HalfOpen closed the circuit. Operators wanting hysteresis on flapping peers can change the constant in a follow-up PR — the migration is byte-faithful, the parameter is now reachable. (3) Probe limiting (`max_half_open_probes`) is pinned at 1 because federation drives one message per probe attempt; pre-#795 this was implicit in the single-write `consecutive_failures` reset, post-#795 it's an explicit constant on `PeerHandle`. The shared breaker's three-state machine (Closed → Open → HalfOpen), atomic hot path, and lock-free reads are preserved unchanged. **Audit completed for the rest of the workspace:** workspace-wide grep for `Circuit\|CircuitState\|HalfOpen\|breaker_state` in non-test source files confirms `rustgate-resilience::circuit::CircuitBreaker` is now the sole circuit-breaker implementation. `rustgate-http::publisher` has consumed the shared primitive since #881; no other crate carried a parallel implementation. The `rustgate-resilience::circuit::CircuitBreaker::state_value` accessor is no longer feature-gated behind `metrics` — downstream crates that translate the numeric state into a crate-local `CircuitState` enum (federation `PeerStatus`) need it unconditionally, and the previous gate would have required mirroring `#[cfg(feature = "metrics")]` on every caller. Net test delta: **+1 test** (`peer_handle_uses_shared_resilience_circuit_breaker` pins the public-API contract by constructing a `rustgate_resilience::circuit::CircuitBreaker` directly through the federation crate's import surface — a future refactor that re-introduces a local `AtomicU8` reimplementation would no longer compile). The pre-existing 23 `peer::tests::circuit_*` tests are preserved unchanged (with two tests updated to call `is_available()` rather than relying on `circuit_state()`'s previously-mutating read, matching the new observation-only contract). The `with_circuit_breaker_custom_params` test now validates the threshold wiring behaviourally rather than poking at private fields that no longer exist.
- **Consolidate Prometheus fallback constructors into `rustgate-core::metrics_util` (closes #794)** — collapses six previously-duplicated helpers (`fallback_counter`, `fallback_gauge`, `fallback_counter_vec`, `fallback_gauge_vec`, `fallback_histogram`, `fallback_histogram_vec`) that lived in three separate crates (`rustgate-server::metrics`, `rustgate-federation::metrics`, `rustgate-http::metrics`) into a single shared module behind the new `metrics` feature on `rustgate-core`. The bodies were identical apart from return type and had drifted in subtle ways — federation referred to `prometheus::IntGaugeVec` via the fully-qualified path while http used a direct import; the server crate kept `fallback_histogram` ~900 lines downstream of the other helpers. The new shared module pins the `OnceLock` + `init()` + accessor pattern documented in `rules/shared-infrastructure.md` so every future crate that exposes Prometheus metrics has one place to import from, with no opportunity for new drift. **Operationally additive only**: the fallback metrics remain unregistered (per-callsite `OnceLock::get_or_init` discipline), so the wire format and `/metrics` exposition are byte-for-byte unchanged across the three migrated crates. The shared helpers use `expect()` with a programmer-error message in place of the previous `std::process::abort()` path, which gives panic-reporting infrastructure a usable diagnostic instead of a silent SIGABRT — the panic remains unreachable in practice because the matching `init()` call site has already validated the same name and label arity at startup, so failure here would mean prometheus is broken rather than the wrapper. Each downstream crate's existing `metrics` feature now activates `rustgate-core/metrics`; existing fallback-helper tests in `rustgate-server::metrics::tests` and `rustgate-http::metrics::tests` continue to exercise the migrated helpers via the shared imports, and a new test module in `rustgate_core::metrics_util` (six tests) pins the contract on the consolidated implementation.

- **Split CI audit into required-vs-soft jobs and unify the ignore list with `deny.toml` (closes #776)** — the previous `audit` CI job ran `cargo deny check` (advisories + licenses + bans + sources, all blocking) followed by `cargo audit` with a hardcoded `--ignore RUSTSEC-2025-0134 --ignore RUSTSEC-2026-0049` list that was NOT mirrored in `deny.toml`. Two failure modes followed: (a) every advisory category — including `unmaintained` informational warnings on transitive deps — was equally merge-blocking, so a new "unmaintained" advisory on a build-only proc-macro could block PR merges identically to a real high-severity CVE; (b) the `cargo audit` ignore list and the `deny.toml` `[advisories].ignore` list could (and did) drift apart, leaving operators with two sources of truth that disagreed about which advisories were knowingly accepted. This PR splits the audit gate into two jobs in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`: **`audit`** runs `cargo deny check` with the `unmaintained`, `yanked`, and `notice` lints demoted to warnings via `--warn` flags, so only the `vulnerability` and `unsound` lint categories — plus the static `licenses` / `bans` / `sources` policies — block merge. The chosen severity threshold for the required gate is **`high`**, matching the `vulnerability` + `unsound` lint categories that carry a CVSS-style severity rating in the RustSec advisory database. **`audit-soft`** runs `cargo audit` with `continue-on-error: true` at the job level and a `|| true` belt-and-braces in the step body, emitting `::warning::` annotations on any unmaintained / yanked / informational findings without ever blocking merge. Both jobs derive their per-advisory exemptions from the SAME source — the `[advisories].ignore` array in `deny.toml` — via a new `scripts/extract-audit-ignores.py` helper that reads the array and emits the equivalent `--ignore RUSTSEC-XXXX-YYYY` flags for `cargo audit`. The hardcoded `--ignore RUSTSEC-2025-0134 --ignore RUSTSEC-2026-0049` flags are removed from the workflow — those IDs were not present in `deny.toml` and were stale. The `[advisories].ignore` array in `deny.toml` is now the documented single source of truth: a header comment block at the top of the file walks contributors through the split-gate model, the severity threshold, and the rule that new ignores belong in that array (never in the workflow YAML). The extraction script is a small pure-stdlib Python helper — no PyPI deps, no `tomllib` requirement so it runs on the same Python that the existing `playbook-lint` job already uses. **Operationally additive**: the new soft job is strictly informational and the required job still gates on real vulnerabilities exactly as before; the only behavioural shift is that an upstream crate going into maintenance mode no longer creates a false-positive merge block. CI YAML changes only — no Rust code is touched.

- **Reconcile `RustgateError` unified-hierarchy docs with per-crate error reality (closes #804, refs IMPROVEMENT-ANALYSIS.md F-114)** — the workspace's contributor-facing error guidance previously described a single unified [`rustgate_core::error::RustgateError`] hierarchy that wrapped every fallible path across the workspace. In practice `RustgateError` is the boundary aggregator only for the `rustgate-core` / `rustgate-transport` / `rustgate-websocket` slice (via the `error::Result` alias), while every other library crate (`rustgate-http::HttpError`, `rustgate-mqtt::MqttError`, `rustgate-enrollment::EnrollmentError`, `rustgate-mavlink::MavlinkError`, `rustgate-stanag4586::Stanag4586Error`, `rustgate-asterix`'s per-category `Cat021Error` / `Cat048Error` / `Cat062Error`, `rustgate-cot::ParseError`, `rustgate-authz::AuthzError`, `rustgate-proto::ProtoError`, `rustgate-client::ClientError`) defines its own typed `thiserror` enum with no `From<*Error> for RustgateError` conversion path; `rustgate-federation` and `rustgate-nats` go further and split per-submodule (`JwtError`/`ReplayStoreError`, `NatsConfigError`/`NatsTlsConfigError`/`RequestError`) without a crate-level umbrella at all. Binary callers in `rustgate-server` propagate every error via `?` and surface them through `anyhow::Error` at the orchestration layer — `RustgateError` is intentionally not the single funnel the prior docs implied. This PR (issue #804 option (a) — accept the per-crate-errors reality) reconciles the documentation to the actual shape: adds a `# Error handling` `//!` module-level note to every library crate's `lib.rs` (`rustgate-core`, `rustgate-transport`, `rustgate-federation`, `rustgate-enrollment`, `rustgate-http`, `rustgate-mqtt`, `rustgate-websocket`, `rustgate-nats`, `rustgate-mavlink`, `rustgate-asterix`, `rustgate-stanag4586`, `rustgate-cot`, `rustgate-authz`, `rustgate-proto`, `rustgate-client`) pointing rustdoc readers at the per-crate error type and explicitly carving out that the type is **not** auto-converted into `RustgateError`. Library crates keep their typed enums so callers can match on specific failure modes (e.g. `EnrollmentError::Csr` vs `EnrollmentError::Signing` for runbook routing); the binary doesn't need that granularity and uses `anyhow` for display + exit. **Pure documentation change**: no public APIs, error variants, conversion paths, or wire formats are altered. No code changes beyond additive `//!` rustdoc comments. Verified via `cargo doc --no-deps --workspace` — every new intra-doc link resolves against the canonical re-exported error symbols.
- **Migrate manual `impl Display` blocks on error enums to `#[derive(thiserror::Error)]` (closes #726)** — aligns three workspace error types with the project's `thiserror`-derive style rule (CLAUDE.md, "Prefer `thiserror` for error types... Never manual `impl Display`"). Migrates `rustgate_cot::delta::DeltaError`, `rustgate_cot::mask::MaskError`, and `rustgate_federation::v2::convert::ConvertError` from hand-written `impl std::fmt::Display` + `impl std::error::Error` blocks to `#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]` with per-variant `#[error("...")]` attributes. The MaskError migration also threads `#[source]` on the `Xml` and `Io` variants so `anyhow::Error::source()` chains continue to surface the inner `quick_xml::Error` and `io::Error` to operators (the bespoke `impl Error::source()` arm is replaced by thiserror's derived equivalent). The pre-existing explicit `From` impls (`From<quick_xml::Error>`, `From<AttrError>`, `From<io::Error>` for `MaskError`; `From<rustgate_proto::ProtoError>` for `ConvertError`) are preserved as-is — `#[from]` only allows one variant per source type and the `AttrError → Xml(quick_xml::Error::from(e))` indirection is intentional, so the `From` bodies stay manual to keep that mapping intact. **Display output is byte-stable**: every migrated variant's `#[error("...")]` template was lifted character-for-character from the prior manual arm, and new tests in each migrated module pin the rendered string so a future refactor that breaks operator log-correlation tooling fails loudly here rather than silently in production grep pipelines. **One error type intentionally not migrated**: `rustgate_federation::jwt::JwtError` keeps its manual `impl Display` because the `UnknownKid(String)` variant renders two distinct messages depending on whether the inner kid is empty (no `kid` header at all) or non-empty — thiserror's `#[error("...")]` is one format string per variant with no template form that branches on field content, and emitting `"unknown kid: "` (trailing space) for the empty case would break byte stability. Splitting `UnknownKid` into separate `MissingKid` + `UnknownKid(String)` variants would let thiserror handle this cleanly but is a breaking change to the public error API and intentionally out of scope. The decision is now documented inline above the manual `impl Display` so the next contributor inherits the rationale, and the `jwt::tests::jwt_error_*` family pins all 14 JwtError variants' output (including both UnknownKid branches) against future drift. The `rustgate-cot` crate gains a `thiserror = { workspace = true }` dependency (was previously absent); `rustgate-federation` already depended on it. Net test delta: **+13 tests** (4 in `rustgate-cot::delta::tests` for `DeltaError`, 2 in `rustgate-cot::mask::tests` for the `Xml` / `Io` Display shapes — the existing `attr_budget_exceeded_display_embeds_limit_value_exactly` and `source_chain_behaves_as_documented_for_every_variant` already cover the third variant and source chain; 0 net for `ConvertError` — the existing 4 Display tests already pin every variant — but a clarifying header comment was added marking those as the byte-stable-pin tests; 7 in `rustgate-federation::jwt::tests` covering every variant including the conditional `UnknownKid` branching, supplementing the pre-existing 3-variant `jwt_error_display` test).
- **`rustgate-federation` migrates off `anyhow` to `thiserror`-typed errors (refs #803, partial — F-92 only)** — the workspace style rule says library crates use `thiserror::Error`-derived enums for typed errors and only the binary tier (`rustgate-server`) may use `anyhow` for top-level glue. The `rustgate-federation` crate was the lone holdout, returning `anyhow::Result<T>` from over a hundred function signatures across `discovery` (DNS-SD / Consul / etcd backends + reconciler), `connector` (mTLS handshake, dynamic peer connector), `manager` (lifecycle / hot-reload / HA adoption), `store` (file-backed + NATS-KV-backed federate persistence), `trust_store` (dynamic CA management), `v1::{client,server}` (length-prefixed XML over mTLS), `v2::client` (gRPC 5-stream handshake), and `ha::{claims,registry}` (NATS KV claim manager + connection registry). This PR introduces a new `crate::error::FederationError` enum with sixteen discriminated variants — `UnknownProtocol`, `InvalidPeerAddress`, `Io`, `Timeout`, `InvalidServerName`, `Tls`, `IdentityExtraction`, `Pem`, `X509`, `Lock`, `Discovery`, `PeerNotFound`, `Serde`, `Storage`, `AlreadyRunning`, `NotInitialized`, `HaClaimManagerMissing`, `V2TlsConfigMissing`, `NoOutboundPeerConfig`, `HaNatsConnect`, `Other` — together with `From<rustgate_core::error::RustgateError>` and `From<std::io::Error>` impls so existing `?` propagation through PEM helpers and filesystem operations still compiles unchanged. Every migrated function preserves its pre-PR Display rendering verbatim (`"federate not found: <id>"`, `"federation manager is already running"`, `"unknown federation protocol: <token>"`, `"invalid peer address '<addr>': <err>"`, `"TCP connect to <addr> timed out after <dur>"`, etc.) so existing operator log greps, runbooks, and the REST-API 404 surface in `crates/rustgate-federation/src/api/handlers.rs` (which formats `{e}` straight into the response body) keep working. The `anyhow` crate moves out of `[dependencies]` and stays out — the federation crate now depends on `thiserror` only — and the `anyhow::Context` / `anyhow!` / `bail!` call sites are gone from every source file in the crate. This is a **partial close of #803**: only sub-item F-92 (replace `anyhow` in library crates) is shipped here. The remaining three sub-items are scheduled as separate PRs that keep #803 open: F-91 (X.509 dep scoping documentation), F-93 (`reqwest` audit), and F-94 (`peer-discovery-*` feature isolation). **Net test delta: +8 new tests** pinning the typed-error contract — `protocol_parse_error_is_unknown_protocol_variant` and `protocol_parse_error_lowercases_input_in_variant_payload` (config), `discover_failure_returns_typed_discovery_variant` (discovery), `update_nonexistent_returns_peer_not_found_variant`, `set_enabled_nonexistent_returns_peer_not_found_variant`, and `set_routing_mode_nonexistent_returns_peer_not_found_variant` (store/file), and `connect_outbound_peer_without_start_returns_not_initialized_variant` and `add_peer_with_invalid_address_returns_invalid_peer_address_variant` (manager).
