The `error.rs` module itself adds a sibling test module that pins Display rendering, source-chain reachability, and the `Send + Sync + 'static` bound surface for every variant. The pre-existing 891-test federation suite (lib + integration) is preserved unchanged and continues to pass; only the few tests that previously asserted on the anyhow Display-string substring have implicit equivalents because the variant `to_string()` rendering is byte-for-byte identical at every migrated call site.
- **Unified HMAC-SHA256 helpers in `rustgate-core::crypto` (closes #799)** — collapses three inlined HMAC-SHA256 constructions across security-critical paths into a single `rustgate_core::crypto::{hmac_sha256_tag, hmac_sha256_verify, HmacError}` surface. The previous sites — `rustgate-transport::store_forward::compute_hmac` (durable client-queue integrity tag), `rustgate-http::auth::{compute_hmac_signature, verify_hmac_signature}` (webhook canonical-payload signing per F-47), and `rustgate-federation::jwt::{SigningKey::sign, VerificationKey::verify}` (HS256 JWT issue/validate) — had subtle divergences in error handling and constant-time-comparison wiring: store-forward used a manual `subtle::ConstantTimeEq::ct_eq` against the trailing tag, http compared the prefixed `sha256=<hex>` envelope via `ct_eq` after re-running the computation, and federation used `mac.verify_slice()` (which routes through `hmac::Output::ct_eq` internally). Concentrating the construction at one boundary means the timing-side-channel and key-length disciplines are now enforced uniformly via the shared helper rather than relying on per-caller correctness; verification always runs through `subtle::ConstantTimeEq::ct_eq` over the raw 32-byte tag. **Operationally additive**: the wire format, ABI, and HMAC byte output are unchanged at every call site — `compute_hmac` in store-forward, `compute_hmac_signature` in http (still returns `sha256=<hex>`), and `SigningKey::sign` in federation all produce byte-identical tags to the pre-migration code. New explicit regression tests pin this byte-for-byte equivalence in each migrated module so a future tweak to the helper cannot silently invalidate (a) any pre-migration on-disk client-queue entry — drain would otherwise reject every record as `TamperedMessage` and discard the backlog; (b) any in-flight signed webhook delivery — the receiver-side verifier would otherwise reject the new signature; or (c) any previously-issued JWT — federation peers would otherwise see a token-verification outage on rollout. The `hmac` and `subtle` workspace deps move out of `rustgate-transport` and `rustgate-federation` (`hmac` only) into `rustgate-core` and into per-crate `dev-dependencies` for the regression tests; `rustgate-http` keeps its `subtle` dep for the prefix-string `ct_eq` defense-in-depth check on the `sha256=` envelope, which protects the verifier against malformed presented signatures (right length, wrong prefix) without leaking the divergence point. **Net test delta: +14 tests** (12 in `rustgate_core::crypto::tests` covering the helper API surface — happy paths, RFC 4231 Test Case 1 vector, all `HmacError` variants, ct_eq source-text guard, determinism, and key/data divergence pins; 1 byte-for-byte regression test in `rustgate-transport::store_forward::tests`; 1 byte-for-byte regression test in `rustgate-http::auth::tests`; 1 byte-for-byte regression test in `rustgate-federation::jwt::tests`). The pre-existing 50+ HMAC-relevant tests across the three callers (cross-endpoint replay, tamper detection, RFC 4231 vector pin, JWT round-trip, etc.) are preserved unchanged and now exercise the helper through every migrated entry point.
- **Unified sliding-window rate limiter in `rustgate-resilience` (closes #798)** — collapses the two near-identical sliding-window rate limiters that previously lived in `rustgate-resilience::conn_rate_limiter::ConnRateLimiter` and `rustgate-enrollment::ratelimit::RateLimiter` into a single parameterized `SlidingWindowLimiter` under `rustgate_resilience::sliding_window`. The new helper preserves every behaviour the two callers relied on: lazy-prune-on-check (no separate sweeper task), the entries-since-last-sweep threshold + elapsed-window double-trigger sweep semantics, the per-key timestamp deque, the `>= max` rejection boundary (rejected calls do NOT append timestamps so an attacker cannot pin a key into permanent rejection), the optional IPv6 `/64` prefix collapsing carried over from the connection limiter, and the optional tracked-key cap with LRU-by-last-seen eviction. The mutex is now `parking_lot::Mutex`, which does not poison on panic — the previous `std::sync::Mutex`-with-`into_inner` (`ConnRateLimiter`) and fail-closed-on-poison (`enrollment::RateLimiter`) policies converge on uniform fail-open semantics under this lock. **Audit emission is now centralized inside the limiter**: every rejection fires `rustgate_core::audit::rate_limit_triggered(peer, category, max)` with `category` configured at construction time (`"connection"` for the MQTT/WebSocket/UDP listeners, `"request"` for the enrollment endpoint), so SIEM dashboards can distinguish enforcement cadences without losing the unified counter — a previously-implicit spread (only `enrollment::handlers::sign.rs` emitted; MQTT/WebSocket/UDP did not) is replaced by uniform coverage. **Migration:** `ConnRateLimiter` survives as a thin `#[deprecated]` shim in `rustgate-resilience::conn_rate_limiter` for one PR cycle so any external consumers compile without churn; every internal caller (MQTT listener, WebSocket listener, UDP transport, WebSocket security tests) is moved to construct `SlidingWindowLimiter::new(max, window, "connection").with_ipv6_64_collapse(true)` directly. The `rustgate-enrollment::ratelimit` module — including `RateLimiter`, `PoisonCallback`, `with_poison_callback`, and `EnrollmentServer::with_rate_limit_poison_callback` — is **deleted outright**: `parking_lot::Mutex` removes the poison failure mode the callback existed to surface, and `EnrollmentServer` now wraps a `SlidingWindowLimiter` directly with `category="request"`. The `rustgate_enrollment_rate_limit_poison_total` Prometheus counter remains registered for dashboard compatibility (now permanently zero) and the accessor is gated behind `#[allow(dead_code)]` with a justification comment pointing at this CHANGELOG entry. **Operationally additive**: every existing caller observes the same admit/reject decisions for the same inputs; the only behavioural shift is the new audit emission from the formerly-silent listener rejections, which is a strict information gain. Net test delta: +13 new tests in `rustgate-resilience::sliding_window::tests` covering the seven scenarios called out in #798 (allows-under-max, rejects-at-max, refills-after-window, audit-on-reject via tracing-subscriber capture, isolates-per-key, lazy-prune-keeps-map-bounded under a 1000-key flood, fail-open-on-mutex-poison via `parking_lot` reuse-after-panic) plus six behavioural-parity tests for the IPv6 `/64` collapse, the tracked-key cap, the rejected-calls-don't-record invariant, the `is_limited`/`try_check` inversion, and the `Debug` projection. The pre-existing `ConnRateLimiter` and `enrollment::RateLimiter` test suites are reduced to the boundary-pin set that exercises the deprecated shim API surface only.
- **`MAX_FEDERATION_HOPS` is now runtime-configurable for tactical topologies (closes #758)** — the V2 inbound federation hop limit was a compile-time constant (`MAX_FEDERATION_HOPS: i64 = 8` in `crates/rustgate-federation/src/v2/server.rs`) before this PR. Operators running multi-region meshes that intentionally route through more than eight hops, or star-shaped two-hub deployments that wanted a tighter loop-prevention bound, had no way to tune the limit short of a rebuild and redeploy. The limit is now a `u8` field on [`FederationService`] (range `1..=255`) configurable via the new [`FederationService::with_max_hops`] builder method, mirroring the existing `with_on_event` / `with_on_blob` / `with_on_rol_event` / `with_on_group_sync` / `with_allowed_peer_groups` builder shape. Also surfaces a new CLI flag `--federation-max-hops <N>` (env `RUSTGATE_FEDERATION_MAX_HOPS`, default 8) gated by `clap::value_parser!(u8).range(1..=255)` so operator typos like `--federation-max-hops 0` or `--federation-max-hops 1000` fail loudly at parse time rather than producing a misconfigured service. The TOML key `federation-max-hops` follows the kebab-case mirror so config-file deployments inherit the same defaults < file < env < CLI precedence chain. **Default-preserving migration:** the new default of `8` matches the historical hard-coded `MAX_FEDERATION_HOPS`, so deployments that do not opt into the knob see no behavior change. The constant `pub const MAX_FEDERATION_HOPS: u8 = 8` remains exported for tests and external callers — it is now documented as the *default-only fallback*, with the active limit living on the per-instance `FederationService::max_hops`. The four hop-validation helpers (`validate_hop_count`, `validate_blob_hop_count`, `validate_rol_hop_count`, `validate_group_sync_hop_count`) and their two observation-stub wrappers (`observe_inbound_rol_event`, `observe_inbound_group_sync`) now read the per-instance limit; spawned drain tasks capture `self.max_hops` by value (u8 is Copy) before `tokio::spawn` so they do not need a `&self` reference. The CLI value widens to `FederationConfig.max_hops: u32` for the V1 outbound metadata path that already consumes the same field, and narrows back to `u8` inside `FederationManager::start` when constructing the V2 service — single source of truth, two consumers. **Removes the only TODO in the workspace** (`federation/v2/server.rs:29`). New test coverage: 5 tests in `crates/rustgate-federation/src/v2/server.rs::tests` (`with_max_hops_overrides_default`, `with_max_hops_default_is_eight`, `hop_validation_uses_configured_max`, `hop_validation_at_boundary`, `with_max_hops_zero_rejected` — the last splits across `cfg(debug_assertions)` so debug builds catch the panic and release builds catch the saturation-to-1 fallback that prevents production federation tear-down on a misconfig) plus 4 tests in `crates/rustgate-server/src/cli.rs::tests` (`cli_federation_max_hops_default_eight`, `cli_federation_max_hops_override`, `cli_federation_max_hops_rejects_zero`, `cli_federation_max_hops_rejects_above_255`). Net test delta: +9 tests.
- **WebSocket rate limit is now configurable end-to-end + mTLS-before-upgrade ordering pinned by test (closes #756, refs IMPROVEMENT-ANALYSIS.md F-59, F-60)** — closes both sub-items #756 calls out in one focused PR. **F-59 (configurability for production fleets):** the per-IP connection rate limit `CONN_RATE_LIMIT = 10/10s` was hard-coded inside `rustgate-websocket` before this change, which left thousand-peer-fleet deployments with no way to raise the cap short of a rebuild and redeploy. The knob is now exposed as `WsListenerConfig::{conn_rate_limit, conn_rate_window}` (already plumbed into the listener constructor; this PR adds the canonical CLI surface), with new CLI flags `--ws-rate-limit-max <N>` (env `RUSTGATE_WS_RATE_LIMIT_MAX`) and `--ws-rate-limit-window-secs <N>` (env `RUSTGATE_WS_RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_SECS`) that thread directly into the listener at server startup. The TOML keys follow the kebab-case mirror of the field names (`ws-rate-limit-max`, `ws-rate-limit-window-secs`), so config-file deployments pick up the same precedence chain (defaults < file < env < CLI flags). The pre-#756 long forms `--ws-conn-rate-limit` / `--ws-conn-rate-window-secs` are retained as `clap::visible_alias` so any operator scripts or runbooks that already reference the older names keep parsing without diff. Defaults remain `max=10, window=10s` — exactly the pre-PR hard-coded constants — so deployments that do not opt into the new knobs see no behaviour change. **F-60 (mTLS-before-upgrade test pin):** adds `tests/ws_security.rs::ws_upgrade_without_client_cert_rejected_at_tls_layer_not_http`, a regression test that builds a `rustls::ClientConfig` with the server CA trusted but `with_no_client_auth()` (no client certificate presented) and attempts a TLS handshake against a `WsListener` configured with mTLS required. The test asserts the connection dies inside the TLS layer — either the rustls connector errors during `connect()`, or the returned stream is unusable on the very first read/write — and explicitly rejects the failure mode where an HTTP response (any byte sequence starting with `"HTTP/"`) crosses the wire on the no-cert connection. The current `WsListener::accept` loop runs `TCP accept → TLS handshake → identity extraction → WS upgrade` in that order, so the existing implementation is already correct; this test is the canary against a future refactor that silently moved the auth checkpoint past the upgrade (e.g. a rewrite that parsed the HTTP `Upgrade` header before invoking the cert verifier — which would let the HTTP machinery accept bytes from a no-cert peer before any auth ran). New test coverage: 4 new CLI tests in `crates/rustgate-server/src/cli.rs::tests` (`ws_listener_config_default_rate_limit_matches_pre_pr_constants` pins the default knob values match `WsListenerConfig::default()` and the pre-PR const values; `ws_listener_config_rate_limit_overridable_via_cli` pins both flags accept overrides and round-trip through the parser; `ws_rate_limit_legacy_aliases_still_parse` pins the `--ws-conn-rate-limit` / `--ws-conn-rate-window-secs` aliases keep working; `ws_rate_limit_toml_key_overrides_default` pins the `ws-rate-limit-max` / `ws-rate-limit-window-secs` TOML keys override the defaults via the `defaults < file` precedence rung) plus 3 new integration tests in `crates/rustgate-websocket/tests/ws_security.rs` (`ws_rate_limit_actually_enforces_configured_max` drives the `ConnRateLimiter` directly with `max=3, window=10s` and pins the 4th attempt is rejected; `ws_listener_accepts_raised_rate_limit_config` is a construction smoke test that a thousand-peer-sized cap binds without panic; the F-60 test described above). Net test delta: +7 tests (+4 server, +3 websocket).
- **Document `ArcSwap` reload eventual-consistency semantics for the Send and Receive PEP (closes #805, refs IMPROVEMENT-ANALYSIS.md F-14)** — adds a new `Reload semantics` section to `docs/authorization.md` covering the eventual-consistency window between Send PEP evaluation in `Router::route_inner` and the per-recipient Receive PEP evaluations that follow. The two sites each call `self.authz.load()` independently against the `arc_swap::ArcSwap<Option<Arc<dyn PolicyEngine>>>` that backs the hot-reload path, so a SIGHUP that lands mid-dispatch can split a single message across two policy versions: Send-allowed under vN, Receive-allowed-or-denied under vN+1, with obligations stacked from the per-PEP `outcome.obligations` that each evaluation produces. The new section walks operators through the `ArcSwap` architecture, the timeline of a message that crosses the swap boundary, the compound effect for obligations (Send-side commits are baked into the envelope before fan-out and cannot be undone by a vN+1 that drops the obligation; Receive-side obligations are policy-current and stack via `RoutedMessage::with_obligations` against whatever guard the per-recipient PEP loaded), the compound effect for ACL group narrowing (membership is cached on `Identity.groups` at session establishment and not re-derived mid-dispatch — Receive-PEP filtering is what catches narrowed access), why this trade-off is correct for a tactical router (a router-wide read lock would either serialize reloads behind the slowest recipient or serialize dispatch behind reloads — both unacceptable), and operator guidance for zero-downtime migrations (trigger during low-traffic windows, correlate reload edges with `rustgate_authz_decisions_total{decision="deny"}` spikes via the `audit::authz_reload_success` / `audit::authz_reload_failed` events emitted from `rustgate_core::audit`, stage a "compatible-with-both" intermediate policy when moving from policy A to policy C, and drain or flush the persistence paths when strict ordering matters). The store-and-forward and SA-replay paths are explicitly carved out as *not* part of the reload window: `filter_offline_messages` and `replay_positions` re-run both PEPs against the current policy snapshot on every drain, so a tightening reload that lands while a recipient is offline catches them on reconnect rather than carrying a stale verdict forward. Documentation only; no code changes.
- **Unified secret-file reader (`rustgate_core::secrets::read_secret_file`, closes #797)** — collapses 5 divergent ad-hoc secret-file readers across the workspace (`rustgate-http::auth::read_secret_file` with the strictest existing discipline, `rustgate-client::connect::build_tls_config`'s bare `std::fs::read` on the private key, `rustgate-federation::connector::PeerConnector::new`'s and `rustgate-federation::manager::FederationManager::start`'s key-file reads, `rustgate-server::main::read_queue_key_file`, and the bearer-token / CA-key reads in `rustgate-server::setup::start_metrics_server` / `rustgate-server::setup::start_enrollment` / `rustgate-server::main`'s ACL-API and management-API token readers) into a single helper in `rustgate-core`. The new helper enforces the strictest existing policy universally — 8 KiB default size cap, Unix mode `0o077` permissions gate (rejects any group/other read access), optional file-owner-uid binding, optional newline trim, and rejection of empty files — and returns `Zeroizing<String>` on every success path so the loaded contents are wiped from memory on drop. Configuration is via the new `SecretFileOpts` knob: callers pin `max_bytes` for larger PEM private keys (the federation, client, and CA-key sites widen to 16 KiB to cover RSA-4096 PKCS#8) and `require_owner_uid` for the strictest "secret dropped by `root`, service runs as `rustgate`" misconfig detection (HTTP auth, server queue-key reader). **This is a security TIGHTENING, not just a refactor**: operators with overly-permissive key files (mode `0o6xx` and above on group/other bits) will now see a hard error at startup — e.g. `secret file '/etc/rustgate/key.pem' has overly-permissive Unix mode 0o644; expected mode 0o077 (group/other bits zero) so a co-tenant cannot read` — instead of a silent passthrough that left every co-tenant on the host able to read the secret. Pre-existing crate error types each gain a `SecretFile(rustgate_core::SecretFileError)` variant via `#[from]` so the structured failure propagates without losing operator-facing detail. The helper itself is exhaustively tested: 10 unit tests pin the contract on the round-trip happy path (default-strict policy with a `\n`-trimmed `0o600` file), the size-cap rejection, the world-readable rejection (Unix-only), the empty-file rejection, the not-found path, the trim-disabled and perm-check-disabled overrides, the invalid-UTF-8 rejection, and the convenience constructor preserving strict defaults when only `max_bytes` is overridden. Operationally additive for any deployment that already follows the documented "chmod 0600 your key files" practice.
- **Concurrency model documentation + DedupCache invariant comment (closes #806)** — adds `docs/concurrency-model.md` as the source of truth for picking concurrency primitives in rustgate, covering mutex discipline (`parking_lot` vs `tokio::sync` vs `std::sync`), per-primitive atomic-ordering rules with rationale tables drawn from real call sites (`CircuitBreaker`, `BackpressureGate`, `TenantQuotaTracker`, `DedupCache`, `PeerHandle`, `TokenBucket`, `ReplayBuffer`), `ArcSwap` discipline including the eventual-consistency window and the no-await-between-load-and-drop rule, callback-shape conventions (`Arc<dyn Fn(...) + Send + Sync>`, not `dyn AsyncFn`), background-task lifecycle helpers (`spawn_background` for fire-and-forget, `SubsystemHandle` for drainable subsystems with a 5s graceful drain), and a decision flowchart contributors can walk to pick the right primitive without re-deriving the rules from the workspace's ~350 existing atomic sites. Pairs the doc with an `// INVARIANT:` comment in `Router::route_inner` that pins the no-`.await`-between-`dedup.load()`-and-the-guard-drop contract that ArcSwap-backed hot-reloadable state requires; the inner `parking_lot::Mutex` makes the comment redundant for the immediate body (the borrow checker would refuse to compile any await against the inner guard), but the outer ArcSwap `Guard` is `Send`, so the comment is the load-bearing documentation for the surrounding scope. Operator guidance: when reviewing PRs that add a new atomic site, walk section 2's pattern table; when adding a new ArcSwap-backed field, copy the `Router::route_inner` comment shape so the next contributor inherits the contract.

### Security

- **Per-sink egress envelope rendering for external sinks (closes #746)** — adds the public `Router::prepare_egress_envelope_for_sink(arc_msg, RecipientClass) -> Result<EgressEnvelope, EgressError>` method that lets every external-sink fan-out helper (TLS / plaintext read loops in `rustgate-server::session`, MQTT publish in `rustgate-mqtt::session`, NATS subscriber loop in `rustgate-nats::subscriber`, federation `on_inbound` in `rustgate-server::setup`, WebSocket read loop in `rustgate-websocket::server`, UDP loop in `rustgate-transport::udp`) render its own post-Send-PEP envelope keyed on the sink's `RecipientClass`. The pre-#746 architecture handed *one* `Arc<RoutableMessage>` from `Router::route_for_egress` to every sink — fine for Direct/Group/Broadcast where the local Send PEP runs at the route boundary, fine for Multicast since #738 wired `prepare_egress_envelope` through the multicast call site — but external sinks addressed by their own `AuthzResource` (a NATS subject, an HTTP webhook endpoint, a federation peer) had no way to apply per-sink Send-PEP rules to the envelope they dispatched. A `MaskPayload`-on-Send rule wired specifically to the HTTP webhook bound to a SIEM would never run on the egress path. This PR closes that gap by routing every wired sink callback through `prepare_egress_envelope_for_sink` first; `EgressError::Denied` and `EgressError::ObligationFailed` suppress dispatch to that sink only — peer sinks still get their own envelope-rendering chance. Obligation actuation runs once per sink per inbound message (the `Arc<EgressEnvelope::message>` cache in the helper is reused across recipients within a single envelope) and the `egress.obligation.applied` audit cadence stays per-envelope. Test delta: +2 tests in `crates/rustgate-router/tests/egress_envelope.rs` pinning (a) per-sink envelope rendering produces one `egress.obligation.applied` event per sink class with the expected `sink` label, and (b) the no-engine path returns the input arc verbatim with empty `applied_obligations`. (closes #746)
- **Federation `on_inbound` egress wired through Send-PEP + NATS/HTTP fan-out (closes #737)** — closes the umbrella by completing the third and final ingress path #737 flagged. The federation `on_inbound` callback in `crates/rustgate-server/src/setup.rs` (formerly inline in `start_federation`) used to call `router.route()` and stop there, which delivered messages from federation peers to local subscribers but left two asymmetries with every other ingress path: (a) the post-route envelope produced by Send-PEP obligations was never observed — `MaskPoint` / `MaskPayload` rules applied to local fanout only — and (b) the message did not fan out to the workspace's external sinks (NATS bus via `NatsPublisher::publish`, HTTP webhooks via `HttpForwardFn`). A `MaskPoint`-on-Send rule on the receiving group therefore zeroed coordinates for in-process recipients only — a SIEM wired downstream of the local rustgate via the HTTP egress bridge would have observed the raw federation-peer coordinates while the directly-connected clients saw the masked form, and the operator's NATS scale-out fanout would have skipped federated messages entirely. This PR closes the gap by mirroring the NATS-subscriber pattern from #1266: extract the inlined `OnInbound` closure into a testable factory `setup::build_federation_inbound_handler(&router, FedInboundForwardingHooks)` that constructs the `RoutableMessage` from `(peer_cn, payload)`, drives it through `Router::route_for_egress` so Send-PEP obligations are baked into the envelope, and fans the resulting `Arc<RoutableMessage>` out to the optional `nats_publish` / `http_forward` callbacks before the spawned task exits. **(1) New `FedInboundForwardingHooks` bundle.** A small struct with two optional callback fields (`nats_publish: Option<rustgate_core::egress::OnNatsPublish>` and `http_forward: Option<HttpForwardFn>` under `cfg(feature = "http")`) plus a `Default` impl that yields the pre-#737 local-only behaviour. The struct intentionally has NO `federation_forward` field — a federation-sourced message must not re-enter the federation forwarder, and the V2 protocol's hop guard (`MAX_FEDERATION_HOPS`, see `validate_hop_count` in `rustgate-federation/src/v2/server.rs`) already drops re-emitted federation messages at the wire layer. The compile-time absence of the field is the load-bearing invariant: a future refactor that adds it back fails the new `federation_inbound_does_not_loop_back_to_federation` test. **(2) `start_federation` accepts hooks.** The signature widens by one parameter (`hooks: FedInboundForwardingHooks`); the inlined closure is replaced with `let on_inbound = build_federation_inbound_handler(router, hooks);`. Existing federation tests that don't care about egress fan-out (e.g. the `manager.start(...)` smoke tests in `rustgate-federation`) continue to compile because they construct their own `OnInbound` directly — they never used the server's `start_federation` orchestrator. **(3) Bootstrap reorder in `main.rs`.** HTTP egress (`setup::connect_http`) now runs BEFORE federation so the `http_forward` callback is in scope when `start_federation` is called. The reorder is purely a wiring change — `connect_http` only consumes `cli` and produces the publisher / forward callback, with no router or federation dependency, so no behaviour relies on the pre-PR ordering. The NATS subscriber's deferred-spawn path from #1266 is unaffected: it still spawns AFTER both federation and HTTP have landed, so the round-trip story is consistent across all three transports. **(4) Echo prevention is intentional asymmetry.** The NATS publisher's case-insensitive `source_protocol == "nats"` echo guard (#1192, line 102 of `rustgate-nats/src/publisher.rs`) does NOT match `"federation"` — a federation-sourced message stamped with `metadata.source_protocol = "federation"` flows through to the NATS bus as intended (no echo-guard update needed; verified by reading the publisher source). The HTTP publisher's `eq_ignore_ascii_case("http")` guard at line 419 of `rustgate-http/src/publisher.rs` likewise does NOT match `"federation"`. Federation→NATS and federation→HTTP fan-out are therefore the intended behaviour of this PR; only federation→federation is the case the design forbids, and that's enforced by the absence of a `federation_forward` field plus the V2 hop guard. **(5) Backward-compatible.** When the binary is built without `--features nats` or `--features http`, the corresponding `nats_publish` / `http_forward` callbacks remain `None` and `fire_federation_inbound_forwarding` is a no-op, exactly matching the pre-#737 behaviour. All 757 federation-crate tests and 551 server-crate tests continue to pass without modification. **Test coverage adds 6 unit tests in `crates/rustgate-server/src/setup.rs::tests::federation_inbound`**: `federation_inbound_fans_out_to_nats` pins the NATS hook fires exactly once with the post-Send-PEP envelope and `source_protocol = "federation"`; `federation_inbound_fans_out_to_http` pins the HTTP hook fires symmetrically; `federation_inbound_does_not_loop_back_to_federation` pins the type-level absence of a federation-forward field on the hook struct (the test fails to build, not at runtime, if the field is added back); `federation_inbound_with_send_pep_obligation_applies_obligation_before_fanout` installs an `AllowWithSendMaskPayloadEngine` and asserts the NATS hook observes the masked envelope (payload bytes stripped, `message_type` rewritten to `Other("masked")`); `federation_inbound_source_protocol_is_federation` pins the metadata invariant both publisher echo guards depend on; `federation_inbound_with_default_hooks_does_not_call_egress` pins that `FedInboundForwardingHooks::default()` is a true no-op so the no-bridge configuration stays no-op. The tests exercise `build_federation_inbound_handler` directly without spinning up a federation manager, so they run in milliseconds and pin the security properties at the closure level rather than depending on V1/V2 wire-protocol round-trips. **Net test delta: +6 unit tests.** **Closes #737** — the umbrella issue is now complete, joining the MQTT sub-item (regression tests in #1263) and the NATS-subscriber sub-item (#1266). (closes #737)
- **RUSTSEC-2024-0436 (`paste` unmaintained) — re-investigated and documented (closes #1249)** — `paste 1.0.15` was archived upstream and surfaced as RUSTSEC-2024-0436 ("unmaintained" informational advisory). #1249 re-investigated whether rustgate could remove the dependency by swapping to the community fork `pastey`. Outcome: **`paste` is purely transitive** through `rustgate-server -> tikv-jemalloc-ctl 0.6.1 -> paste 1.0.15` (chain confirmed by `cargo tree --workspace -e normal --all-features -i paste`); no workspace crate has a direct `paste = "..."` declaration, no `use paste::*` import, and no `paste!` macro invocation. We cannot adopt `pastey` ourselves because the consumer is `tikv-jemalloc-ctl`, not rustgate — a swap would require forking that upstream. Upstream is tracking the same migration in `tikv/jemallocator#130` (open: replaces `paste` with `preinterpret`); we are waiting on that PR rather than carrying a downstream fork. The existing `cargo deny check advisories` ignore for RUSTSEC-2024-0436 (originally added in #714) is retained, with the justification in `deny.toml` updated to (a) cite the upstream PR by URL, (b) record the explicit removal trigger ("drop the ignore after `tikv-jemalloc-ctl` ships a release that no longer pulls in `paste` and we bump past it"), and (c) document the risk-surface argument that justifies the deferral (paste is a build-time proc-macro with no runtime footprint, the advisory is informational rather than a vulnerability, and `cargo deny check sources` gates any malicious upstream release before it reaches a build). No code, lock-file, or feature-flag changes — the conclusion is documentary. (Closes #1249, refs RUSTSEC-2024-0436, refs `tikv/jemallocator#130`.)
- **NATS-subscriber egress wired through Send-PEP + federation/HTTP fan-out (refs #737, NATS-subscriber sub-item)** — closes the second of the three ingress paths #737 flagged as historically calling `Router::route` instead of `Router::route_for_egress`. Pre-this-PR the JetStream pull-consumer loop in `crates/rustgate-nats/src/subscriber.rs` decoded each inbound NATS message into a `RoutableMessage` and dispatched via `router.route(routable)`, which (a) skipped the post-route `Arc<RoutableMessage>` that carries Send-PEP obligations baked into the envelope and (b) had no fan-out to the workspace's external sinks (federation peers, webhook / SIEM targets). A `MaskPoint`-on-Send rule on the receiving group therefore zeroed coordinates for in-process recipients only — a federation peer wired in front of the NATS subscriber observed nothing at all, and any operator hoping to ship a NATS-bridged message onward to a SIEM via the HTTP egress bridge would have to plumb the dispatch path themselves. **(1) Subscriber struct gains forwarder bundle.** `NatsSubscriber` adds three new optional callback fields (`nats_publish: Option<OnNatsPublish>`, `federation_forward: Option<OnFederationForward>`, `http_forward: Option<OnHttpForward>`) plus matching `with_*` builder methods, mirroring the `MqttForwardingHooks` shape so the same `rustgate_core::egress` aliases plug into every transport that fans out. The `nats_publish` field is included for shape parity even though every invocation short-circuits on the publisher's case-insensitive `eq_ignore_ascii_case("nats")` echo guard from #1192 — the subscriber stamps `metadata.source_protocol = "nats"` via `WireEvent::into_routable`, so a future change to the echo discipline surfaces as a single-site edit at the publisher rather than at every transport. **(2) Consumer loop dispatches through `route_for_egress`.** The single-line `router.route(routable)` is replaced with `router.route_for_egress(routable)` plus a `fire_forwarding` helper that walks the optional callbacks against the returned `Arc<RoutableMessage>`. A `None` return means the router dropped the message (dedup, TTL, Send-PEP deny, oversize multicast) and every fan-out is skipped — external sinks see exactly what local sessions saw. **(3) Server orchestration plumbs the forwarders.** `rustgate-server::setup::connect_nats` is split: it now returns a `NatsConnectOutcome { publisher, subscriber }` with the subscriber pre-configured for metrics but **deferred from spawn**, and a new `setup::start_nats_subscriber` helper attaches the federation / HTTP / NATS-publish forwarders and spawns the consumer loop. `main.rs` calls `start_nats_subscriber` AFTER `fed_forward` and `http_forward` are constructed, so an inbound NATS-bridged message reaches the same external sinks every other transport already feeds. **(4) `source_protocol` stamping.** Already in place via `WireEvent::into_routable` (no new code) — pinned by a new regression test so the loop-prevention contract is now defended at the subscriber side as well as the publisher side. **(5) Backward-compatible.** When the binary is built without `--features federation` or `--features http`, the corresponding `with_federation_forward` / `with_http_forward` calls do not happen and the subscriber behaves exactly as before; existing NATS subscriber tests pass unchanged. **Test coverage adds 5 integration tests in `crates/rustgate-nats/tests/integration.rs`**: `nats_subscriber_publish_fans_out_to_federation` pins the federation forwarder fires exactly once with the post-Send-PEP `(payload, groups, metadata)` triple; `nats_subscriber_publish_fans_out_to_http` pins the HTTP egress forwarder fires exactly once with the post-Send-PEP `RoutableMessage`; `nats_subscriber_with_send_pep_obligation_applies_obligation_before_fanout` installs an `AllowWithSendMaskPayloadEngine` and asserts both the local recipient AND the federation forwarder observe the masked envelope (payload bytes stripped, `message_type` rewritten to `Other("masked")`) — `MaskPayload` is used rather than `MaskPoint` because the NATS wire form is JSON and `MaskPoint`'s non-XML branch would silently forward unmasked bytes; `nats_subscriber_does_not_re_publish_to_nats` pins the publisher's `eq_ignore_ascii_case("nats")` echo guard short-circuits the new `nats_publish` callback so no publish loop can form; `nats_subscriber_source_protocol_stamped_correctly` pins the `metadata.source_protocol = "nats"` invariant the echo guard depends on. Each test spins up an ephemeral `TestNatsServer` via `require_nats!`. **Net test delta: +5 integration tests.** **Issue #737 stays open** — the third sub-item (federation `on_inbound` callback) ships in a separate follow-up PR; this PR uses `Refs #737` and explicitly does NOT close it. The MQTT sub-item is already covered by the regression tests in #1263. (refs #737)
- **MQTT publish path egress fan-out test coverage (refs #737, MQTT sub-item)** — pins two security invariants on the inbound MQTT PUBLISH dispatch the wiring closed by #1129 first introduced. Issue #737 flagged three ingress paths (MQTT, NATS subscriber consumer loop, federation `on_inbound`) that historically called `Router::route` instead of `Router::route_for_egress` and therefore (a) did not apply Send-PEP obligations to the post-route envelope and (b) did not fan the message out to the NATS / federation / HTTP egress sinks. The MQTT path itself was already migrated to `route_for_egress` in #1129 and the `MqttForwardingHooks` bundle is wired into the publish path in `crates/rustgate-mqtt/src/session.rs::handle_publish_v5` and `handle_publish_v4` (and the matching `handle_pubrel_*` QoS 2 deliver step), so this PR is a coverage-only follow-up that adds two integration tests in `crates/rustgate-mqtt/tests/mqtt_integration.rs` to keep those properties honest under future churn. **(1) `mqtt_publish_with_send_pep_obligation_applies_obligation_before_fanout`** installs an `AllowWithSendMaskPointEngine` policy that attaches `Obligation::MaskPoint` on every `Action::Send` evaluation, has Alice publish a CoT `<event>` with non-zero `<point lat="38.8977" lon="-77.0365" hae="125.4">` to a group Bob is subscribed to, and asserts that (i) Bob's delivered MQTT PUBLISH carries `lat="0.0"` / `lon="0.0"` and contains neither `38.8977` nor `-77.0365`, (ii) the recorded `nats_publish` egress copy carries the same masked form, (iii) the local-subscriber payload is byte-identical to the egress copy — pinning the `Arc<RoutableMessage>` shared between the local fan-out and the egress return value of `route_for_egress`. A regression that fired the egress callbacks against the pre-PEP form would leak raw coordinates to a SIEM, federation peer, or webhook target while the in-process delivery looked compliant; the byte-equality assertion catches the alternative regression where the local copy and the egress copy diverge after the route returned. **(2) `mqtt_publish_does_not_loop_back_to_mqtt_subscriber_via_nats`** drives the bidirectional echo-loop break: the test injects a synthetic `RoutableMessage` with `source_protocol = "nats"` directly into the router via `Router::route_for_egress` (simulating the future NATS-subscriber consumer loop sub-item of #737), confirms the MQTT subscriber receives the wire bytes, and asserts that NONE of the three `MqttForwardingHooks` callbacks (`nats_publish`, `federation_forward`, `http_forward`) fire — the MQTT-side fan-out helper is wired only on the inbound PUBLISH dispatch, never on the local-recipient delivery path, so an MQTT-sourced message arriving back via a NATS subscriber consumer cannot loop back out through MQTT egress. The test then has Bob publish a fresh message and asserts (a) `nats_publish` fires exactly once, (b) the recorded envelope's `metadata.source_protocol == "mqtt"` so the NATS publisher's case-insensitive `eq_ignore_ascii_case("nats")` echo guard from #1192 trips on any return trip — closing the round-trip loop documented as the canonical broker echo failure mode in #737. **No production code changes** — the wiring already existed; the security property was already correct. The tests exist to keep it correct under future refactors. The two remaining sub-items of #737 (NATS subscriber consumer loop + federation `on_inbound` callback) ship in separate follow-up PRs; this PR uses `Refs #737` and does NOT close it. (refs #737)
- **Audit and document CN normalization across identity / ACL / authz layers (closes #723)** — audited the Common Name (CN) string flow from cert extraction → `Identity` construction → group ACL match → authz Cedar engine evaluation for normalization drift that could let an attacker who controls their CN spoof a different principal across layers. Audit outcome: **no exploitable drift** — the per-layer rules are deliberately divergent (cert extraction preserves bytes verbatim, `Identity::new` validates without normalizing, the group ACL applies ASCII-only lowercase at both allow-list construction AND lookup, the authz native / Cedar engine does byte-identical `==` comparison) and the AND-composition of "ACL allow" ∧ "authz allow" means the more restrictive of the two normalization rules always wins. A Unicode lookalike like Turkish dotless-i `alıce` (U+0131) does NOT match an ASCII `alice` allow list at any layer because (1) ASCII-only lowercase deliberately does not fold non-ASCII codepoints, (2) the authz engine compares bytes, and (3) Identity preserves bytes verbatim — every layer independently rejects the lookalike. The PR ships a new `docs/identity-normalization.md` spelling out which rule applies at each layer, why we deliberately do NOT push normalization into `Identity::new` (would silently merge cert-rotation-separated sessions in the authz cache, would collapse forensic visibility, would silently shift Cedar policy meaning across releases, and would collapse the AND-composition defense to a single layer), and an explicit threat-model table walking through case-mismatched / Unicode-lookalike / NFD-NFC / leading-whitespace attacker scenarios and showing each one fail closed. Test coverage adds 13 invariant-pinning tests across the three layers: 5 in `rustgate-core::identity::tests` (`identity_preserves_cn_bytes_verbatim`, `identity_does_not_lowercase_at_construction`, `nfd_and_nfc_construct_different_identities`, `leading_trailing_whitespace_is_preserved_verbatim`, `unicode_lookalike_does_not_match_legitimate_cn` — the load-bearing security regression guard); 4 in `rustgate-transport::acl::tests` (`acl_match_is_case_insensitive_at_both_construction_and_lookup`, `acl_does_not_fold_unicode_lookalikes`, `acl_does_not_trim_or_nfc_normalize_input`, `acl_already_normalized_input_consumes_without_re_normalization`); and 4 in `rustgate-authz::compile::tests` (`compiled_subject_pred_cn_eq_is_case_sensitive`, `compiled_subject_pred_cn_eq_does_not_fold_unicode_lookalikes`, `compiled_subject_pred_cn_eq_does_not_trim_or_normalize_input`, `compiled_subject_pred_already_normalized_input_consumes_without_re_normalization`). Each test carries a comment explaining the regression class it traps, so a future "well-meaning" refactor that adds NFC + lowercase to `Identity::new` (or that swaps `to_ascii_lowercase()` for full Unicode case folding in the ACL, or that adds normalization to the authz `==` comparison) will fail one of these tests locally before reaching CI. **Operationally additive** — no behavior change, no wire-format change, no audit-record shape change. The PR is the contract documentation + invariant pins; the existing layer behavior was already correct, and the tests exist to keep it correct under future churn.
- **Canonical obligation chaining order (refs #882, sub-item 2 of 3 — obligation chaining; partial close)** — pre-this-PR, when multiple obligations applied to a single message (e.g. Send-PEP attaches `MaskPoint` and Receive-PEP attaches `TagClassified`, or a future downstream policy attaches `AuditExtended` on top), the dispatcher applied them in encounter order — exactly the order the engine emitted them in the `Vec<Obligation>` returned alongside an allow decision. Different code paths could encounter the same obligations in different sequences (Send PEP runs before Receive PEP on `route_inner`; multicast egress builds a per-group union via `HashSet<Obligation>` whose iteration order is NOT input-stable; cache-replay reconstructs the obligation list from a flat-buffer that may reorder during round-trip), producing inconsistent post-PEP byte output for the same input. Without a defined ordering, downstream invariants that key on byte identity — dedup, position cache, federated forwarding correlation — silently broke when the same logical obligation set arrived via two different paths. This PR defines a canonical 3-group ordering enforced by a stable sort before actuation: **Group 1 — Redactors** (`MaskPoint`, `MaskPayload`; priority 0; remove information from the payload, run first so subsequent groups see the redacted form); **Group 2 — Classifiers / Taggers** (`TagClassified`; priority 1; attach new fields to the already-redacted message); **Group 3 — Auditors** (`AuditExtended`; priority 2; emit audit events without changing message bytes, run last so the audit record reflects the final post-redact-post-tag state). Within each group ordering is alphabetical by `Debug` repr — deterministic, no per-variant configuration needed. The dispatcher (`rustgate_transport::obligations::apply_obligations_with_limiter`) now performs a `sort_by_cached_key(Obligation::chain_sort_key)` (Rust's stable sort) on a local clone of the input slice before iterating, so the engine's emission order remains observable upstream of the dispatcher while the actuation path sees the canonical order. **Forward compatibility for `#[non_exhaustive]`**: `Obligation::priority(&self) -> u8` includes a wildcard arm returning `2` (Group 3, Auditors) — the safest default for a transport build older than the policy engine, since auditing the final state lets every known redactor and tagger run first regardless of which unknown variant the engine returned. New variants must declare their group in the variant docstring per the discipline this PR establishes; the doc rule is the contract the next contributor inherits. **Byte-stable output guarantee.** The load-bearing security property is now: two permutations of the same obligation set produce byte-identical post-PEP output. Test coverage adds 4 inline tests in `rustgate-authz::model::model_tests` (`obligation_priority_pins_canonical_group_assignment` pins each known variant's group; `obligation_chain_sort_key_is_priority_then_debug_repr` pins the tuple shape so a regression that swapped (priority, name) for (name, priority) lands here; `obligation_chain_sort_key_orders_alphabetically_within_group` pins `MaskPayload < MaskPoint` lexicographically and that group priority dominates within-group alphabetical; `obligation_chain_sort_key_canonicalizes_permutations` pins the full 4-variant scrambled-input round-trip) and 6 inline tests in `rustgate-transport::obligations::tests` (`obligations_apply_in_canonical_order_redactors_first` pins the deliberately-wrong `[TagClassified, MaskPoint]` input applies as `[MaskPoint, TagClassified]`; `obligations_within_group_sort_alphabetically` pins both forward and reverse-input round-trip to the same canonical alphabetical output; `obligation_chaining_produces_byte_stable_output_under_input_reorder` pins the byte-stable claim end-to-end through `apply_obligations` with two arbitrary permutations of the full known set; `unknown_variant_assigned_to_group_3` pins `AuditExtended.priority() == 2` as the documented `#[non_exhaustive]` fallback bucket plus the per-variant group assignments; `dispatcher_byte_stable_when_only_redactor_mutates_payload` pins the same byte-stable claim through the dispatcher with an obligation set without `MaskPayload` so the sort actually has to put `MaskPoint` first for the claim to hold — without this complement the previous test could pass trivially if a regression silently dropped the sort). **Operationally additive — no wire-format change**: the only externally-visible shift is that obligation actuation now produces deterministic byte output across permutations; pre-this-PR callers that happened to emit obligations in the canonical order already see byte-identical output post-this-PR. **Issue #882 stays open** — the third sub-item (replay filter non-CoT bypass) ships in a separate follow-up PR; this PR partial-closes the "obligation chaining" sub-item only. (refs #882)
- **Operator-configurable `MaskDetailLevel` for secondary position-bearing field redaction (refs #882, sub-item 1 of 3 — point masking detail leakage; partial close)** — `rustgate_cot::mask::strip_coordinates` zeroed `<point lat lon hae />` but left every secondary position-bearing field documented in the CoT spec untouched: `<contact callsign>` (callsign is identity-linked to position, so a receiver who sees `callsign="ALPHA-1"` plus a masked `<point>` can still derive sector membership over time), `<__group name role>` (unit affiliation reveals tactical structure), `<takv version platform>` (TAK device family — ATAK-CIV / WinTAK / iTAK identifies the operator's hardware role), `<status battery>` (battery level can correlate with patrol duration under a sufficiently aggressive threat model), and any vendor-defined custom attribute whose name contains `lat`/`lon`/`alt`/`pos`/`loc` (which would re-introduce position the masker did not know to look for). The legacy single-tier behaviour was the most permissive choice — appropriate for a deployment that trusts every receiver to handle the secondary metadata, inappropriate for one that treats the receiver as semi-trusted and wants the event shape but not the operator's identity. This PR adds a new `pub enum MaskDetailLevel { Coarse, Medium, Strict }` (`#[non_exhaustive]`, `Default = Coarse`) and a new `pub fn strip_coordinates_with_level(payload, level) -> Result<Bytes, MaskError>` entrypoint that lets the caller select how aggressively the secondary fields are scrubbed without committing to the all-or-nothing `Obligation::MaskPayload`. **`Coarse`** (default, the legacy behaviour) masks only `<point lat lon hae />`. **`Medium`** also redacts `<contact callsign>` and the `<__group name role>` attributes — every callsign-or-affiliation field collapsed to the static `[REDACTED]` token (the brackets distinguish "operator masked this" from "sender omitted this", and survive parsers that strip empty attributes). **`Strict`** further redacts `<takv version platform>`, `<status battery>`, and any attribute on any element whose name contains (case-insensitively) one of `lat`/`lon`/`alt`/`pos`/`loc` — a substring scan rather than an exact match so vendor extensions like `<x my_lat="…">` and `<custom pos_estimated_x>` are also caught. The three canonical `<point>` numeric attributes still receive `0.0` rather than `[REDACTED]` even at Strict so a numeric parser does not error on the spec shape; only custom position-named attributes on `<point>` (e.g. `<point my_lat="…">`) get the bracket-style redaction. Element matching for every target is case-insensitive and namespace-prefix-tolerant — same shape as the existing `is_point_tag` discipline so a sender cannot bypass the masker by emitting `<Contact>` or `<cot:contact>`. A new per-element attribute-count cap `MAX_DETAIL_ATTRIBUTES = 64` is applied to every element the stricter levels touch, mirroring the pre-existing `MAX_POINT_ATTRIBUTES` cost-amplification protection; crafted XML packing thousands of attributes onto a single `<contact>` fail-closes via `MaskError::AttrBudgetExceeded` rather than amplifying per-recipient masking cost on a broadcast. **Backward compatibility.** The legacy `strip_coordinates(xml)` entrypoint is preserved and now dispatches to `strip_coordinates_with_level(xml, MaskDetailLevel::Coarse)`, so every pre-#882 caller (the `MaskPoint` obligation dispatcher in `rustgate_transport::obligations` plus the integration / fuzz callers) sees byte-identical Coarse-level output. Operators who want stricter redaction call `strip_coordinates_with_level` with the level of their choice; the existing dispatcher is unchanged in this PR (a follow-up will thread the operator-configured level into the obligation actuation site once the level-selection knob lands on the policy-engine surface). **Audit vocabulary.** The 4-variant recovery-token vocabulary established by #1205 (`forwarded_binary` / `forwarded_unmasked` / `forwarded_unknown` / `dropped`) gains a 5th constant `audit::MASK_RECOVERY_FORWARDED_PARTIAL = "forwarded_partial"` so SIEM dashboards can see when masking was applied at an operator-selected Medium/Strict tier. The token is reserved for the dispatcher to emit in the follow-up obligation-actuation-site PR; this PR ships the constant, its documentation, and the audit-emission contract test so the dashboard side has a stable token to key on as soon as the dispatcher wires it. **Operationally additive — no wire-format change for existing callers**: every existing `strip_coordinates()` call continues to produce Coarse-level output byte-for-byte; the new `MaskDetailLevel::Medium` and `MaskDetailLevel::Strict` paths are opt-in via the new entrypoint; the new audit token is reserved (no new emission in this PR). Test coverage adds 22 inline tests in `rustgate-cot::mask::tests` (`coarse_masks_point_only`, `coarse_does_not_mask_callsign`, `medium_also_masks_callsign`, `medium_also_masks_group_affiliation`, `medium_does_not_mask_takv_or_battery`, `strict_masks_takv_platform`, `strict_masks_status_battery`, `strict_masks_custom_lat_attr`, `strict_masks_uppercase_custom_lat_attr`, `strict_does_not_redact_unrelated_attributes`, `strict_includes_every_medium_redaction`, `byte_stable_for_inputs_with_no_secondary_fields`, `strip_coordinates_default_is_coarse`, `mask_detail_level_default_is_coarse`, `mask_detail_level_redacts_predicates_match_documented_tier_table`, `medium_handles_namespaced_contact_element`, `medium_handles_uppercase_contact_element`, `detail_attr_budget_caps_per_element`, `medium_xml_intent_malformed_payload_is_rejected`, `strict_self_stable_on_redacted_output`, `medium_at_attribute_budget_is_accepted`, `point_inside_strict_with_custom_lat_attr_redacts_custom_attr_only`) and 2 inline tests in `rustgate_core::audit::tests::authz` (`forwarded_partial_token_is_distinct_from_other_recovery_tokens` pins the 5-token-uniqueness contract; `forwarded_partial_is_emitted_as_recovery_field_value_at_medium_or_strict` exercises the audit-emission round-trip through a thread-local subscriber and pins the JSON `"recovery":"forwarded_partial"` wire shape). The existing `mask_recovery_tokens_are_stable_strings` test gains a 5th literal-pinning assertion. **Net test delta: +25 tests across the workspace.** **Issue #882 stays open** — the other two sub-items (obligation chaining, replay filter non-CoT bypass) ship in separate follow-up PRs in different batches; this PR partial-closes the "point masking detail leakage" sub-item only.

- **Send-PEP obligations applied on multicast egress (closes #738)** — closes an egress hole where `Router::route_for_egress` returned the unmasked source `Arc<RoutableMessage>` for `Destination::Multicast` messages. The top-level Send PEP in `route_inner` intentionally bypasses multicast (per-group granularity is handled inside `send_to_group_excluding` for the local fanout), so the per-recipient session copies were correctly masked while the egress arc returned to NATS / federation / HTTP forwarders carried the raw pre-obligation payload. A `MaskPoint`-on-Send rule on group `alpha` therefore zeroed coordinates for in-process recipients but forwarded the unmodified `<point lat="…" lon="…">` to a SIEM, federation peer, or webhook target. This PR adds a per-group Send-PEP pass on the egress path: each addressed group is evaluated under `Action::Send`, the union of allow-side obligations is computed across the multicast list (`HashSet<Obligation>` dedupes the common case where every group carries the same masking rule), and the union is applied to a separate clone of the source message that becomes the egress arc. The local-fanout perf carve-out is preserved — `send_to_multicast` still runs first on the unmasked envelope and per-group obligations are applied recipient-side inside `send_to_group_excluding` exactly as before, so the in-process delivery path takes no extra clone and no extra obligation evaluation. The egress side is additive: when no engine is installed, no group produces payload-mutating obligations, or the only obligations are audit-shaped (`TagClassified` / `AuditExtended`), the egress arc is the original unmodified `Arc<RoutableMessage>` and zero allocation is added. When obligation actuation fail-closes under `UnknownObligationPolicy::FailClosed`, `route_for_egress` returns `None` for the egress copy — external sinks receive nothing rather than a leaked unmasked payload, matching the existing oversize-multicast suppression contract. Audit emission is pinned: per-group `authz_denied` events are NOT re-emitted on the egress path because `send_to_group_excluding` already audited any denies during the local fanout, and `authz_classified_delivery` remains recipient-paired in the Receive PEP — the egress copy is a single artefact with no per-recipient envelope. The semantic choice — apply the *union* of allow-side Send obligations across the addressed groups — is the strictest-wins rule: egress sinks are not group-aware, so if any group's policy author intended a `MaskPoint`, the masked form is what reaches the external sink. Test coverage adds 3 integration tests in a new `crates/rustgate-transport/tests/multicast_egress_pep.rs` binary: `multicast_egress_applies_send_pep_obligations` pins a `MaskPoint`-on-Send policy and asserts the egress arc has `lat="0.0"` / `lon="0.0"` for a CoT `<point>` payload; `multicast_local_fanout_remains_unmasked_when_no_send_obligation` pins the converse direction (a Receive-only obligation leaves the egress arc unmodified while the local recipient still sees the Receive-side mask, preserving the perf carve-out); `multicast_destination_emits_audit_when_obligation_applies` installs an `AuthzObserver` and asserts at least two `Action::Send` evaluations fire for a two-group multicast — covering both the local fanout and the new egress-side per-group evaluations. The existing inline `multicast_*` tests in `rustgate-transport::router::tests` continue to pass unchanged because they exercise only the no-engine path, where the egress arc is `MulticastEgress::Unchanged` and round-trips bytes-for-bytes with the input payload.

- **Static `reason` vocabulary on obligation audit emissions (closes #775, refs IMPROVEMENT-ANALYSIS.md F-4)** — extends the static-label discipline established by #1205 (MaskPoint recovery tokens) to every obligation audit `%err` site. Pre-this-PR the `audit::authz_obligation_failed` helper accepted an `error: &str` field that callers populated either with a hard-coded prose string (`"payload is not XML"` at the non-XML pass-through site) or with `MaskError::kind()`'s discriminant (`"xml_parse_error"` / `"io_error"` / `"attr_budget_exceeded"`). That made SIEM dashboards group on a field whose name (`error`) suggested unconstrained content, and provided no documented vocabulary that operators or dashboard authors could pin against. A future contributor adding a third call site could plausibly have logged the underlying error's `Display` directly — re-introducing exactly the F-4 risk the issue was filed to close, since `quick_xml::Error::Display` echoes payload-derived tag names (`EndEventMismatch { expected, found }`) that drift across releases and can leak fragments of a classified payload that failed to parse. The new contract pins the dashboard grouping field with: (1) five `&'static str` constants in `rustgate_core::audit` — `OBLIGATION_REASON_MASK_POINT_NON_XML`, `OBLIGATION_REASON_MASK_POINT_XML_ERROR`, `OBLIGATION_REASON_MASK_POINT_IO_ERROR`, `OBLIGATION_REASON_MASK_POINT_ATTR_BUDGET_EXCEEDED`, `OBLIGATION_REASON_UNKNOWN_VARIANT` — each documenting the exact emission case and pinning the literal token (`"mask_point_non_xml"`, `"mask_point_xml_error"`, `"mask_point_io_error"`, `"mask_point_attr_budget_exceeded"`, `"unknown_variant"`); (2) a `audit::obligation_reason_for_mask_error_kind(kind: &str) -> &'static str` helper that maps `MaskError::kind()` discriminants to the matching reason token, with a documented fallback to the highest-severity bucket (`mask_point_xml_error`) for any future `MaskError` variant landing without a companion update — so a stale build cannot accidentally drop to a non-XML token and under-report the failure class; (3) the `authz_obligation_failed` audit field renamed from `error` to `reason` (signature parameter renamed to match) so SIEM rules grep on a field whose name matches its constraint, with the orthogonal `recovery` token from #1205 still riding alongside; (4) the `authz_obligation_unknown` event picks up a new `reason = OBLIGATION_REASON_UNKNOWN_VARIANT` field — fixed at the audit-emission site rather than passed by the caller because the `obligation` field already carries the `{:?}` variant rendering, and the `reason` field exists so SIEM rules can group every unknown-variant event under a single alerting key. Both `rustgate_transport::obligations::apply_mask_point` call sites now pass static reason tokens drawn from the constant vocabulary; the `tracing::debug!` line on the XML-parse-failed branch additionally surfaces the resolved `reason` alongside the existing `error_kind` so an operator triaging a verbose log stream can correlate the operational log line with the audit record without re-deriving the mapping. **Operationally additive — no wire-format change for the recovery token vocabulary, no audit-record shape change beyond the field rename**: `recovery` continues to carry `dropped` / `forwarded_binary` / `forwarded_unmasked` / `forwarded_unknown` for the four #1205 buckets unchanged, the new `reason` field is strict information gain, and the rename is a deliberate breaking change that shows up at every dashboard-author touch point so an upgrade is a coordinated decision rather than a silent re-bucketing of every alerted-on event. SIEM dashboards keyed on the old `error` field name need to migrate to `reason` — there is no transitional dual-emission, since the rename is the load-bearing signal that the field semantics now match a documented vocabulary. Test coverage adds 4 inline tests in `rustgate-core::audit::tests::authz` (`obligation_reason_tokens_are_stable_strings` pins the literal value of every constant; `obligation_reason_for_mask_error_kind_maps_known_discriminants` pins the `xml_parse_error` / `io_error` / `attr_budget_exceeded` round-trip; `obligation_reason_for_mask_error_kind_falls_back_to_xml_error` pins the future-`MaskError`-variant safety net) and 4 audit-emission integration tests in a new `crates/rustgate-transport/tests/obligation_static_reason_audit.rs` (`audit_obligation_failed_emits_static_reason_label_for_xml_error` drives a truncated XML payload through the masker end-to-end and asserts `reason="mask_point_xml_error"` plus `recovery="dropped"`; `audit_obligation_failed_emits_static_reason_label_for_io_error` exercises the `MaskError::Io` audit shape via the public audit API since the `Vec<u8>` writer makes the variant unreachable from real traffic; `audit_obligation_failed_emits_static_reason_label_for_attr_budget_exceeded` drives a crafted oversized `<point>` payload through the masker and additionally asserts the prose fragment `"attribute count exceeded"` does NOT appear in the audit emission; `audit_obligation_unknown_emits_static_reason_label` pins the unknown-variant audit shape with `reason="unknown_variant"`). The integration-test binary isolation is required because tracing caches per-callsite `Interest` globally — same rationale that motivated the existing `mask_point_recovery_audit.rs` and `position_replay_rate_limit_audit.rs` integration binaries. Net test delta: +4 inline + 4 integration = +8 tests across the workspace. Existing `mask_point_recovery_audit.rs` integration tests pass unchanged because they assert only on the `recovery` and `source_protocol` fields, not on the renamed `error` → `reason` field.
- **Cap log-field cardinality by hashing operational CN/peer_id at info/debug (closes #773, refs IMPROVEMENT-ANALYSIS.md F-30)** — closes the operational companion to #802. Pre-this-PR, operational `info!`/`debug!`/`trace!` log lines across `rustgate-federation` (manager, V1 client, HA claims, HA registry, trust store), `rustgate-server` (session, setup), and `rustgate-mqtt`/`rustgate-server` rate-limit + replay-detect debug arms emitted the raw `cn` and `peer_id` fields straight into structured `tracing` records. A SIEM ingesting the log stream (Loki / Splunk / Elasticsearch) indexes by field value, and the value space is user-controlled — an attacker who churns CNs (or compromises a fleet of clients with random / generated CNs) can inflate the SIEM index to multi-GB by emitting unique values per request, with the secondary effect that legitimate CN-based queries get drowned in churn. **The boundary discipline.** This PR adopts a hash-by-default discipline for operational logs at info/debug level: every such site now wraps the value with `rustgate_core::masking::hash_cn(...)` before it reaches a structured field, capping the SIEM index cardinality at the bounded fleet-CN count (a deployment property, not attacker-controlled per session). Error and warn paths intentionally keep the raw value — those are the forensic-correlation logs an operator needs to reconstruct a session under investigation, and they are already audit-sanitized at the `rustgate_core::audit` boundary by #1197 (audit records sanitize at emission, so raw CN in a `warn!` cannot reach a tampered audit chain). **Why hard-hash over LRU-gated cap.** Two designs were considered: (1) a `LogFieldCardinalityGate` LRU that tracked `(field_name, value)` tuples and switched to hashed output only after a threshold; (2) hash unconditionally at every operational log site. We picked (2) — it's stateless, has predictable cardinality bounds (the SIEM will see at most `2^48` distinct hashes regardless of attacker effort, and in practice will see one hash per fleet CN), avoids the per-emission lookup cost of an LRU, avoids the re-tuning footgun where an operator might accidentally widen the threshold and re-expose the index, and lets a future SIEM correlation query group by the stable hash without the LRU's "below-threshold prefix is raw, above-threshold suffix is hashed" discontinuity. The `hash_cn` helper has been the canonical correlation primitive since #802; this PR finishes the migration that #802 partially shipped (security-critical sites only, leaving operational logs raw). **Sites migrated.** `rustgate-federation::manager` (12 info/debug peer_id sites — replay-buffer rehydrate, peer-claimed-by-other-pod, V1/V2 client started + adoption variants, V1/V2 client stopped + claim-lost variants, peer-added enable/inbound/outbound variants, peer-already-connected, peer-adopted-successfully, replay-buffer-removed, peer-claim-lost dedup-callback debug arm, circuit-breaker-recovered info, V1-dedup-duplicate-dropped debug); `rustgate-federation::v1::client` (6 info/debug peer_id sites — V1 connect, replay-on-reconnect, disconnect-clean, reconnect-delay-info, drained-on-exit-debug, finished-replay-debug, V1-shutdown-requested-debug, V1-heartbeat-received-debug, V1-heartbeat-sent-debug); `rustgate-federation::ha::claims` (6 info/debug peer_id sites — claim-acquired, claim-reclaim-own, claim-already-held-by-other, claim-released, claim-expired-during-refresh, expired-claim-reclaim-success, peer-available-for-adoption-debug, refreshed-claim-debug); `rustgate-federation::ha::registry` (2 debug peer_id sites — connection-registered, connection-unregistered); `rustgate-federation::trust_store` (3 cn sites — debug load, info added, info removed); `rustgate-server::session` (8 cn sites — debug TakProtocolSupport advertisement sent, info protobuf-upgrade requested + complete, info staying-XML, debug rate-limit-drop both TLS and plaintext arms, debug replay-detected both arms); `rustgate-server::setup` (1 info peer_id site — adopting-orphaned-peer); `rustgate-mqtt::session` already used `hash_cn` at every CN log site from #802 (no migration needed; this PR adds an info/debug boundary regression test at the module test surface). Total migrated: 38 log sites across 8 source files. **What stays raw — and why.** Every `warn!`/`error!` path with `cn` or `peer_id` keeps the raw value: TLS handshake failures, certificate-validation rejections, federation-circuit trips, V1/V2 client failed-to-register, V1 reconnect-max-reached, group-join-quota-rejected, group-limit-quota-rejected, persisted-replay-delete-failed, fencing-token-stale-during-adoption, federation-failed-to-add-from-discovery, federation-failed-to-adopt-peer, federation-claim-lost-disconnect, message-dropped-no-store-forward-queue, MaskPoint-unparseable-XML — these are the forensic events an operator wires into SIEM alerting and pages on; collapsing them to a hash would defeat the per-event correlation that incident response needs. The audit-boundary-sanitization landed in #1197 keeps these records safe from log-forging via embedded CR/LF in the raw CN. **Operationally additive — no wire-format change, no API change, no audit-record shape change.** The visible operator shift is that 38 operational log sites now emit a 12-char hashed identity token instead of the raw value; operators querying the SIEM should switch their dashboards to filter on the hashed field and use the unmodified warn/error sites for raw-CN forensic queries. **Test delta**: +2 tests in `rustgate_core::masking` (`hash_identity_idempotent_through_log_field` pins the SIEM-grouping property — the same CN must hash to the same token across repeated calls, including across owned/borrowed binding sources, so a single identity collapses to a single index entry; `hash_identity_collision_resistance_smoke` pins the 1000-CN smoke set producing 1000 distinct hashes — a regression to a much shorter truncation, e.g. first 8 bits, would collapse the smoke set into ~256 buckets and trip here); +1 in `rustgate_mqtt::session::tests` (`mqtt_session_operational_logs_hash_cn_at_info_debug_boundary` pins that the module's `hash_cn` import resolves to the public helper rather than a stray crate-local copy, plus the 12-char hex-only token contract the SIEM cardinality cap depends on); +1 in `rustgate_federation::manager::tests` (`manager_uses_shared_hash_cn_for_peer_id_log_cardinality_cap` pins the same import-resolution contract for the federation manager's many `peer_id` sites). Net workspace test delta: +4. (closes #773)

- **Document the `RUSTSEC-2024-0436` ignore in `deny.toml` against issue #714** — `RUSTSEC-2024-0436` flags the `paste 1.0.15` proc-macro crate as no longer maintained (the upstream repository was archived by the author). It is an "unmaintained" advisory, not a vulnerability — `paste` runs at compile time and produces no runtime code, so it carries no exploitable surface in shipped binaries. `paste` enters rustgate's dependency graph only when the `jemalloc` feature is enabled, transitively through `tikv-jemalloc-ctl 0.6.1` (the latest release still depends on `paste`). Replacing the chain would require forking `tikv-jemalloc-ctl` itself to swap in the `pastey` community fork, which is not justified for an informational advisory on a build-only macro crate. The `deny.toml` `[advisories].ignore` already carried `"RUSTSEC-2024-0436"` (added in commit `83c6275` when the advisory first surfaced); this PR rewrites the inline justification to (a) correctly identify the upstream chain (`tikv-jemalloc-ctl`, not `tikv-jemallocator`), (b) reference issue #714 explicitly so the ignore can be removed alongside that issue's resolution, and (c) document the upgrade-trigger ("remove this ignore when `tikv-jemalloc-ctl` ships a release that no longer pulls in `paste`"). No source-code change; `cargo deny check` and `cargo audit` continue to report `advisories ok` with the suppression in place. (closes #714)

- **MaskPoint audit distinguishes binary-protocol pass-through from unparseable XML (closes #742, refs IMPROVEMENT-ANALYSIS.md F-2)** — `rustgate_transport::obligations::apply_mask_point` previously emitted a single `recovery="forwarded_unmasked"` audit token for every non-XML-intent payload that arrived at the masker. That collapsed three forensically distinct cases — a legitimate binary framing where masking is N/A by design (MAVLink, TAK protobuf, ASTERIX), an XML-text protocol whose bytes did not parse and may have leaked a position the masker missed, and an unrecognised protocol identifier from a misconfigured upstream — into one audit string, forcing operators to re-derive the distinction from the `source_protocol` field by hand. This PR splits the audit token into a three-variant vocabulary keyed on `source_protocol`: `forwarded_binary` for known binary framings (the new lowest-severity bucket — pass-through is correct by design), `forwarded_unmasked` for `source_protocol` claiming `cot` or `xml` but the payload non-parseable (the higher-severity bucket, label preserved from the pre-issue-#742 vocabulary so existing SIEM rules keep firing on exactly this case), and `forwarded_unknown` for anything else (operator-visibility bucket for misconfigured upstreams). The vocabulary is exposed through stable `&'static str` constants `MASK_RECOVERY_FORWARDED_BINARY`, `MASK_RECOVERY_FORWARDED_UNMASKED`, `MASK_RECOVERY_FORWARDED_UNKNOWN`, and `MASK_RECOVERY_DROPPED` in `rustgate_core::audit` so a SIEM dashboard author and the dispatcher reference one source of truth, and a new `audit::classify_mask_recovery_for(source_protocol)` helper performs the bucket decision with ASCII case-insensitive matching (a federation hop that re-stamps `MAVLink` or `MAVLINK` does not flip the recovery bucket). The known-binary list explicitly accepts both `tak-protobuf` (the spelling `Codec::protocol_id()` returns) and `tak_protobuf` (the spelling older config keys used) so the historic identifier divergence does not split a single forensic event across two audit streams. The XML-intent fail-closed path continues to emit `recovery="dropped"` unchanged — that's the security boundary where a crafted `<event><point lat="…"/>…` payload that aborts parsing immediately after `<point>` was already emitted to the writer must NOT leak coordinates via pass-through, and the migration to the named constant is purely cosmetic. **Operationally additive**: the `forwarded_unmasked` token is preserved for the unparseable-XML case, so dashboards keyed on the existing string keep firing on exactly the same forensic event class they did before; the new `forwarded_binary` and `forwarded_unknown` tokens are strict information gain. Test coverage spans (a) the recovery-token string-stability contract in `rustgate-core::audit::tests` (4 tests pinning each constant's literal value plus the classifier's bucket decisions across known-binary, known-XML, and unknown protocols, with ASCII-case-insensitive coverage); (b) the dispatcher-side side-effect contract in `rustgate-transport::obligations::tests` (5 tests pinning that `apply_mask_point` passes a payload through byte-for-byte regardless of which binary or XML or unknown framing it claims to be — no regression where a future refactor starts mutating MAVLink / TAK protobuf / ASTERIX bytes); and (c) the end-to-end audit-emission shape in a new `crates/rustgate-transport/tests/mask_point_recovery_audit.rs` integration test (6 tests pinning the JSON-shape audit record for MAVLink, TAK protobuf both spellings, ASTERIX, unparseable CoT, and an unrecognised protocol — the integration-test binary isolation is required because tracing caches per-callsite `Interest` globally and a thread-local subscriber installed in a unit test cannot capture an audit-target event whose Interest was already cached as `never` by an earlier test in the same binary, the same rationale that motivated `tests/position_replay_rate_limit_audit.rs` and `tests/store_forward_dwell_audit.rs`). Net test delta: +15 tests across the workspace.
- **Rate-limit unknown-obligation audit emissions + add Prometheus counter (closes #769)** — closes both sub-items of the issue in one focused change. **F-3a (audit-flood mitigation)**: pre-this-PR a misconfigured policy that returned an unknown obligation variant on every routed message produced one `audit::authz_obligation_unknown` emission per delivery, which at modest message rates would have flooded the hash-chained audit log (`rustgate_core::audit_chain::HashChainWriter`) with effectively duplicate forensic noise and blown past disk budgets in long-running deployments. The new `rustgate_transport::obligations::ObligationRateLimiter` gates audit emission via a per-`(policy_id, variant_name)` `rustgate_resilience::token_bucket::TokenBucket`, defaulting to `DEFAULT_UNKNOWN_OBLIGATION_AUDIT_PER_MIN = 60` emissions per minute per key. The keyspace is `(policy_id, variant_name)` so two distinct broken variants each retain their own audit allotment, and a policy reload (which changes `policy_id`) re-arms the bucket — `Router::swap_authz` and `Router::clear_authz` now call `ObligationRateLimiter::forget_policy` on the previous engine's id so map growth stays bounded across reloads and the freshly-installed policy's first-minute emissions are not pre-suppressed by the previous policy's audit-rate state. Excess emissions are silently dropped at the audit-emit site, but counted in the new metric (F-3b) so operators retain visibility into the actual rate. **F-3b (operator-visible counter)**: new `rustgate_authz_obligation_unknown_total{variant}` Prometheus `IntCounterVec` registered in `rustgate_server::metrics` under the existing OnceLock + accessor pattern. The counter increments BEFORE the rate-limit check via the `ObligationRateLimiter::with_on_unknown` callback (`OnObligationUnknown = Arc<dyn Fn(&str) + Send + Sync>`), so the counter reflects every unknown-variant encounter — operators page on `rate(rustgate_authz_obligation_unknown_total[5m])` regardless of whether audit emissions for that key have been silenced. The callback is wired in `rustgate_server::main` at router construction time (gated behind `feature = "metrics"`) so the counter is the load-bearing operator visibility signal, with the audit log providing forensic detail at most `audit_per_min` times per minute per key. The existing `apply_obligations` free function keeps its pre-#769 signature for the fuzz target and any caller without engine context; the new `apply_obligations_with_limiter` entrypoint threads `policy_id` and an optional `&ObligationRateLimiter` through to the unknown-variant audit + metric path. The `RoutedMessage::with_obligations` helper grew the same two parameters and every call site in `Router` (Send PEP, Receive PEP, replay path, store-and-forward drain, multicast fan-out) now threads the engine's `policy_id()` and the router's installed rate limiter. Test coverage adds 7 new tests in `obligations::tests` (`obligation_unknown_audit_rate_limited_after_threshold` pins the F-3a spec mirror — 100 emissions cap to the per-minute allotment; `obligation_unknown_metric_counts_all_emissions_not_just_audited` pins the F-3b spec mirror — counter sees all 100 emissions; `obligation_unknown_per_variant_isolation` pins the (policy_id, variant) keyspace — saturating variant A leaves variant B's allotment intact; `obligation_unknown_per_policy_isolation` pins the policy_id half — same variant under a different policy gets a fresh bucket; `obligation_unknown_forget_policy_clears_only_that_policy` pins the reload re-arm contract; `obligation_rate_limiter_default_audit_per_min` pins the documented default of 60; `obligation_rate_limiter_zero_per_min_is_clamped_to_one` pins the never-fully-suppressed signal floor) and 3 new tests in `metrics::tests::authz_obligation_unknown_counter` (`obligation_unknown_registered_under_documented_name` pins the Prometheus name + single `variant` label dimension; `obligation_unknown_increments_variant_label` pins the increment hot path; `obligation_unknown_distinguishes_variants` pins label isolation). The fuzz target `obligation_apply.rs` continues to use the back-compat `apply_obligations` free function and is unaffected.
- **Promote `hash_cn` to `rustgate-core::masking` and expand log sanitization across security-critical paths (closes #802, refs IMPROVEMENT-ANALYSIS.md F-94)** — closes the F-94 log-hygiene gap that the audit-boundary sanitization landed in #1197 left half-finished.
