Three discrete fixes ship in one focused PR. **(1) `hash_cn` is now a public, top-level helper.** The 48-bit SHA-256-truncated correlation token previously lived as a crate-private `fn hash_cn` inside `rustgate-transport::router` and could not be reached from `rustgate-mqtt`, `rustgate-websocket`, `rustgate-federation`, `rustgate-server`, `rustgate-transport::cache`, or `rustgate-transport::listener` — every site that wanted PII-safe identity correlation either reinvented it or logged the raw CN. The function had already been moved to `rustgate_core::masking::hash_cn` in a prior unrelated refactor (the router was importing it from there); this PR finishes the job by adding a top-level `pub use masking::hash_cn` re-export from `rustgate-core`'s `lib.rs` so downstream crates can reach it as `rustgate_core::hash_cn` without spelunking through the masking module path, and pins the public-API contract through four explicitly-named regression tests in `rustgate_core::masking::tests`: `hash_identity_returns_hex_with_documented_length` (12 hex chars = 48 bits), `hash_identity_is_deterministic` (same input → same output across calls), `hash_identity_distinguishes_different_inputs` (collision-resistance acknowledgement against the 48-bit birthday bound), and `hash_identity_handles_pathological_inputs` (empty, 1-MiB, all-NUL, CR/LF + ANSI CSI, multi-byte Unicode + control-byte payloads — every variant must yield a 12-char hex token without panic). The `sanitize_for_log` helper from `rustgate-core::sanitize` is also re-exported from the crate root for the same convenience-and-discoverability reason. **(2) Migrated 10 call sites at security-critical boundaries.** Walked the workspace for `tracing::*!(.. cn = %.. ..)` and similar patterns, identified the highest-value sites where a hostile peer's CN reaches a log field, and either wrapped with `hash_cn` (security-relevant info/warn at connection boundaries) or with `sanitize_for_log` (when the CN is not yet a validated `Identity` and the goal is log-injection defense rather than PII protection). Sites migrated: `rustgate-transport::listener` (TLS-authenticated client log), `rustgate-transport::cache` (position-cache eviction warning), `rustgate-server::session` (TLS connect/disconnect, plaintext TCP connect/disconnect, tenant-quota rejection, negotiation failure, generic session-error debug — both TLS and plaintext arms), `rustgate-server::setup` (federation inbound peer-identity rejection — `peer_cn` here is bytes from a remote peer that failed `Identity::plaintext` construction so the cert-extraction sanitizer hasn't run yet; sanitize before the structured-log field), `rustgate-federation::v1::server` (V1 inbound peer connect/disconnect/heartbeat-received), `rustgate-federation::v1::client` (V1 outbound peer connect), `rustgate-federation::connector` (mTLS server-identity-extracted CN log), `rustgate-websocket::lib` (WebSocket TLS authenticated + handshake established), `rustgate-mqtt::listener` (MQTT TLS authenticated), `rustgate-enrollment::est` (re-enrollment CN-mismatch — `client_cn` is from validated Basic Auth and safe; `requested_cn` is attacker-controlled CSR subject bytes so sanitize before logging), `rustgate-enrollment::handlers::sign` (CSR signing v1/v2 — `client_uid` query-param is truncated to 128 chars but not stripped of CR/LF, sanitize once on extraction and reuse for all subsequent log fields). For sites where the CN comes through cert extraction (and thus already through `extract.rs::sanitize_for_log`), the migration uses `hash_cn` for PII protection rather than re-sanitizing — defense-in-depth, not redundant work. The router itself was already on `hash_cn`; the regression test `router_uses_hash_identity_for_access_log` pins that the access-log dst field formatting still routes through the public helper rather than a stray crate-local copy. **(3) The migration follows the audit-boundary discipline (#1197).** Audit emission paths sanitize at the audit boundary inside `rustgate_core::audit`; this PR sanitizes at the call site for tracing logs. Defense-in-depth: even if a future caller forgets to wrap, the audit record stays safe because the audit helpers wrap on their side. **Operationally additive — no wire-format change, no ABI change, no audit-record shape change.** The visible operational shift is that 10 log sites now emit a 12-char hashed identity token instead of the raw CN, and 5 sites emit a sanitized-for-log string (control bytes replaced with U+FFFD) instead of the raw CN. Operators correlating across log entries should switch to the hashed-CN field which is stable per-CN-per-process. **Partial migration is intentional**: the audit-boundary work in #1197 is the load-bearing security boundary; this PR is operational defense-in-depth for the highest-value subset of the remaining log call sites. A full per-line migration of every `cn = %identity.cn` in the workspace would touch 100+ files for diminishing security return — the unmigrated sites mostly log CNs that have already passed through `extract.rs::sanitize_for_log` so an embedded CR/LF cannot reach them. Test delta: +6 in `rustgate-core::masking` (the four `hash_identity_*` tests + the existing `hash_cn_*` tests are kept), +1 in `rustgate-transport::router::tests` (`router_uses_hash_identity_for_access_log` regression), +1 in `rustgate-federation::v1::server::tests` (`v1_server_uses_shared_hash_cn_for_peer_logs`), +1 in `rustgate-mqtt::listener::tests` (`mqtt_listener_uses_shared_hash_cn_for_authenticated_log_field`).

- **HTTP HMAC signing binds method + path into the canonical signed payload (closes #747, refs IMPROVEMENT-ANALYSIS.md F-47)** — extends `rustgate_http::auth::AuthState::apply` (and the underlying `compute_hmac_signature` helper) so the bytes fed into HMAC-SHA256 now follow an AWS SigV4-style canonical layout `<timestamp>.<METHOD>.<path>.<body>` instead of the prior body-only `<timestamp>.<body>`. Pre-fix the signature was endpoint-agnostic — every replay-relevant attribute except the body was unbound from the cryptographic envelope, so a captured request from a compromised webhook URL could be replayed against a different endpoint on the same host (e.g. an authenticated `POST /alert` body re-issued at `POST /shutdown`) and the receiver's HMAC verifier would happily attest the forged request as authentic. The new canonical layout joins each segment with a single `.` byte separator, places the raw body bytes last (so a body containing `.` characters remains unambiguous), and uppercases the HTTP method at the call site (`reqwest::Method::as_str()` already returns the canonical uppercase form). The `apply` signature changes to `apply(builder, method: &str, path: &str, body: &[u8])`; the only in-tree caller is `rustgate_http::publisher::send_request`, which threads `target.method.as_str()` and a new `target.url_path: String` (cached at `TargetState` construction by parsing the configured URL once with `reqwest::Url::parse`, fall-back to empty on the unreachable parse-failure branch — empty path produces a signature that simply cannot match any well-formed receiver reconstruction, so no silent-bypass risk). A symmetric `verify_hmac_signature(secret, method, path, body, timestamp, presented)` helper lands alongside the signer with a constant-time comparison via `subtle::ConstantTimeEq::ct_eq` per the workspace credential-equality discipline; the helper is `cfg_attr(not(test), allow(dead_code))`-gated as a forward reference until an inbound webhook receiver crate consumes it. The function-level rustdoc on `compute_hmac_signature` now spells out the four-segment canonical layout and the SigV4 alignment so a future contributor reading just the helper sees the full security contract (timestamp → freshness, method → semantics, path → endpoint, body → payload integrity). **WIRE-FORMAT BREAK — read this before upgrading**: a sender on the new canonical layout produces signatures that an old receiver (still reconstructing `<timestamp>.<body>`) will reject as forged, and an old sender produces signatures the new receiver rejects for the symmetric reason. Operators running mixed-version webhook fleets MUST coordinate the upgrade — there is no transitional dual-format mode, and there cannot be one without re-introducing the very replay vector this change closes (a verifier that accepts both layouts can be tricked into matching the body-only format on a request the new sender intended to bind to `/alert`). For deployments where the receiver is operator-controlled, upgrade the receiver first (it stays compatible with old senders during the rollout window because the receiver doesn't *initiate* signed requests), then upgrade senders. For deployments calling out to third-party webhook endpoints (Splunk HEC, Elastic, Loki, custom alerting), confirm the receiving service has been updated to the canonical layout before flipping the sender — every call will fail HMAC verification until both sides are aligned. Test coverage adds 5 unit tests in `auth.rs::tests` pinning the contract: `hmac_signed_payload_includes_method_and_path` (the canonical bytes spec mirror — fails if any segment is reordered or dropped), `hmac_replay_to_different_path_rejected` (the load-bearing security regression — sign with `/alert`, verify with `/shutdown`, assert reject), `hmac_replay_with_different_method_rejected` (the verb-binding mirror — sign with POST, verify as GET, assert reject), `hmac_round_trip_succeeds_for_matching_method_path_body_timestamp` (happy-path regression guard so the load-bearing tests can't pass on a verifier that always returns false), and `hmac_constant_time_compare_used` (defense-in-depth — confirms last-byte mismatch and all-zero digest both reject, plus a source-introspection assertion that pins `subtle::ConstantTimeEq::ct_eq` is used at the comparison site so a future refactor cannot silently regress to `==`). Crate test count goes from 263 to 268 (+5). The legacy in-place tests (`hmac_signature_known_vector`, `hmac_signature_empty_body`, `hmac_signature_deterministic`, `hmac_different_data_different_signature`, `hmac_different_timestamp_different_signature`, plus the `apply`-path tests) are updated to thread method+path through every call site so a future contributor cannot accidentally restore the old body-only signature without one of the existing tests failing first.

- **MAVLink frame codec defaults to v2 + signature required, rejects v1, and panic-proofs the CRC-EXTRA lookup (closes #752, refs IMPROVEMENT-ANALYSIS.md F-72 and F-73)** — closes both sub-items of #752 in one focused change. **F-72 (default-secure signing posture)**: `rustgate_mavlink::MavlinkFrameCodec::default()` now starts with `require_signing = true` and `allow_v1 = false` — unsigned v2 frames (those whose `INCOMPAT & SIGNED` bit is clear) and v1 frames (which have no signature field at all) are rejected at the framing layer with the typed `MavlinkError::UnsignedFrameRejected` and `MavlinkError::V1FrameRejected` errors before the payload is buffered. The previous behaviour silently accepted both wire forms and left signing verification to a never-arrived future layer, which let an attacker who could inject MAVLink frames forge identities without crossing any cryptographic boundary at all. Operators running mixed fleets opt back in via `MavlinkFrameCodec::with_allow_v1(true)` and `MavlinkFrameCodec::with_require_signing(false)` (both stance-setters, so the choice is explicit at wiring time, not silently inherited from a default), and the same opt-out is exposed at the binary surface through new CLI flags `--mavlink-allow-v1 <bool>` (env `RUSTGATE_MAVLINK_ALLOW_V1`, default `false`) and `--mavlink-require-signing <bool>` (env `RUSTGATE_MAVLINK_REQUIRE_SIGNING`, default `true`). Rejection sites consume only the offending magic byte (not the whole header), so a single hostile v1 prefix cannot stall a stream that delivers a valid signed v2 frame immediately afterwards — covered by `strict_codec_rejects_v1_and_recovers_on_following_v2_signed_frame` and the matching unsigned-v2 recovery test. The codec also gains a new `OnMavlinkRejection` callback (`Arc<dyn Fn(RejectionReason) + Send + Sync>`) wired through the new `with_on_rejection` builder; the listener crate (future PR) installs a closure that emits the matching `audit::mavlink_v1_rejected` and `audit::mavlink_unsigned_rejected` events (already in `rustgate-core`) through `rustgate_core::audit`, plus a forthcoming audit fn for the unknown-msg-id case, and increments a Prometheus counter labelled by reason, so a SIEM correlating signing-rollout progress can distinguish "fleet still has v1 senders" from "signing rollout incomplete on v2" from "non-standard dialect or attacker fishing for unknown IDs". The `RejectionReason` enum is `#[non_exhaustive]` so a future class (e.g. CRC mismatch once the signing layer lands) can be added without a breaking API change. **F-73 (CRC-EXTRA panic-source elimination)**: a new `rustgate_mavlink::crc_extra` module ships an `Option`-returning `crc_extra(msg_id: u32) -> Option<u8>` lookup against a static table of common-dialect message IDs. The decoder now extracts every accepted frame's `MSG_ID` and consults the table; a frame whose ID is not in the table surfaces as the typed `MavlinkError::UnknownMessageId { id }` error WITHOUT allocation and WITHOUT panic. The pre-this-PR threat shape was: any future CRC-EXTRA implementation that reached the lookup via `unwrap()` on `HashMap::get` (the canonical Rust pattern) would have been a panic gadget — a hostile sender streaming frames with random `MSG_ID` values could panic the receiver in a release build (`unwrap_used = "deny"` is the workspace lint, but a future PR could regress) or, if the lookup defaulted to `entry().or_insert()`, drive a per-frame allocation that exhausts memory. The shipped lookup is allocation-free by construction (a `&'static [(u32, u8)]` slice with linear scan, no `HashMap` involved) and the `Option` return is the type-system enforcement that "unknown ID" is always a real outcome the caller has to handle — there is no `unwrap()` to regress to. The static table covers HEARTBEAT (MSG_ID 0), the common-dialect position/attitude/command frames the rustgate workspace inspects, and the v2 SETUP_SIGNING message (MSG_ID 256) so an operator rotating signing keys cannot lock themselves out by having the key-rotation message itself rejected as "unknown". Adding a new ID is a one-line PR. **Test coverage delta**: 64 → 84 tests in the `rustgate-mavlink` crate (+20). New tests pin the F-72 spec mirror set (`v1_frame_rejected_by_default`, `v1_frame_accepted_with_allow_v1_opt_in`, `v2_unsigned_frame_rejected_by_default`, `v2_unsigned_frame_accepted_with_require_signing_false`), the F-73 spec mirror set (`unknown_msg_id_rejected_without_panic`, `unknown_msg_id_rejection_burst_does_not_panic_on_release`), the rejection-observer wiring contract (`mavlink_unsigned_rejected_audit_event_fires_on_v1`, `rejection_observer_fires_for_unsigned_v2`, `rejection_observer_fires_for_unknown_msg_id`, `rejection_observer_quiet_on_clean_decode`), the CRC-EXTRA table invariants (`known_message_ids_resolve`, `unknown_message_id_returns_none_no_panic`, `table_is_sorted_by_msg_id`, `table_has_no_duplicate_msg_ids`, `lookup_is_allocation_free_in_principle`), and the new `parse_msg_id` helper's contract (`parse_msg_id_handles_unknown_magic`, `parse_msg_id_v1_extracts_byte_5`, `parse_msg_id_v2_extracts_24_bit_little_endian`); the error variant tests pin `unknown_message_id_display_includes_id` and `from_unknown_message_id_into_io_error_is_invalid_data`. Three new server CLI tests (`mavlink_signing_defaults_are_secure`, `mavlink_allow_v1_overridable_via_cli`, `mavlink_require_signing_overridable_via_cli`) pin the binary-surface knobs and the `cli_env_vars_declared` test learns about `RUSTGATE_MAVLINK_REQUIRE_SIGNING` and `RUSTGATE_MAVLINK_ALLOW_V1`. **Out of scope**: the listener crate that drives the codec, threads the rejection callback through to `rustgate_core::audit::mavlink_*_rejected`, and increments a Prometheus counter labelled by `RejectionReason` is queued as a separate follow-up PR (the listener wiring will compose with the existing `OnMavlinkHeartbeat` plumbing landed in #1183); the CRC-16/MCRF4XX trailer verification itself (which uses the `crc_extra` byte the new module exposes) lives in the future signing module along with the replay-timestamp monotonicity check. This PR ships the framing-layer signing policy and the panic-source elimination — two security surfaces that are correct without the listener and that would be silently regressable if deferred until the listener was ready.
- **Sanitize user-controlled strings at the audit-emission boundary (closes #725)** — pushes the `sanitize_for_log` discipline into `rustgate_core::audit` itself so every audit helper now scrubs control characters, newlines, and ANSI CSI escape sequences from its `&str` parameters before the underlying `audit!` macro emits the structured tracing record. Previously the `sanitize_for_log` helper existed in `rustgate_core::sanitize` but was applied inconsistently at call sites: some crates wrapped CN, group, topic, error, and resource-id strings explicitly (e.g. `rustgate-mqtt`'s session.rs, `rustgate-federation`'s v2/server.rs), but the audit functions themselves accepted raw `&str` and trusted callers — which meant a new caller, or any of the dozens of existing call sites that already forgot, could let an attacker-controlled CN with an embedded newline forge a fake log line visible to a SIEM operator. Concrete forge payload before this PR: a client whose enrollment certificate carries a CN of `alice\nattacker_log_line` calls into `audit::client_disconnected("alice\nattacker_log_line", session_id=1)` and the resulting JSON record splits across two log lines, the second of which the SIEM parses as a forged event. The fix is defense-in-depth: every audit function in the module's API now binds each user-controlled `&str` parameter to a sanitized `String` local before passing it to the macro, so even a brand-new caller that forgets to pre-sanitize cannot produce a forgeable record. The wire format is unchanged for any input that was already free of control characters — `sanitize_for_log` replaces dangerous bytes with the Unicode replacement codepoint U+FFFD, which is a single Unicode scalar value and round-trips cleanly through serde-json serialization, so the audit-record JSON shape and field types remain identical. For inputs that DID contain control characters, the wire-format change is exactly the intended mitigation (one U+FFFD per dangerous byte). Sanitization is idempotent: existing call sites that already wrap with `sanitize_for_log` (the pre-PR discipline pattern) continue to work unchanged because running sanitization twice produces the same string as running it once. Numeric, boolean, and typed fields (`PeerId`, `SocketAddr`, `bool`, `u8`/`u32`/`u64`/`usize`/`i64`) bypass sanitization because their `Display`/`Debug` impls cannot produce attacker-controlled control bytes. Functions touched: 32 audit helpers across the categories named in `shared-infrastructure.md` (`client_*`, `connection_rejected`, `tls_accept_error`, `negotiation_result`, `federation_*`, `enrollment_*`, `crl_reload_*`, `cert_rotation_*`, `spiffe_svid_*`, `authz_*`, `tls_handshake_failed`, `rate_limit_triggered`, `chain_*`, `server_started`, `http_*`, `verifier_rebuild_failed`, `store_forward_*`, `mavlink_unsigned_rejected`, `mavlink_v1_rejected`, `mqtt_will_published`); five purely-numeric helpers (`federation_circuit_tripped`, `federation_circuit_recovered`, `mavlink_heartbeat_received`) need no string handling and are unchanged. The `federation_group_claim_rejected` helper additionally sanitizes each entry of its `claimed_groups: &[String]` before the `?val` debug-format emission so a hostile peer cannot smuggle CR/LF through the wire-claimed group list. Module-level `//!` docs explain the boundary discipline and document sanitization-vs-disclosure as orthogonal concerns (e.g. `authz_classified_delivery` keeps plaintext-CN identity attribution for forensics by design — the access-control of the audit sink, not log-injection hardening, is the disclosure control there). Test coverage: four new tests in `audit::tests::sanitization` capture the audit-target tracing output, parse the JSON record, and pin the contract — `audit_sanitizes_cn_with_newline_injection` (the canonical log-forging payload), `audit_sanitizes_cn_with_control_char_injection` (C0 control bytes 0x01-0x03), `audit_sanitizes_group_with_log_forging_payload` (CR/LF + ANSI CSI), and `audit_does_not_double_sanitize_already_safe_input` (idempotency). Pre-existing call-site sanitization (e.g. `rustgate-mqtt`'s `sanitize_for_log(&will.topic)` before passing to `mqtt_will_published`) keeps working unchanged thanks to idempotency; new code does not need to wrap. Crate test count for `rustgate-core` goes from 36 to 40 audit tests.
- **Rate-limit position replay per CN on reconnect (closes #724)** — closes the flap-loop authz-DoS vector the security audit of PR #716 (`feat/authz-obligations`) flagged. `Router::replay_positions` runs the Send + Receive PEP for every cached position before delivery; before this change the replay path had no per-CN gate, so a client flap-looping (connect → disconnect → connect) drove the authz engine at an uncapped rate proportional to `cache_size × reconnect_rate` — a 10k-position cache with a 10×/sec reconnect produced 200,000 authz evaluations/sec from a single client and crowded out evaluations for legitimate traffic. The fix adds a per-CN [`TokenBucket`] gate (the existing `rustgate_resilience::token_bucket` primitive) keyed on the reconnecting client's CN. Each call to `replay_positions` consumes one token; when the bucket is empty the replay is skipped entirely with a `tracing::warn!` line and a structured `position_replay.rate_limited` audit event (PII-safe `hash_cn` for the session field, plus `attempted` and `allowed` counts so SIEMs can track flap-loop magnitude over time). Defaults are operationally permissive — `rate_per_sec=100`, `burst=200` — chosen so a normal-cadence reconnect is never limited (a single replay is always served by the burst) while a flap-loop attack is bounded at 200 replays/sec instead of 200k authz evals/sec. The bucket map is a `parking_lot::Mutex<HashMap<String, Arc<TokenBucket>>>` that grows lazily on first replay per CN and is **pruned on session disconnect** in `Router::unregister` so a CN-churning attacker that opens and closes thousands of distinct CNs cannot inflate the entry table without bound (the `position_replay_rate_limit_token_bucket_pruned_on_disconnect` test pins this contract). Operators who need different defaults can override via `--position-replay-rate-per-sec` (env `RUSTGATE_POSITION_REPLAY_RATE_PER_SEC`) and `--position-replay-burst` (env `RUSTGATE_POSITION_REPLAY_BURST`); the CLI knobs flow through the existing `defaults < file < env < CLI flags` precedence chain via the `define_config_file!` macro and `Router::with_position_replay_limit`. New test coverage: 5 router unit tests (`replay_positions_consumes_tokens` pins burst exhaustion, `replay_positions_refills_over_time` pins TokenBucket refill semantics, `replay_positions_per_cn_isolation` pins one CN's exhaustion does not affect another's bucket, `replay_positions_default_rate_permissive_for_normal_use` pins the operator-safe defaults, `position_replay_rate_limit_token_bucket_pruned_on_disconnect` pins the prune-on-disconnect anti-DoS invariant — the existing `replay_positions_filters_by_group` and `replay_positions_allows_shared_group` continue to pass under the default-permissive config), 1 audit-trail integration test in `crates/rustgate-transport/tests/position_replay_rate_limit_audit.rs` (`replay_positions_emits_audit_on_rate_limit` runs in its own integration-test binary so the thread-local audit subscriber does not race other in-process subscribers, parses the `position_replay.rate_limited` JSON line, and pins target/level/event_type/action/result/allowed/session/attempted fields against the documented contract), and 1 audit-helper smoke test in `rustgate-core::audit::tests::rate_limit::test_position_replay_rate_limited`. Net delta: +7 tests across the workspace.

- **Harden TAK protocol-version negotiation against empty-string forced-upgrade and slow-negotiate exhaustion (closes #754, refs IMPROVEMENT-ANALYSIS.md F-64 and F-65)** — closes both sub-items of #754 in one focused change. **F-64 (forced-upgrade via empty version strings)**: `rustgate_proto::negotiate::parse_tak_request` previously treated an empty `min_proto_version` or `max_proto_version` (the proto3 default for unset fields) as "accepts anything" and silently mapped the missing bound to the server's `MIN_PROTO_VERSION` / `MAX_PROTO_VERSION`. A malicious client could therefore force negotiation to `MAX_PROTO_VERSION` by sending two empty strings, bypassing any deployment that had narrowed the allowed range on the client side. The hardened parser now requires both fields to be present and parseable as `u32`; empty or whitespace-only values surface as a new typed `ProtoError::BlankVersion(field)` variant rather than negotiating to a forced upgrade. The session-layer caller logs the rejection through `tracing::warn!` with the peer CN routed through `rustgate_core::sanitize::sanitize_for_log` so an attacker cannot inject CR/LF into the structured log field. The integration and unit tests that pinned the legacy "empty versions accepted" behaviour are flipped to assert rejection, and four new unit tests cover the empty-min, empty-max, whitespace-only, and happy-path cases (the last is a regression guard so the hardening cannot break legitimate clients). **F-65 (slow-negotiate handshake-slot exhaustion)**: the previous `NEGOTIATION_TIMEOUT = Duration::from_secs(30)` was a `const` baked into `read_tak_request`. Combined with `rustgate_transport::DEFAULT_MAX_HANDSHAKES` (~100–256 concurrent slots in production deployments), a mass slow-negotiate attack — clients that complete the TLS handshake but then sit on the negotiation read indefinitely — could park every handshake slot for a full 30-second window. The default is now `NEGOTIATION_TIMEOUT_DEFAULT_SECS = 10` (a healthy TAK negotiation completes in well under a second, so 10s is comfortable for real clients while tightening the abuse window threefold), and operators can override it through the new `--negotiation-timeout-secs` CLI flag (env: `RUSTGATE_NEGOTIATION_TIMEOUT_SECS`). The new value is threaded from `Cli` into `SessionDeps::negotiation_timeout` and consumed by `rustgate_proto::read_tak_request_with_timeout`, a new public entrypoint that takes an explicit `Duration`; `read_tak_request` keeps its old signature and now delegates to the with-timeout variant using `DEFAULT_NEGOTIATION_TIMEOUT`. The CLI carries the literal `default_value_t = 10` so the binary still compiles without `--features proto`, and a `cli_negotiation_timeout_default_matches_proto_const` test (gated on `feature = "proto"`) asserts the literal agrees with the authoritative `rustgate_proto::NEGOTIATION_TIMEOUT_DEFAULT_SECS` so a future single-source bump in the proto crate is reflected at the binary surface. Zero is rejected by `parse_nonzero_u64` (zero would short-circuit every negotiation and is never the operator intent). New test coverage: four `parse_tak_request_*` unit tests in `negotiate::tests` for F-64, one `negotiation_timeout_default_is_ten_seconds` regression-guard test, plus three CLI tests (`cli_negotiation_timeout_override`, `cli_rejects_zero_negotiation_timeout`, `cli_negotiation_timeout_default_matches_proto_const`) and an env-var presence assertion in `cli_env_vars_declared`.
- **NATS publisher echo prevention is now case-insensitive (closes #748)** — the `NatsPublisher::publish` echo guard previously compared `msg.metadata.source_protocol == "nats"` exactly, so a federated message whose `source_protocol` had been normalized to `"NATS"` or `"Nats"` by an upstream peer slipped past the check and was re-published onto NATS — forming a publish loop between rustgate and a federated NATS bridge that would only break under topology change. The check now uses `eq_ignore_ascii_case("nats")`, matching the `rustgate-http` publisher's discipline (which had already adopted the case-insensitive comparison precisely to defend against inconsistent casing across transport adapters), and emits a `tracing::debug!` line on trigger so operators can correlate echo-prevention drops against incoming source-protocol casing in their logs. Three regression tests pin the contract end-to-end against a real `nats-server` subprocess via the existing `require_nats!` skip-if-absent harness: `echo_prevention_matches_uppercase_source_protocol` exercises the literal `"NATS"` case, `echo_prevention_matches_mixed_case` exercises `"Nats"`, and `echo_prevention_does_not_block_non_nats_sources` pins the negative — messages from MQTT, federation, TCP and other transports must still be republished to NATS, since over-blocking would silently break legitimate cross-transport routing. No data-loss exposure existed prior — only the loop-amplification path — but the bypass would compound under a federated bridge configured to renormalize protocol identifiers.

- **MQTT Maximum Packet Size advertisement + structured DISCONNECT 0x95 on oversize (closes #753, refs #880)** — closes the F-58 production hazard the security label on #753 calls out: rustgate's MQTT broker enforced a 16 MiB packet cap at the parse layer (`PacketCodec::new(stream, max_packet_size)`) but never told the client about it. MQTT 5.0 §3.2.2.3.6 says CONNACK MUST advertise `Maximum Packet Size` so a compliant client short-circuits oversized publishes locally rather than sending a 200 MB payload that gets silently dropped server-side; without the advertisement the spec default is "no limit beyond the protocol's remaining-length encoding ceiling" and a well-behaved client has no way to know what the broker will accept. This PR ships both halves of the spec mitigation in one focused change. **CONNACK side**: `write_connack_v5` (the only v5 CONNACK emission path in the crate) now unconditionally sets `properties.max_packet_size = Some(self.max_packet_size as u32)` on every CONNACK — Success, NotAuthorized, ImplementationSpecificError, TopicNameInvalid — so a client that gets refused for any reason still learns the broker's cap before the connection drops. The configured cap saturates at `u32::MAX` rather than refusing to set the property if the operator's input exceeds the wire field (a 4-byte integer per spec); the saturation preserves the "broker has a limit" signal even on misconfigured input, and in practice the default 16 MiB is well below the u32 ceiling so this never trips. **Inbound rejection side**: `try_parse` and `try_parse_connect` (both protocol arms — v3.1.1 and v5.0) now map `mqttbytes::Error::PayloadSizeLimitExceeded(size)` to the typed `MqttError::PacketTooLarge { size, max }` variant instead of folding it into `MqttError::Malformed(...)`. The typed mapping is what makes the DISCONNECT 0x95 path reachable: when the read loop returns `Err(PacketTooLarge)` from `mqtt_read_loop`, the session loop in `run_session` writes a `Disconnect { reason_code: PacketTooLarge, properties: None }` packet to the writer half before dropping the TLS stream — gives the client a structured reason (MQTT 5.0 §3.14.2.1 reason code 0x95) instead of an unexplained TCP RST. The DISCONNECT emission is best-effort; the `tokio::select!` between read and write loops cancels the write-loop future on read-loop error and tokio I/O is not cancel-safe, so the writer-half state is unspecified at the moment of read-error. The integration test pins both happy-path (DISCONNECT arrives and parses) and fallback-path (clean EOF) outcomes and rejects the only failure mode that matters — a hung connection with no diagnostic, which is exactly the F-58 production shape #753 was filed against. v3.1.1 has no server-initiated DISCONNECT packet by spec, so the v4 path simply drops the connection (the typed `PacketTooLarge` mapping still fires for accurate logging / metrics distinguishing "client too noisy" from "client emitted garbage" in the operator's dashboard). New test coverage: four unit tests in `packet.rs::tests` (`v5_connack_advertises_configured_maximum_packet_size` builds and parses a CONNACK with the property to pin the wire format, `try_parse_v5_size_violation_returns_packet_too_large` and `try_parse_v311_size_violation_returns_packet_too_large` exercise the post-handshake size-cap rejection in both protocol arms, `try_parse_connect_rejects_oversized_connect_with_packet_too_large` covers the connect-time symmetry that an oversized CONNECT itself produces the typed variant — `write_v5_to_buf` skips CONNECT in its server-only allowlist so the test serialises via `connect.write` directly), plus a tightened `max_packet_size_rejects_oversized_publish` integration test that drops the previously permissive "any of EOF / read-error / bytes" outcome match in favour of a streaming parse loop that demands either a structured DISCONNECT 0x95 or stream close (no other packet types accepted, no hung connection accepted) and asserts the CONNACK property echoes the configured 64-byte cap end-to-end. Crate test count goes from 178 to 182. **Out of scope**: Receive Maximum (§3.2.2.3.3 flow control) and Topic Alias Maximum (§3.2.2.3.8) — the other two advertised-cap properties — are separate follow-up PRs; this change only addresses the security-labelled item. Builds on the v5-CONNACK-properties scaffolding already in place from #1146 (retain), #1150 (will), #1153 (retain hooks), and #1154 (will audit), and closes the security-labelled audit item from the broader MQTT production-completeness work in #880.

### Added

- **Criterion benchmark for router fanout hot path (closes #785)** — adds `crates/rustgate-transport/benches/router_fanout.rs` so future PRs touching the router can detect regressions in fanout latency / throughput without an operator having to hand-roll a custom harness. Pre-this-PR the only criterion bench in the transport crate was `benches/codec.rs`, which exercises the length-prefixed and XML-stream codecs but never goes through `Router::route_for_egress` — meaning the cross-cutting cost of dispatching one routed message to N session channels (the path every NATS / federation / HTTP / MQTT egress depends on) was invisible to local profiling and to any "did this refactor get faster or slower" loop. The new harness measures three destination shapes covering the full router-state-shape surface: (1) `Destination::Group("alpha")` parameterised over `[1, 10, 100, 1000]` subscribers via `bench_with_input`, the canonical group-fanout cost curve called out in the issue and the shape that scales linearly with the membership-set size of the addressed group; (2) `Destination::Broadcast` parameterised over the same subscriber-count sweep with each subscriber holding a unique singleton group, so a broadcast visits every group in the engine's group map and exercises the full session iteration path rather than the single-group shortcut; (3) `Destination::Direct(target_identity)` as a single-recipient floor for routing cost when no fanout is involved at all — useful as a reference point for what fraction of the group/broadcast cost is dispatch overhead vs. actual fan-out work. The hot path under test is `Router::route_for_egress` (not `Router::route`), matching the project rule that egress forwarders MUST consume the post-Send-PEP form so that data-plane obligations such as `Obligation::MaskPoint` and `Obligation::MaskPayload` are applied to the local-fanout copy AND to the egress copy uniformly — a regression that quietly broke this method's fast path would otherwise manifest as cross-cutting NATS / federation / HTTP / MQTT egress latency without any per-bridge unit-level test triggering. **Construction**: each scenario builds a fresh `Router::new()`, registers the sender plus the parameterised number of subscribers (each with their own bounded `mpsc` channel pair sized at `4 × (PRIORITY_CHANNEL_CAPACITY + NORMAL_CHANNEL_CAPACITY)` for headroom over the criterion warm-up + measurement burst), and spawns a per-session drainer task on the same `current_thread` tokio runtime so that `try_send` never trips the `SessionHandle` consecutive-drops circuit breaker mid-measurement. Channel headroom plus an active drainer is the right shape here because a smaller channel under criterion's measurement burst would surface as `try_send` failures inflating the reported routing latency with circuit-breaker accounting, and an unbounded channel would unbalance the bench against the actual `mpsc::channel(N)` shape every production session uses. The bench message is a 256-byte `MessageType::Chat` payload (rides the normal-priority channel; the priority channel is reserved for `Position` / `Alert` and would skew drainer wakeup patterns across the three scenarios), constructed fresh per iteration so the bench measures dispatch + per-recipient `try_send` + obligation-application + `Arc::clone`, not a frozen `RoutableMessage::clone`. **No baseline numbers are committed** — operators run criterion locally for tuning, matching the existing `codec.rs` discipline. The benchmark is intentionally NOT gated in CI by an absolute-threshold guard; criterion's per-run noise floor on shared CI runners is too high to support a sub-microsecond latency budget without false positives, and the PR template's own `cargo bench --quick` smoke is the right stop-gap for "this still compiles and runs" coverage. Operators investigating a suspected regression diff `target/criterion/router_fanout_*/base/estimates.json` against a fresh run on the same hardware. **Wiring**: the workspace already declared `criterion = { version = "0.8", features = ["html_reports"] }`; this PR adds the `async_tokio` feature to the `rustgate-transport` dev-dep override (`criterion = { workspace = true, features = ["async_tokio"] }`) so `b.to_async(&runtime).iter(|| async { ... })` resolves to the tokio AsyncExecutor impl, and adds the `[[bench]] name = "router_fanout"` entry to the crate manifest beside the existing `codec` bench. The bench file carries `#![allow(clippy::panic, clippy::unwrap_used, unused_results)]` per the project's bench-file convention and stays free of any production code change. The benchmark's shape — three destination scenarios with a parameterised subscriber-count sweep — is what's load-bearing for regression detection; absolute numbers depend on the hardware and are intentionally not pinned in either the source or the changelog. References IMPROVEMENT-ANALYSIS.md F-125.
- **Graceful TLS certificate rotation integration test (closes #790)** — pre-this-PR, `crates/rustgate-transport/src/cert_reloader.rs` carried unit tests that exercised the `RwLock`-backed swap mechanism in isolation but no integration test bound a live `TlsListener` through `build_reloadable_server_config`, drove a real client handshake against it, rotated the on-disk material, and asserted the next handshake observed the new cert while the previously established TLS session kept working. Operators have flagged cert rotation as a recurring source of incident pain (the reloader runs on every production deployment but the swap path was only verified by direct unit calls), so this PR pins the full hot-path against regression with five integration scenarios in `crates/rustgate-transport/tests/cert_rotation.rs`: (1) `rotation_swaps_server_cert_for_new_connections` rotates the cert files on disk, calls `CertReloader::reload`, and asserts the next client handshake presents a different leaf-cert serial than the pre-rotation handshake observed; (2) `rotation_does_not_drop_in_flight_connections` opens a TLS stream on cert A, rotates to cert B, and asserts a second `write_all` on the pre-rotation stream still succeeds (TLS session state is bound to the cert active at handshake time, so the rotation must not tear down established sessions); (3) `rotation_failure_keeps_old_cert_active` writes garbage PEM into the cert file, asserts `reload()` returns `Err`, asserts subsequent handshakes still present cert A's serial, and verifies the audit subsystem emitted a `cert.rotation_failed` event with `action="rotate"`/`result="failure"`; (4) `rotation_emits_audit_on_success` pins the on-the-wire shape of the `cert.rotated` event after a successful rotation — `target=audit`, `action=rotate`, `result=success`, and `new_serial` matching the cert observed on the next handshake — so SIEM correlation tools can rely on the field names being stable; (5) `rotation_with_concurrent_handshakes_does_not_race` spawns five concurrent client handshake tasks, lands a rotation while they are in flight, and asserts each task's handshake completed observing *either* cert A's serial or cert B's serial — never a torn read of the underlying `Arc<CertifiedKey>`. Scenario (5) is the regression guard for the `RwLock` read discipline documented in `.claude/rules/shared-infrastructure.md` (cf. the `ArcSwap` `Guard` pattern used elsewhere in the router); a regression that introduced an `await` boundary inside the resolver's read path would surface here as either a panicked spawn task or a third unexpected serial value. Audit assertions reuse the `tracing-subscriber` JSON-layer + `MakeWriter` capture pattern already in use across `tests/store_forward_*_audit.rs`, scoped to the `audit` target so non-audit telemetry does not pollute the snapshot. The fixture binds an ephemeral `127.0.0.1:0` port (no hardcoded ports), generates all material via `rustgate_test_utils::TestCa`, drains its accept loop on `JoinHandle::abort()` at teardown, and stays under the test-utils `unsafe_code = "forbid"` posture. Test count delta on the `rustgate-transport` crate's `cert_rotation` integration binary: +5 named scenarios alongside the pre-existing 2 retained guards (`reload_unchanged_returns_false`, `reload_corrupted_cert_returns_error`), bringing the binary to 7 tests. No production-code changes — the reloader, listener, and audit helpers are all exercised through their existing public surfaces.
- **`rustgate check-config` dry-run subcommand (closes #793)** — new diagnostic that loads and validates a rustgate TOML config without starting any listeners, NATS connections, federation discovery, or other I/O. Wired into CI pipelines and `helm test` hooks where the goal is to confirm a rendered config would start cleanly before the pod is allowed to bind ports. The subcommand exits `0` for a valid config, `1` for a config that loaded but failed cross-field validation (range error, federation prerequisites, ACL reload-interval guard, etc.), and `2` for a config that could not even be read (path missing, permission denied, malformed TOML). Output formats: human-readable plain text by default, and `--json` emitting `{status, config_path, strict, errors, warnings}` for machine integration. The optional `--strict` flag additionally walks every cert / ACL / authz / secret-bearing file the config references; a missing referenced file becomes a hard error, and (on Unix) any secret-bearing file (TLS key, metrics token, CA private key, archive key) without `0o077`-conforming permissions is rejected with the same wording the runtime `read_secret_file` helper uses so the dry-run and real-start verdicts agree. Crucially the subcommand never constructs a tokio runtime, never dials NATS, and never binds a TCP listener — a meta-test (`check_config_does_not_bind_listeners`) grabs an ephemeral port, runs check-config against a config configured to bind that exact port, and asserts the port is still rebindable after the run. New module `rustgate_server::diagnostics::check_config` ships behind the existing diagnostic-subcommand pattern (parallel to `cert-info`, `crl-info`, `check-cert-expiry`, `test-connection`, `generate-config`). Net test delta: +17 unit tests in `crates/rustgate-server/src/diagnostics/check_config.rs` covering the report shape, exit-code contract, strict-mode permission audit, missing-file detection, JSON serialization stability, the human-render shape, the warnings surface, and the no-listeners meta-test, plus +8 integration tests in `crates/rustgate-server/tests/cli_parsing.rs` driving the real binary as a subprocess so the clap dispatch wiring is exercised end-to-end.
- **Operator-initiated graceful drain endpoint `POST /api/drain` (closes #791, completes #818)** — closes the canary-deployment surface gap that #818 left open: the helm `values-canary.yaml` preStop hook curls `http://localhost:9090/api/drain` to signal a graceful drain before SIGTERM, but pre-this-PR no such endpoint existed and the curl call was `|| true`'d so the actual drain still happened via SIGTERM + SubsystemHandle 5s grace. The operator-visible signal is now real. The endpoint lives alongside every other management API route (`/api/cert/`, `/api/crl/`, `/api/dedup/`, `/api/clients/`, `/api/dlq/`, `/api/reload`) and follows the same discipline: bearer-token auth via constant-time `subtle::ConstantTimeEq` comparison; fires the same shared `tokio::sync::Notify` shutdown trigger that SIGTERM does, so the existing SubsystemHandle drain runs unchanged (no separate "API drain code path" — the `notify_one()` transitions the accept loop into the same drain code SIGTERM would); returns IMMEDIATELY with `200 OK` and `{"status": "drain_initiated", "source": "api"}` after firing the notify, so the K8s preStop hook can sleep separately for whatever bounded wait is required (the rustgate drain itself runs under SubsystemHandle's 5s grace timeout). New `rustgate_core::audit::admin_drain_triggered(source: &str)` audit helper emits `event_type="admin.drain_triggered"`, `action="drain"`, `result="initiated"` with `source` sanitized at the audit boundary per the #1197 discipline; new `rustgate_admin_drain_triggered_total{source}` Prometheus counter (registered in `rustgate_server::metrics` under the existing OnceLock + accessor pattern) lets SIEM and dashboards distinguish API-initiated drains from SIGTERM-initiated ones, which would otherwise collapse into one indistinguishable stream during a Kubernetes rolling upgrade. The `MgmtApiState` struct gains a new `drain_notify: Arc<tokio::sync::Notify>` field threaded from `main.rs` where the same `Arc` is also captured by `shutdown_signal()` so a single `notify_one()` from either surface unblocks the accept loop. The existing dispatcher in `crates/rustgate-server/src/metrics.rs::serve` was extended to route `/api/drain` (a bare path like `/api/reload`, not a prefix) and `/api/dlq/` to the management handler — `/api/dlq/` was previously declared in `MGMT_PATH_PREFIXES` but missing from the dispatcher's path filter, an unrelated bug this PR clears as a side effect of pinning bare paths via the new `MGMT_EXACT_PATHS` constant. The `helm/values-canary.yaml` preStop hook keeps its `|| true` fallback so the hook stays portable for clusters running without `--mgmt-api-token-file` (in that build the management API is not registered and the curl call would otherwise fail the preStop step). New test coverage: 7 tests in `crates/rustgate-server/src/mgmt_api.rs::tests` (`admin_drain_returns_200_with_valid_token` pins the wire-format envelope and the literal `"drain_initiated"` status string; `admin_drain_returns_401_without_token` pins the bearer-auth boundary so a refactor that moves the auth check out of `handle_request` cannot silently expose drain to anonymous callers; `admin_drain_emits_audit_event` captures the audit-target tracing output via a thread-local subscriber and asserts the event_type / source / action / result fields; `admin_drain_increments_metric` snapshots the counter pre/post and asserts the strict +1 delta on the `source="api"` label; `admin_drain_triggers_shutdown_notify` registers a `notified()` waiter, calls the endpoint, and pins that the waiter observes the wake-up within a 1s bounded timeout — a regression that no-ops the `notify_one()` would hang the test until timeout; `admin_drain_wrong_method_returns_405` pins the `GET` returns 405 not 404 distinction so a script that types the wrong verb gets a precise diagnostic; `admin_drain_does_not_block_on_completion` pins the immediate-return contract via a 100ms wall-clock bound that is two orders of magnitude looser than the actual hot-path latency), 1 test in `crates/rustgate-core/src/audit.rs` smoke-testing the new helper across the documented sources plus boundary inputs, and 1 sanitization test pinning the audit-boundary contract for the `source` field against a CR/LF + ANSI CSI payload. The pre-existing `mgmt_path_prefixes_cover_all_endpoints` test gained two new assertions for the bare paths in the new `MGMT_EXACT_PATHS` constant. Verified end-to-end with `helm template helm -f helm/values-canary.yaml` (clean — the YAML still parses).

- **Helm canary values + reload-rollback observability (closes #818)** — two operational items shipped together because both target the rolling-upgrade lifecycle. (1) **F-142 — `helm/values-canary.yaml`**: a new chart overlay that converts the default Deployment into a manual-canary rolling upgrade with `maxSurge=1` / `maxUnavailable=0` / `minReadySeconds=30` and a preStop drain hook (best-effort POST to the management API drain endpoint with `|| true` so the hook stays portable across rustgate versions, then `sleep 5` so the load balancer can rotate the pod out before SIGTERM). The chart's `helm/templates/deployment.yaml` now reads `deployment.strategy`, `deployment.minReadySeconds`, `deployment.lifecycle`, `deployment.readinessProbe`, `deployment.livenessProbe`, and `podAnnotations` from values, all empty by default so the existing baseline render is byte-identical without the overlay. The overlay also annotates pods with `config.linkerd.io/proxy-await=enabled` and the Prometheus scrape pair so service-mesh canary integration works without further config. Documented in a new top-level `helm/README-canary.md` covering usage, rollback, verification, and Linkerd/Istio integration. Verified end-to-end with `helm template helm -f helm/values-canary.yaml` (clean), `helm template helm -f helm/values-production.yaml -f helm/values-canary.yaml` (production+canary stack — clean), and the default `helm template helm` render (unchanged from pre-this-PR baseline). (2) **F-144 — reload-rollback audit + metric**: a new `rustgate_core::audit::authz_reload_rollback(reason, previous_policy_id)` event paired with a new `rustgate_reload_rollback_total{subsystem}` Prometheus counter (helper: `rustgate_server::metrics::record_reload_rollback("authz")`). Pre-this-PR, when a config hot-reload failed and the broker silently rolled back to the previously installed policy, the operator only learned about the rollback by correlating tracing logs — the metric and audit pair now give SIEM dashboards a single structured signal to alert on (e.g. `rate(rustgate_reload_rollback_total{subsystem="authz"}[5m]) > 0`). Wired at every reload-failure call site in `crates/rustgate-server/src/authz_reloader.rs` (read / parse / validate / compile failures + the spawn-blocking task-panic path) and at the two startup fail-open paths in `crates/rustgate-server/src/main.rs` (Cedar and Native backends). The audit emission follows the boundary-sanitization discipline already established for the sibling `authz_reload_failed` and `authz_reload_success` helpers — both `reason` and the optional `previous_policy_id` are run through `sanitize_for_log` inside the helper before the `tracing::info!` call, so a malicious upstream policy id with embedded newlines or ANSI CSI escapes cannot forge a separate audit line. Test coverage spans (a) the audit-shape contract (`event_type="authz.reload_rollback"`, `action="rollback"`, `result="success"`, both fields rendered as JSON strings via `tracing-subscriber`), (b) the boundary-sanitization contract on both string fields against a CR/LF + CSI payload, (c) the documented Prometheus name and the single `subsystem` label dimension via `Collector::desc()`, and (d) the per-subsystem isolation contract (a `record_reload_rollback("acl")` call must not bleed into the `crl` time series). The pre-existing `authz_reload_failed` event still fires alongside the new rollback event so a SIEM rule can correlate the two by timestamp; the new event is the operator-visible signal that the failure was caught by the rollback safety net rather than by an outage.

- **Store-forward dwell-time observability (closes #729)** — closes the audit-correlation gap where drain records carried only `received_at` and `delivered_at` but no signal for how long a message actually sat in the offline queue. A message could have been routed live for 4h59m and only queued in the last minute, OR could have been queued for the full 5h — the audit record made both indistinguishable, forcing operators to infer queue dwell from two timestamps that happened to bracket several non-queue intervals (live routing, federation hops, transport switch). This PR captures an explicit `queued_at` Unix-millisecond timestamp at admission (in `ClientQueue::enqueue`, before the writer-task hand-off, so the recorded admission time reflects the moment the queue accepted custody rather than when the writer-task happened to commit, which under load can lag by hundreds of milliseconds and would understate dwell), threads it through the on-disk envelope as a new field after `received_at_ms`, and on drain emits both a new `audit::store_forward_drained` event carrying `count`, `dwell_seconds_mean`, `dwell_seconds_min`, `dwell_seconds_max`, `expired_count`, and `tampered_count`, plus a per-message observation through the new `OnDrainObservation` callback that `rustgate-server` wires to the new `rustgate_store_forward_dwell_seconds` Prometheus histogram. The histogram buckets — `[1.0, 10.0, 60.0, 300.0, 1800.0, 7200.0, 21600.0]` seconds — span the operationally meaningful range from sub-second (a client briefly disconnected during a TCP retransmit storm) up to 6 hours (an extended outage); anything above 6h almost certainly means queue retention policy is misconfigured rather than dwell continuing to accumulate, which is a separate signal from "messages rode a long but bounded outage". Per-message observation (not per-batch): a 5h drain of 100 messages records 100 datapoints so the histogram percentiles reflect message experience, not batch experience. **Backward compatibility**: the on-disk envelope version bumps from 1 to 2; the decoder accepts both and falls back `queued_at = received_at` for legacy v1 records, preserving pre-PR audit semantics on existing queues until they cycle to v2-only entries — operators with queues that survived a previous-version restart see the legacy path until the queue drains, with no operational change required. Encoder always emits v2. Audit field names are stable for SIEM correlation; the integration test `tests/store_forward_dwell_audit.rs` pins the JSON shape end-to-end. Test coverage delta: +4 unit tests in `crates/rustgate-transport/src/store_forward.rs::tests` (`admission_records_queued_at_timestamp` round-trips through the real writer task and redb; `drain_dwell_histogram_observes_drain_event` pins per-message callback cardinality; `legacy_record_without_queued_at_falls_back_to_received_at` pins the v1→v2 fallback) plus +1 new integration test (`tests/store_forward_dwell_audit.rs::drain_audit_includes_dwell_seconds`) pinning the JSON-shape audit emission, plus +1 smoke test in `crates/rustgate-core/src/audit.rs` covering the new helper's degenerate inputs.
- **Audit-chain corruption verification runbook (closes #774)** — adds `docs/runbooks/audit-chain-corruption.md` documenting how operators respond when `rustgate-core::audit_chain` verification fails. Covers detection signals (`VerifyError::HashMismatch`, `VerifyError::PrevMismatch`, `VerifyError::MissingSeq`, `VerifyError::Gap`, `VerifyError::InvalidSeq`) emitted by `verify_audit_log()` at startup or from offline runs; a three-step diagnostic decision tree that separates a torn write from an unexpected shutdown (failure on the LAST record only, recoverable via `read_chain_tip` truncation or an offline `truncate -s` on the last newline) from an external rotation event (failure near the start of the new segment with mismatched `prev_sha256` against `GENESIS_PREV` and `seq` not equal to `1`, recoverable by anchoring the previous segment via `write_anchor` and documenting the cutover in a secondary log) from genuine tamper or hardware corruption (failure in the middle of a continuous write window with no restart or rotation event, NOT silently recoverable); offline verification with code samples for `verify_audit_log()` plus an example `VerifyReport` walkthrough showing healthy output, torn-write `InvalidJson`, and tampered-file `HashMismatch` cases; recovery procedures per scenario including the forensic-preservation discipline for tamper (`cp --preserve=all`, `stat`, `sha256sum` for chain-of-custody, escalate to security team, do NOT continue writing — start a fresh chain at a new path); and SIEM alert design guidance covering the high-severity `audit_chain_corrupt` page, a five-minute `verify_audit_log_failure_count` secondary, and an `audit_seq_regression` watermark alert that catches the tail-truncation-and-rewrite attack the hash chain alone cannot detect. Cross-references the implementation in `crates/rustgate-core/src/audit_chain.rs` and the broader runbook collection. Pure documentation — no behavioural change.
- **Customer-facing `SECURITY.md` threat model (closes #808)** — adds a top-level `SECURITY.md` documenting the trust model (mTLS root, CA/CRL trust path, mTLS/route-dispatch boundary, SPIFFE workload identity, federation V1/V2 peer authentication), the in-scope attacker capabilities the project mitigates (network-level MITM, compromised peer, resource exhaustion, log injection, timing side-channels in credential comparison, wire-format fuzzing), explicit out-of-scope items (compromised host OS, CPU side-channels, operator misconfiguration, insider threats, physical attacks, volumetric DDoS, classifications above CUI), per-crate attack surface for all 14 production crates with notable hardening calls (`MAX_FRAME_SIZE`, `HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT`, `ConnRateLimiter`, `subtle::ConstantTimeEq`, fuzz targets), data-classification guidance (tactical and SBU/CUI in scope; S/TS/SCI explicit non-goal), known-safe deployment patterns (mTLS + CRL refresh, dedup, rate limiting, audit chain, jemalloc, federation peer allowlists) with a representative production CLI invocation, and a responsible-disclosure section pointing at GitHub Security Advisories with a `security@rustgate.example` placeholder. Cross-references `docs/threat-model.md` for the deeper STRIDE breakdown and `.claude/rules/shared-infrastructure.md` for the implementation-side discipline. Pure documentation — no behavioural change.

- **STANAG 4586 LOI 4 payload calibration command frame (refs #1122)** — continues the LOI 4 graduation kicked off by #1170 (waypoint upload), #1174 (sensor pointing), #1176 (mission abort), #1177 (GCS handover), #1179 (route upload), #1180 (payload control), and #1182 (emergency status request), shipping the **eighth command-side** message in the `rustgate-stanag4586` crate. Where the prior seven command-side frames each direct the platform to *do something now* — fly to a waypoint, slew the optics, terminate the mission, transfer authority to another GCS, upload a multi-leg route, start/stop a recorder, or interrupt the telemetry cadence to emit a fresh snapshot — `PayloadCalibrationCommand` instructs an onboard payload to perform a **sensor calibration cycle**: a self-contained, time-bounded routine that brings a sensor back into trim before (or in the middle of) a mission rather than running it open-loop with whatever drift has accumulated since the last calibration. **Operational scenario**: inertial gyros drift once the airframe has been on the ramp for a while; a magnetometer that was trimmed at the field of origin no longer reads true once the platform has been ferried to a deployment site with a different local magnetic declination; an EO/IR sensor's dark-frame baseline shifts as the optics warm; a turret's boresight drifts after a hard landing or cargo-bay handling. None of these failures will trip a BIT-report fault — the sensor is operating, just operating *biased* — so the operator needs an explicit re-trim lever. The GCS picks a [`CalibrationKind`](crate::payload_calibration_command::CalibrationKind) selecting which routine to run ([`GyroAlignment`](crate::payload_calibration_command::CalibrationKind::GyroAlignment) for an IMU re-trim, [`MagnetometerCompensation`](crate::payload_calibration_command::CalibrationKind::MagnetometerCompensation) for a heading sensor that has been displaced, [`DarkFrameCapture`](crate::payload_calibration_command::CalibrationKind::DarkFrameCapture) for an EO/IR baseline once the optics have warmed, [`BoresightAlign`](crate::payload_calibration_command::CalibrationKind::BoresightAlign) for a turret that took a knock, [`FullSelfTest`](crate::payload_calibration_command::CalibrationKind::FullSelfTest) for the "run everything you have" pre-flight check), a [`Mode`](crate::payload_calibration_command::Mode) biasing how the platform schedules the routine ([`Manual`](crate::payload_calibration_command::Mode::Manual) runs the routine once and waits for the operator's next command, [`Automatic`](crate::payload_calibration_command::Mode::Automatic) runs the routine through to completion without further interaction, [`ScheduledRecurring`](crate::payload_calibration_command::Mode::ScheduledRecurring) asks the platform to repeat the routine at its own internal cadence until told to stop — the load-bearing tier for periodic mid-mission re-trim where pulsing a fresh command on every iteration would waste link budget), an `iteration_count` (`0` is the documented "single pass" sentinel — run the routine once and stop; non-zero values request the platform re-run the routine N additional times after the first pass for averaging — the documented use-case is long-baseline gyro alignment where averaging over multiple samples reduces residual drift below what a single pass can achieve), and a `timeout_secs` (`0` is the documented "no timeout" sentinel — let the calibration run as long as it needs; non-zero values let the operator put a hard ceiling on calibration duration so a stuck sensor cannot block the platform's command loop indefinitely). The platform applies the command, surfaces progress through the existing LOI 2-3 telemetry surfaces ([`sensor_status`](crate::sensor_status), [`payload_status`](crate::payload_status), [`bit_report`](crate::bit_report) — a `FullSelfTest` will exercise multiple subsystems and surface their states through several frames; a single-sensor routine like `MagnetometerCompensation` only touches the relevant subsystem), and either runs the routine once or to its natural completion or repeats on its internal cadence per the chosen `Mode`. **Cross-frame correlation**: `payload_id` (u32 at wire offset 4, big-endian) is **wire-byte-compatible** with [`PayloadStatus::payload_id`](crate::payload_status::PayloadStatus::payload_id) from #1157 and [`PayloadControlCommand::payload_id`](crate::payload_control_command::PayloadControlCommand::payload_id) from #1180 — both frames put the field at offset 0 of the payload-scoped wire layout (and this command frame puts it at offset 4 after the leading `vehicle_id`), so the four-byte big-endian representation of the same logical payload identifier is byte-for-byte identical between the LOI 2-3 telemetry frame, the prior LOI 4 payload-control frame, and this calibration frame. Without that guarantee, an operator who copied the bytes verbatim from a status frame into a calibration command could end up calibrating a different payload — a silent footgun the codec is explicitly designed to prevent. The contract is pinned by a dedicated `payload_id_field_matches_payload_status_module` test that builds both frames at the same logical `PAYLOAD_ID` and asserts the four wire bytes are byte-for-byte identical (and additionally pins the literal big-endian encoding of the test value `42` as `[0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x2A]` so a future refactor that swaps the wire format on either frame still trips the test). **Wire format** (32 bytes fixed, NATO big-endian, mirrors the existing LOI 4 32-byte fixed-frame siblings): `vehicle_id` (u32 @ 0, matches the same field across every LOI 2-3 telemetry and LOI 4 command frame), `payload_id` (u32 @ 4, cross-frame correlated), `calibration_kind` (u8 @ 8, [`CalibrationKind`](crate::payload_calibration_command::CalibrationKind) enum), `mode` (u8 @ 9, [`Mode`](crate::payload_calibration_command::Mode) enum), 2 reserved bytes @ 10..12, `iteration_count` (u32 @ 12, big-endian, `0` = single pass), `timeout_secs` (u32 @ 16, big-endian, `0` = no timeout), 4 reserved bytes @ 20..24, `timestamp_unix_ms` (u64 @ 24, big-endian). Reserved blocks are zero-filled on encode; the decoder does NOT validate them so a future spec revision that allocates the bytes for a calibration sequence number, a per-routine tolerance threshold, or a cryptographic nonce binding the command to the issuing GCS authority stays backward-compatible at the frame-length level. Trailing bytes beyond 32 are tolerated (covered by `decode_extra_trailing_bytes_are_ignored` with a 32-byte trailer). Truncation surfaces as `Stanag4586Error::FrameTooShort { actual, expected: 32 }` covering input lengths `[0, 1, 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 31]` (truncation sweep test). **Two enum designs**: [`CalibrationKind`](crate::payload_calibration_command::CalibrationKind) covers the five named routines (`GyroAlignment` = 0x01, `MagnetometerCompensation` = 0x02, `DarkFrameCapture` = 0x03, `BoresightAlign` = 0x04, `FullSelfTest` = 0x05) plus a forward-compat `Other(u8)` catch-all so a future spec revision allocating a new routine (an `AltimeterZero` for a pressure-altimeter ground reference, an `OpticsFocus` for a motorised focus mechanism, a `PayloadLinkBudget` for a streamer's receive-side gain-trim sweep) stays decodable on a receiver running today's build. [`Mode`](crate::payload_calibration_command::Mode) covers the three named scheduling tiers (`Manual` = 0x01, `Automatic` = 0x02, `ScheduledRecurring` = 0x03) plus the same forward-compat `Other(u8)`. `0x00` deliberately falls into `Other` for both enums — the encode side never emits `0x00` for a named variant, so observing one on decode means the upstream sent something unintended and the operator should be able to see the raw byte value in a log line. Both enums implement `Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq` plus `to_byte`/`from_byte` mirroring every sibling LOI 2-3 / LOI 4 frame's enums. **Test coverage delta**: 14 new tests bring the crate from 185 → 199. Coverage matrix: 3 hand-built fixture round-trips (zero-valued, `GyroAlignment`/`Manual` typical, `FullSelfTest`/`Automatic` with iteration-count averaging), 2 zero-as-sentinel acceptance pins (`decode_accepts_zero_iteration_count_as_single_pass`, `decode_accepts_zero_timeout_as_no_timeout`), 1 golden-fixture decode pinning literal hex bytes for `vehicle_id` (0x1122_3344), `payload_id` (0xAABB_CCDD), `calibration_kind` (0x01 = `GyroAlignment`), `mode` (0x02 = `Automatic`), `iteration_count` (0x0000_0005), `timeout_secs` (0x0000_003C = 60s), and `timestamp_unix_ms` (0xFEDC_BA98_7654_3210), 1 truncation sweep covering `[0, 1, 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 31]`-byte inputs, 1 trailing-bytes-ignored test with a 32-byte 0xAA trailer, 1 `CalibrationKind` enum round-trip covering all named variants plus `Other(0xFF)` plus a sweep of unknown bytes including `0x00` and `0x06`, 1 `Mode` enum round-trip covering all named variants plus `Other(0xFF)` plus a sweep of unknown bytes including `0x00` and `0x04`, 1 cross-frame `payload_id` correlation test against [`PayloadStatus`](crate::payload_status::PayloadStatus) (mirrors #1180's same-shape test against the same module), 1 `encode_to_vec` method-vs-function parity, 1 `encode_into` non-clearing-of-destination, and 1 256-case proptest exercising every numeric-field range and every enum-byte value. **Public surface**: `pub mod payload_calibration_command` exporting `PayloadCalibrationCommand` (the message struct), `CalibrationKind` (the routine enum), `Mode` (the scheduling enum), `PAYLOAD_CALIBRATION_COMMAND_FRAME_LEN` (the fixed wire-frame length constant, `32`), `encode(&PayloadCalibrationCommand) -> Vec<u8>`, `encode_into(&PayloadCalibrationCommand, &mut BytesMut)`, `decode(&[u8]) -> Result<PayloadCalibrationCommand, Stanag4586Error>`, plus the convenience method `PayloadCalibrationCommand::encode_to_vec(&self) -> Vec<u8>`. Re-exported from `rustgate_stanag4586::{CalibrationKind, Mode, PayloadCalibrationCommand}` at the crate root mirroring every sibling frame's re-export pattern. **Out of scope**: the calibration response message — the platform's "routine started, expected duration N seconds" / "routine complete, residual error E" / "routine aborted, sensor stuck" reply — is surfaced through the existing LOI 2-3 read-side telemetry frames ([`sensor_status`](crate::sensor_status), [`payload_status`](crate::payload_status), [`bit_report`](crate::bit_report)) plus a dedicated calibration-result frame that is a separate follow-up read-side PR rather than a command-side concern; per-sensor calibration parameter overrides (operator-supplied gain trim values, white-balance temperature anchors, per-axis bias deltas) are deliberately not in the minimum-viable command set and belong in a follow-up extended-command PR that allocates the existing reserved bytes for the override payload; mode change is the remaining LOI 4 minimum-viable command-side message and ships in a follow-up PR with its own wire format and validation rules; bidirectional command-response handshake messages (the platform's "calibration accepted, will run at T+50ms" / "calibration rejected, sensor unavailable" reply) are a separate follow-up PR; UDP/TCP listener wiring stays out of scope — this module is pure encode/decode over `&[u8]`, mirroring the every-prior-LOI-4-PR boundary.

- **ASTERIX CAT-021 outbound encoder + `data_source_id` decode fix (refs #1121)** — ships the encode-side complement to the decode-only MVP that landed in #1166 and the fuzz target that landed in #1169, completing the bidirectional CAT-021 ADS-B codec for the forwarding-with-modification deployments that the airframe-side detect-and-avoid stack needs. Where #1166's `decode_cat021` parses an inbound CAT-021 datablock from the wire (typically a UDP-multicast datagram from an SBS-3 / BEAST receiver feeding ADS-B traffic into the routing layer), the new `encode_cat021(reports: &[Cat021Report]) -> Result<Vec<u8>, Cat021EncodeError>` and zero-extra-allocation `encode_cat021_into(reports, &mut bytes::BytesMut)` re-emit a `Cat021Report` (or a slice of them) as a CAT-021 datablock that bytes-precisely round-trips back through `decode_cat021`. The motivating use-case is **mask-the-target-address-and-re-broadcast-to-a-less-privileged-consumer**: a tactical UAS deployment sometimes wants to re-emit the surveillance picture downstream with sensitive identifiers stripped (the 24-bit ICAO `target_address` is the canonical aircraft-to-flight correlator across consecutive position reports — a downstream consumer that should see "aircraft at lat/lon/FL" but NOT "this is N12345" gets a synthesised report with `target_address: None`), and the integration-test pattern of "decode a real wire trace, mutate one field, encode back, assert the byte sequence rustgate would write" is the end-to-end correctness contract the encoder unblocks. **Round-trip self-stability invariant**: a `Cat021Report` decoded from N bytes, when re-encoded, produces a datablock that decodes back to a `Cat021Report` with the SAME `Some(...)` field set. The encoder walks FRNs 1..=48 in ascending order (matching the wire UAP and `decode_record`'s decode walk) and sets FSPEC bits ONLY for fields whose `Option` is `Some(...)`; an all-`None` `Cat021Report::default()` emits a single 0x00 FSPEC octet with no following field bytes (a 4-byte datablock: CAT + 2-byte LEN + 1-byte FSPEC), and any subset of the MVP fields produces a datablock whose FSPEC chain extends to exactly the highest-set FRN's octet (FRN 21 → 3-octet chain via FX bits, FRN 29 → 5-octet chain) without any spare bits. This is the property that makes the encoder safe to compose with the decoder for the forwarding-with-modification path: `decode → mutate → encode → decode` is byte-stable on the field set, so a SIEM that tails the egress side can treat the re-emitted bytes as semantically equivalent to the ingress side modulo the explicitly-mutated field. **BEHAVIOUR CHANGE — decode now populates `data_source_id`**: pre-this-PR, FRN 1 (I021/010 Data Source Identifier) was decoded as a length-2 skip — the wire bytes were consumed but no struct field was populated. As of this PR, `Cat021Report` carries a new `data_source_id: Option<u16>` field that decode populates with the SAC (high byte) + SIC (low byte) packed as a u16. This is a load-bearing change for the round-trip invariant: without it, a real-world CAT-021 record (which always carries FRN 1 — the Data Source Identifier is mandatory in practice per Eurocontrol's UAP usage notes even though the spec marks it as optional via FSPEC) would round-trip as `Some(addr) → encode → decode → None`, breaking the self-stability property the encoder is documented to provide. The behaviour change is bounded: pre-existing test fixtures that don't carry FRN 1 continue to decode unchanged (every field stays `None`), and pre-existing tests that DO carry FRN 1 (`decode_minimal_datablock_with_only_data_source_id`, `decode_full_ads_b_record_with_all_mvp_fields`) have been updated to assert the now-populated field rather than expecting `Cat021Report::default()`. A downstream consumer that was relying on FRN 1 being silently skipped would observe one new `Some(0x...)` field on every decoded report — operationally additive (no field that was previously `Some` becomes `None`, no error path that was previously `Ok` becomes `Err`). **New `Cat021EncodeError` enum** (deliberately distinct from the decode-side `Cat021Error` because encode and decode have non-overlapping failure surfaces): `TargetAddressOutOfRange { value: u32 }` rejects a caller-supplied `target_address` with any of the high 8 bits set rather than silently masking off to 24 bits — the type-level container is `u32` because Rust has no native `u24` and the unsanitised mask would let a 32-bit value lay down as a different aircraft's hex code on the wire; `UnencodableIdentification { value: String, reason: &'static str }` rejects a `target_identification` longer than 8 characters or containing characters outside the ICAO Annex 10 6-bit alphabet (uppercase A-Z, digits 0-9, ASCII space) — the only three reasons a callsign won't fit the wire format losslessly, and surfacing them as a typed error rather than silently substituting `?` characters means the upstream component decides whether to upper-case, drop, or substitute; `DatablockTooLarge { len: usize, max: usize }` guards the 16-bit ASTERIX LEN header — a caller batching a very large slice of reports into one datablock that would exceed `u16::MAX` (65 535) bytes can hit this ceiling, surfaced explicitly so the caller fragments the slice rather than emitting a corrupt LEN header. Float-domain fields (`time_of_day_seconds`, `flight_level`, the WGS-84 lat/lon pair) saturate to wire-representable extremes on NaN / out-of-range input rather than panicking — the 1/128-second time-of-day saturates to the 24-bit ceiling, the 0.25-FL flight level saturates to `i16::{MIN, MAX}`, the 180/2^23-deg semicircles saturate to the i24 endpoints; healthy round-trips never exercise the saturation, but a caller that passes `f64::NAN` from a sensor fault gets the closest representable wire value rather than a no-panics-in-production guideline violation. **Test coverage delta**: 43 → 54 tests in the `rustgate-asterix` crate (+11 tests). `encode_minimal_record_round_trips_through_decode` pins the load-bearing single-FRN case (`target_address` only); `encode_full_mvp_record_round_trips_through_decode` exercises every MVP FRN simultaneously and pins the emit-in-ascending-FRN-order discipline by asserting equality on every decoded field; `encode_multiple_records_in_one_datablock` pins the multi-record case for parity with `decode_cat021`'s multi-record support; `encode_fspec_chain_extends_when_high_frn_set` pins the FX-chain layout for an FRN-21-only record (3-octet chain, FX bits at octets 0-1, FRN 21 bit at octet 2 with FX clear); `encode_target_address_out_of_range_returns_err` and `encode_unencodable_identification_returns_err` pin the two value-domain typed errors; `encode_pads_short_callsign_with_six_bit_space` pins the ICAO 6-bit space (0x20) padding for a 4-character callsign; `encode_record_with_no_fields_set_emits_zero_fspec` pins the all-`None` minimum (4-byte datablock with single 0x00 FSPEC octet); `encode_position_wgs84_round_trip_preserves_at_lsb_precision` pins the geographic round-trip at the wire LSB precision (180/2^23 deg ≈ 2.145e-5 deg, ≈ 2.4 m at the equator); `decode_data_source_id_now_populated_after_encoder_addition` pins the BEHAVIOUR CHANGE on decode with a hand-built fixture (SAC=0x42, SIC=0x07 → packed `Some(0x4207)`); `encode_into_appends_to_existing_buffer` pins that the `_into` variant does not pre-clear the caller's `BytesMut` so a batch encoder can reuse one output buffer across many datablocks. The fuzz target #1169 is **not extended** in this PR — the existing `fuzz_targets/asterix_cat021.rs` already exercises the decoder against arbitrary input bytes and pinning the additional `decode(encode(decode(x))) == decode(x)` self-stability invariant is queued for a separate small follow-up PR rather than mixed into this encode-side change. **Out of scope (called out as explicit follow-ups, not silent gaps)**: (a) **compound items remain decode-`TruncatedField` and are not encodable** — the four FRNs that decode_cat021 currently surfaces as `Cat021Error::TruncatedField` (FRN 31 Met Information, FRN 34 Trajectory Intent, FRN 39 Mode S MB Data, FRN 42 Data Ages) carry primary-subfield bitmaps with per-subfield content; fully decoding the subfield catalogue is out of scope for the issue-#1121 MVP, and matching encode-side support is correspondingly absent — a `Cat021Report` cannot today carry a "compound item present" marker for the encoder to re-emit, by design, until the decode side grows the field types; (b) **fuzz target extension** — adding the `decode(encode(decode(x))) == decode(x)` invariant to the existing `fuzz_targets/asterix_cat021.rs` is queued as a separate small follow-up PR; (c) **UDP listener wiring** — this crate is pure encode/decode over `&[u8]` slices; the network glue (binding to a CAT-021 multicast group, feeding the decoder, and emitting re-encoded forwards) lives in a separate listener crate following the same pattern as `rustgate-mavlink`'s codec → listener split; (d) **mapping `Cat021Report → RoutableMessage`** — that belongs in the integration layer (issue #847) so this crate stays free of routing concepts. Builds on #1166 (decode-only MVP — direct dependency the encoder is the inverse of) and #1169 (fuzz target — establishes the no-panics-on-arbitrary-bytes invariant the encoder's saturation logic preserves on the encode side).
