Pinning the order with `trigger_drain_returns_unknown_target_before_check_channel_state` blocks an attacker from starving legitimate triggers by hammering the endpoint with an invalid target name (which would otherwise eat 32 channel slots before the validation fires). On the server side, `crates/rustgate-server/src/mgmt_api.rs` gains a new `pub http_publisher: Option<rustgate_http::HttpPublisher>` field on `MgmtApiState` (feature-gated on `http`, since `rustgate-http` is itself an optional workspace dependency), the `/api/dlq/` prefix is added to `MGMT_PATH_PREFIXES` so the metrics-server dispatcher routes those paths to this handler, and a new `dlq_replay_handler(target, state)` synchronous function maps `TriggerDrainError` variants onto precise HTTP status codes: `DlqNotConfigured` → `503 Service Unavailable`, `UnknownTarget` → `404 Not Found`, `ChannelFull` → `429 Too Many Requests`, `ChannelClosed` → `503 Service Unavailable`. An empty target segment (`POST /api/dlq//replay`) is rejected with `400 Bad Request` *before* dispatching to the publisher, so operators get a precise diagnostic instead of a misleading `404`. When `http` is not compiled in, the prefix is still in `MGMT_PATH_PREFIXES` and the handler short-circuits to `503 "HTTP egress not compiled in"` rather than the generic `404 "not found"` — operators see "this server cannot do that" instead of "this URL doesn't exist", which materially shortens debugging when a build is mis-configured. Authentication is unchanged: the same constant-time `Authorization: Bearer <token>` check that gates every other management endpoint, with the bearer prefix required and the token wrapped in `Zeroizing`. The handler emits `audit::http_dlq_drain_started(target, 0)` on every successful trigger so the SIEM trail records who-asked-when alongside the auto-recovery edge — a `segment_count` of 0 is documented as legal in the existing audit function so the manual-trigger path does not lie about how many segments existed at the moment of trigger (the actual segment scan happens inside the worker after the trigger arrives). Six new unit tests in `publisher.rs` pin the publisher contract: `trigger_drain_returns_dlq_not_configured_when_no_dlq` (no DLQ → `DlqNotConfigured` with empty `targets`), `trigger_drain_returns_unknown_target_for_unconfigured_name` (DLQ on, target list does not match → `UnknownTarget`), `trigger_drain_succeeds_for_configured_target` (happy path with valid name returns `Ok(())`), `trigger_drain_returns_unknown_target_before_check_channel_state` (saturate the channel with valid triggers, assert an unknown-target call still surfaces `UnknownTarget` not `ChannelFull` — order-of-checks regression guard), `trigger_drain_error_display_strings_are_stable` (Display contract for downstream JSON/audit/runbook stability), and `target_names_returns_configured_targets_in_order` (config-order preservation for diagnostics consumers). Six new in-file tests in `mgmt_api.rs` pin the HTTP surface across both feature configurations: `dlq_replay_without_publisher_returns_503` (no publisher → 503 with "HTTP publisher" in error body), `dlq_replay_wrong_method_returns_405` (GET on the path → 405 not 404, since the path is recognised), `dlq_replay_empty_target_returns_400` (empty `{target}` segment → 400 with structured diagnostic), `dlq_replay_unknown_target_returns_404` (publisher present, target not in config → 404 with `"unknown HTTP target"` in error body), `dlq_replay_known_target_returns_200` (happy path returns 200 with `{"data": {"target": "...", "triggered": true}}` JSON envelope), and `dlq_replay_without_auth_returns_401` (missing `Authorization` header → 401 — pin the auth-still-applies behaviour against future refactors that might split mutating endpoints out of `handle_request`). The `mgmt_path_prefixes_cover_all_endpoints` test gains `/api/dlq/webhook-prod/replay` to its assertion set so a future change that drops the new prefix from `MGMT_PATH_PREFIXES` fails loudly. The startup log message that lists the registered endpoints now includes `/api/dlq/`, and the doc-comment table at the top of `mgmt_api.rs` adds the row alongside the other write endpoints. Third and final PR for #881; with this and #1143 (`delivery_id` idempotency key) and #1144 (auto-drain on recovery), the HTTP egress DLQ has full lifecycle support: persistence with stable id, automatic replay on confirmed recovery, and operator-initiated replay with precise error semantics.
- **HTTP DLQ auto-drain on circuit recovery (refs #881)** — when an HTTP target's circuit breaker transitions from `HalfOpen` to `Closed` (confirmed recovery after a successful probe), the publisher now automatically replays every sealed DLQ segment for that target against the live endpoint. The recovery edge is observed by a new `build_circuit_observer(target_name, drain_tx)` helper attached to every `TargetState` via `CircuitBreaker::with_on_state_change`; on the load-bearing `(HalfOpen → Closed)` transition the observer `try_send`s the target's own name through a bounded `tokio::sync::mpsc::Sender<String>` (buffer = 32, created once at `HttpPublisher::new` time and cloned per target). A dedicated `drain_worker` task — spawned only when a DLQ is configured, to avoid burning a task on a no-op channel for publishers without forensic persistence — consumes the trigger channel and calls `drain_target(name, &targets, &dlq)` for each recovery edge. The drain sequence per pass: (1) `DeadLetterQueue::rotate_active_segment(name)` seals the live writer so any entries that never hit a size-based rotation become replayable, (2) `list_sealed_segments(name)` returns every `{target}_*.dlq.enc` on disk sorted oldest-first by mtime (ties broken lexicographically) so the replay preserves original dead-letter ordering, excluding the currently-active path which has no terminator chunk, (3) each segment is decrypted via `DeadLetterQueue::read_segment` and iterated entry-by-entry, (4) per entry the drain calls a new `replay_entry` helper that reconstructs a synthetic `RoutableMessage` (CN and groups from the entry, empty fingerprint/tenant/spiffe/attributes because the original cert material is not captured at DLQ write time — same as the offline `rustgate-replay-dlq` tool), runs the target's rate limiter and `max_payload_bytes` check, serializes via the target's configured format, and calls `send_request` **directly with a SINGLE attempt** — NOT the full `publish_with_retry` loop — because replay runs inside the recovery window and burning the retry budget here would re-trip the circuit on a mass replay against a flapping target, (5) on 2xx the entry is counted as `replayed` and silently dropped from disk when the segment is removed, on non-2xx or transport error the entry is re-persisted via the new `dead_letter_with_id(target, msg, "replay_failed", &delivery_id)` method that **preserves the original `delivery_id`** so a receiver that actually accepted the first replay but failed our 2xx read (e.g. TCP RST after response send) dedups the second replay on the same id — without this the retry cycle would duplicate on every receiver, and (6) the sealed segment is removed regardless of per-entry outcome, because failed entries were re-persisted under a fresh segment so leaving the drained file on disk would cause an infinite replay loop on every subsequent recovery trigger. Entries whose payload base64 decode fails or whose serialization errors out are classified as `ReplayOutcome::Dropped` and NOT re-persisted, because no retry can fix a corrupted record; the operator observes the drop via the per-result counter rather than by the entry silently reappearing in the next drain. Mid-drain circuit re-trip is handled by feeding `CircuitBreaker::record_failure()` from the replay path: a mass replay against an endpoint that is still unhealthy re-opens the circuit quickly, which prevents the worker from burning through the backlog pointlessly — the remaining entries re-DLQ under the same pass and await the next recovery cycle. 4xx client errors do NOT affect the circuit (matching the live dispatch path's classification), so a schema mismatch between producer and consumer will not masquerade as an availability failure. Two new audit events bracket every pass for the SIEM trail: `audit::http_dlq_drain_started(target, segment_count)` (`segment_count` = 0 is a legal value and emitted — operators see every recovery edge) and `audit::http_dlq_drain_completed(target, replayed, failed)` where `replayed + failed` is the total entry count read from the drained segments so dashboards can reconcile against the per-entry counter rate without a subtraction. New metric `rustgate_http_dlq_replayed_total{target, result}` counts every processed entry with `result` in `success|failed|dropped`; a climbing `failed` rate after recovery is the operator signal that the target is unhealthy in a way the circuit breaker missed (accepting the probe but rejecting the backlog — a pattern that symptomizes rate-limiter exhaustion on the receiver side). The drain channel is **fire-and-forget by design**: a full channel (another drain is already queued or running) coalesces the extra trigger to a `debug`-level log rather than blocking the circuit hot path, and a closed channel (publisher already shutting down) degrades to the same `warn`-log-only path the non-DLQ configuration takes. The drain worker terminates on `shutdown.notified()` with the same `tokio::select!` pattern as the dispatch worker, so `HttpPublisher::shutdown` drains both workers under the existing 5s graceful-shutdown budget. `build_circuit_observer` keeps its existing gauge-update side effect on the `(Open → HalfOpen)` edge (probe window visibility) intact; the four existing observer tests (`circuit_observer_sets_gauge_to_halfopen_on_open_to_halfopen`, `circuit_observer_ignores_unrelated_transitions`, `circuit_observer_fires_via_real_breaker_transition`, `circuit_observer_is_send_and_sync`) pass `None` as the new `drain_tx` parameter since they exercise only the metrics side — drain behaviour has its own test suite. Four new integration tests in `crates/rustgate-http/tests/dlq_drain_integration.rs` pin the end-to-end contract against a live wiremock. The trip phase deliberately publishes TWO messages: the first takes the terminal 5xx that trips the circuit (terminal failures are dropped, not DLQ'd, by `publish_with_retry` design), the second is shed against the now-open circuit and lands in the DLQ where the drain can pick it up — reflecting the real-world sequence rather than the (incorrect) shortcut that a terminal 5xx and a DLQ write are the same event. `drain_replays_dlq_entries_on_circuit_recovery`: 500 → trip → second publish DLQ'd → cooldown → probe → replay; wiremock `expect(2)` on the 200 mock panics on drop if probe + replay do not both land. `drain_preserves_delivery_id_across_replay`: the replay mock gates on `header_exists("X-Rustgate-Delivery-Id")` AND a charlie-body discriminator so the match itself fails if the drain forgets the header, and `server.received_requests()` is inspected post-hoc to assert the wire value is 32 lowercase hex chars (pinning the wire shape — a regression to empty string or a format marker would still fail here even though `header_exists` alone would tolerate it). The test reads the delivery id from the WIRE rather than from the encrypted segment because the active DLQ segment is unsealed (no AEAD terminator) while the publisher is running, so `read_dlq_file` would refuse to decrypt it — the wire is the only pre-shutdown vantage point. `drain_requeues_failed_entries_and_preserves_id`: mocks 500 on the replay (500 on charlie-body, 200 on bob-body) so `dead_letter_with_id` fires, captures the wire id from `received_requests`, and after `publisher.shutdown()` seals the re-DLQ'd segment reads it via `dlq_reader::read_dlq_file` and asserts the sealed entry's `delivery_id` matches the wire id — the load-bearing property that `dead_letter_with_id` preserves the caller-supplied id rather than minting a fresh one, which is what keeps receiver-side dedup working across retry cycles. `drain_is_noop_when_no_sealed_segments_exist`: recovery trigger with an empty DLQ dir must not panic and must not produce spurious replay requests. Three unit tests in `publisher.rs` pin the new `parse_message_type` helper (the inverse of `MessageType::Display` used to reconstruct the variant from the string field stored in each DLQ entry): `parse_message_type_round_trips_every_named_variant`, `parse_message_type_preserves_other_variant_tail` (including the single-pass prefix peel for `other:ns:subtype`), and `parse_message_type_falls_back_to_other_for_unknown_strings` (graceful degradation when a newer producer emits a variant an older consumer's parser does not yet recognise). Two new `rustgate_core::audit` functions gain coverage in `test_http_dlq_drain_started` and `test_http_dlq_drain_completed`, matching the shape of every other audit event test. Opt-in: a publisher configured without `dlq_dir` / `dlq_key_file` sees no behaviour change — the drain worker is only spawned when a DLQ exists, and the circuit observer's `drain_tx` argument gracefully short-circuits to a no-op on the recovery edge. Second of three PRs for #881; the admin `POST /api/dlq/{target}/replay` endpoint ships as the third so operators can trigger a manual drain without waiting for a circuit recovery.
- **HTTP DLQ entry idempotency key (`delivery_id`) for replay deduplication (refs #881)** — every record written by `rustgate_http::dlq::DeadLetterQueue::dead_letter` is now stamped at dead-letter time with a stable 128-bit `delivery_id` field, serialised as exactly 32 lowercase hex characters — the same entropy budget, wire format, and generator shape as the live publish path's `X-Rustgate-Delivery-Id` HTTP header (reserved as a publisher-owned header name in `HttpConfig` validation since #905). The generator is a private `dlq::generate_delivery_id()` helper that draws 16 bytes from `fastrand::fill` and renders them through `hex::encode`, mirroring `publisher::generate_delivery_id` byte-for-byte so a dead-lettered delivery id is indistinguishable from one produced by the live path — this matters because the follow-up replay tooling (PR B: auto-drain on circuit recovery; PR C: admin replay endpoint) will forward the stamped id verbatim on the wire as the `X-Rustgate-Delivery-Id` header so receivers can deduplicate replayed deliveries against the original attempt without any additional server-side state on the rustgate side. The reader side (`rustgate_http::dlq_reader::OwnedDlqEntry`) gains a matching `pub delivery_id: String` field guarded by `#[serde(default)]`, which keeps the reader **backward-compatible with pre-migration DLQ archives**: an operator replaying a `.dlq.enc` file produced before this release sees entries with an empty `delivery_id` string, and replay consumers are expected to treat an empty id as "generate a fresh one" rather than forwarding the empty sentinel as a header value — pinned by `deserialization_tolerates_missing_delivery_id_for_backward_compat`, which feeds a legacy JSON record (no `delivery_id` key) through the deserializer and asserts `entry.delivery_id.is_empty()`. Entry order is deterministic — the field is positioned in the serialised struct between `reason` and `source_cn`, same as in the reader — so `jq`-level tooling sees a stable column order across the producer/consumer pair. Five new tests pin the contract: `delivery_id_is_lowercase_hex_128_bits` (regression guard for the format — any future generator swap must preserve the 32-char lowercase hex shape or the test fails loudly), `delivery_id_generator_is_non_constant` (two calls must produce different ids — defends against a broken `fastrand` seed or an accidentally-deterministic refactor), `dead_letter_stamps_delivery_id_on_every_entry` (end-to-end writer → reader round-trip with two dead-lettered messages, asserts both entries carry 32-char ids and the two ids differ), `deserialization_preserves_delivery_id_verbatim` (fresh JSON with `delivery_id":"deadbeefcafef00d0011223344556677"` preserves the value byte-for-byte), and `delivery_id_round_trips_through_encrypted_segment` (three dead-letters → encrypt → decrypt → consumer cycle; asserts all three ids are 32-char lowercase hex and mutually distinct). The two existing `dlq_entry_serializes_to_json` and `dlq_entry_json_contains_all_documented_fields` tests were updated to include the new field in their literal `DlqEntry` constructions — a DLQ entry without a `delivery_id` now fails to compile, which is the desired compile-time guard against a future writer regression that forgets to stamp the field. No behavioural change for operators who do not yet have replay tooling wired up — the field is additive, the encryption/AEAD wire format is unchanged (`delivery_id` is plaintext JSON inside the existing ChaCha20-Poly1305 envelope), and `dlq_max_bytes` / `dlq_max_target_bytes` accounting still reflects the actual on-disk byte count. First of three PRs for #881: this one lays the idempotency-key infrastructure, the auto-drain-on-circuit-recovery and admin replay endpoint ship as follow-ups now that the stable `delivery_id` exists for receivers to deduplicate against.
- **NATS dead-letter subject for poison message preservation** — new optional
  `NatsConfig::dead_letter_subject: Option<String>` field lets operators
  designate a NATS subject where the subscriber republishes the original
  payload before ACKing a message it cannot process locally. The four
  drop paths wired to DLQ are: oversized payloads that exceed
  `max_payload_bytes`, JSON that fails to deserialize as `WireEvent`,
  CoT reports carrying the `ce/le` position-unknown sentinel, and
  messages whose embedded identity (empty CN, CN longer than 256 bytes,
  etc.) fails `Identity::plaintext` validation. Before this change those
  four branches silently ACKed to keep the pull consumer moving past
  stuck sequences, leaving operators with no way to inspect what garbage
  the upstream producer sent. The helper forwards the original bytes
  unchanged so forensic tooling sees exactly what arrived, and attaches
  three diagnostic headers: `X-Rustgate-DLQ-Reason` (one of `oversized`,
  `unparseable`, `unknown-position`, `invalid-identity` — identifies
  which drop path fired so alerting can fan out per root-cause),
  `X-Rustgate-DLQ-Original-Subject` (preserves the live-stream subject
  the poison message arrived on — critical for tenant attribution when
  the live stream captures a `{prefix}.>` wildcard spanning many
  groups), and `X-Rustgate-DLQ-Timestamp` (Unix millis at DLQ publish
  time so DLQ traffic can be correlated with subscriber logs even when
  the original payload has no timestamp of its own). The feature is
  **strictly opt-in** — default is `None`, which preserves today's
  silent-drop behaviour and guarantees that existing deployments see no
  change on upgrade. Publication is **best-effort**: a failed DLQ
  publish is logged at `warn` with `dlq_subject`, `reason`,
  `original_subject`, and the underlying error, but does NOT block the
  ACK of the original message; the whole point of DLQ is that operators
  give up on a stuck sequence and advance the consumer, so allowing a
  transient publish error to keep the poison message in the pending
  set would defeat the purpose and could wedge the consumer on one
  unlucky payload. Validation catches two misconfiguration classes at
  `NatsConfig::validate()` time: (1) wildcards (`*`, `>`) in the DLQ
  subject are rejected with the same rule that applies to
  `subject_prefix` — the subscriber publishes to one concrete subject,
  wildcards have no meaning on the publish path and almost certainly
  indicate operator confusion between DLQ and `subject_filters`; and
  (2) DLQ subjects that start with `{subject_prefix}.` are rejected
  with an error message that mentions the word `loop`, because the
  live JetStream stream captures `{subject_prefix}.>` with a wildcard,
  so a DLQ subject inside that namespace would be recaptured,
  redelivered, re-classified as poison, republished to DLQ, and so on
  indefinitely — an unbounded feedback loop that would wedge the
  consumer on one poisoned payload. The canonical deployment pattern
  is a disjoint sibling namespace (e.g. `subject_prefix = "points"`,
  `dead_letter_subject = "rustgate.dlq"`) optionally captured by a
  second JetStream stream for durable archival. Edge case preserved
  deliberately: a DLQ subject **equal to** the bare `subject_prefix`
  (no trailing dot) is accepted because the live-stream wildcard only
  captures the `{prefix}.` sub-namespace, not the bare token. Twelve
  new unit tests cover the validation matrix (default-None, multi-level
  subject accepted, single-token subject accepted, wildcards rejected,
  asterisk rejected, empty string rejected, control char rejected,
  non-ASCII rejected, prefix-conflict rejected with loop-mentioning
  error message, equal-to-prefix accepted, unrelated-prefix accepted,
  round-trip). Two new integration tests exercise the end-to-end path
  against a real nats-server: `dead_letter_publishes_unparseable_payload`
  asserts that bogus bytes published to `points.ALPHA` surface on
  `rustgate.dlq` with the exact original payload, the `unparseable`
  reason slug, the preserved original subject, and a parseable
  unix-millis timestamp header; `no_dead_letter_when_subject_not_configured`
  guards the opt-in contract by verifying that when
  `dead_letter_subject` is `None` (the default), no traffic arrives on
  any speculative DLQ subject even in the presence of poison messages.
  Refs #883.
- **`test-connection` diagnostic CLI subcommand** — operator-facing reachability pre-flight that probes a single remote endpoint without starting the server or loading any TLS material. Intended to be wired into cron, Ansible, or `systemd`'s `ExecStartPre=` so firewall, DNS, or service-outage problems surface before `rustgate` itself tries to start and fails at a less-diagnosable point. Exactly one target flag must be supplied: `--tcp HOST:PORT` runs a dumb three-way TCP handshake that works against every listener type (TLS, WebSocket, MQTT, plaintext, enrollment, metrics) because it sends zero application-layer bytes; `--nats nats://HOST:PORT` (feature-gated on `nats`) adds a read of the server's `INFO` greeting so listeners that accept TCP but reject NATS (misconfigured auth, wrong service on the port) are distinguished from healthy targets; `--http URL` (feature-gated on `http`) sends `GET / HTTP/1.0` and classifies by status line so 2xx/3xx/4xx report `connected` (the server is answering) while 5xx reports `refused`. Every probe honours a single `--timeout-secs` budget (default `5`) covering DNS resolution, TCP handshake, and any protocol-level exchange so a hung target cannot stall the caller. Exit codes form a monotonic severity ladder — `0` connected, `1` refused (TCP RST / ECONNREFUSED / 5xx / NATS non-`INFO`), `2` timeout, `3` any other error (bad URL, DNS, unexpected I/O) — so downstream scripts branch on the code alone without having to parse the report body. The stable JSON contract exposes `target_type`, `target`, `timeout_seconds`, `status` (one of `connected` / `refused` / `timeout` / `error`), `elapsed_ms`, and `error` (non-null whenever status is not `connected`); the key set is pinned by a `json_contract_is_stable` unit test so a rename or removal is caught at build time. The new module `crates/rustgate-server/src/diagnostics/test_connection.rs` builds its own single-threaded tokio runtime on the fly so the subcommand runs before the server's normal runtime/tracing/config init — the same self-contained pattern the existing `cert-info` / `crl-info` / `check-cert-expiry` / `generate-config` subcommands use. Eleven new unit tests pin the contract: the status-to-exit-code ladder is monotonic, status string tokens are stable, TCP probe against an open listener reports `connected`, TCP probe against a closed port reports `refused`, TCP probe against an unparseable target reports `error`, human rendering includes all headline fields and the error line only when present, JSON keys are exactly the documented set, HTTP status-line classifier buckets 2xx/4xx as `connected` and 5xx as `refused`, HTTP URL parser handles `http://` + `https://` default ports and missing-path shorthand, NATS scheme-strip accepts both `nats://h:p` and bare `h:p` and rejects `tcp://`. As a side effect the top-level `Cli` parser gains `subcommand_negates_reqs = true` so `--cert` / `--key` / `--ca` are no longer incorrectly marked as required when the user invokes a diagnostic subcommand — a latent UX bug on all four existing subcommands (`cert-info`, `crl-info`, `check-cert-expiry`, `generate-config`) that forced operators to pass dummy TLS paths to run any of them. (Refs #900)
- **`generate-config` diagnostic CLI subcommand** — introspects the clap schema for [`Cli`] at runtime and emits an annotated TOML configuration template covering every option rustgate reads from a config file. Operators run `rustgate generate-config > rustgate.toml`, uncomment the keys they want to override, and hand the result to `--config`; the existing `defaults < file < env < CLI flags` precedence chain takes over from there. The output is grouped into sixteen human-labeled sections (TLS / mTLS, Framing and encoding, NATS / JetStream bridge, HTTP egress bridge, Certificate enrollment / EST, Prometheus metrics endpoint, Connection limits and backpressure, WebSocket transport, MQTT transport, Plaintext TCP / UDP transports, Federation, Client rate limiting, Authorization (ACL and authz engine), Archives, audit log, access log, OpenTelemetry tracing, Deduplication and CoT delta encoding) that mirror the field order in the `define_config_file!` invocation — mechanically stable so that `diff`ing the template between releases highlights exactly which options were added, removed, or changed. Each block carries the full help comment from the clap arg (wrapped to 72 columns so the `# `-prefixed line stays within a 79-column envelope for editor readability), the `env:` variable name when one is configured, a `default:` line, and the `key = value` pair itself. Required fields (`cert`, `key`, `ca` when `--spiffe` is not set) are emitted *uncommented* with a `REPLACE_ME` placeholder so a copy-pasted template fails loudly at server startup rather than silently running with an empty string; every other field is emitted commented-out with its actual default so uncomment-to-override works without having to consult the reference docs. Optional fields with no default (`crl`, `nats_url`, `otel_endpoint`, and ~30 others) get a commented-out `#key = "<unset>"` placeholder so operators can see the TOML syntax for the key — the `<unset>` string is deliberately not a valid runtime value, signalling that uncommenting alone will not opt the option in. Default value rendering is type-aware via `clap::builder::ValueParser::type_id()` compared against `std::any::TypeId::of::<T>()` for each primitive: `bool`, `i8`..`i128`, `isize`, `u8`..`u128`, `usize`, `f32`, `f64` render as bare TOML literals (so `fips-required = false` and `federation-max-hops = 10` come out as operators would write them by hand), while `String`, `PathBuf`, and `ValueEnum`-derived types render double-quoted with `"` and `\` escaped per TOML basic-string rules. This fixes a landmine where the `tls-min-version` default `"1.2"` would otherwise render as a bare `1.2` (valid TOML float but the server's `ConfigFile` mirror deserializes into a `String` and would reject the float) — a regression test pins this exact case. Schema drift between [`Cli`] and [`ConfigFile`] is caught loudly: the template emits a `# SCHEMA_DRIFT:` marker (deliberately not the word "WARNING", which appears legitimately inside multi-line help text — e.g. the `--acl-api-bind` arg — and would confuse a naive `grep WARNING` check in CI) whenever a `CONFIG_FILE_FIELDS` entry has no matching Cli `#[arg]`. The `define_config_file!` macro was extended to emit a new `pub(crate) const CONFIG_FILE_FIELDS: &[&str]` listing every field name in source order so both the macro (single source of truth for which keys load from TOML) and the generator (walks that list to decide what to render) cannot drift. The new module `crates/rustgate-server/src/diagnostics/generate_config.rs` uses the same self-contained no-runtime-no-tracing pattern as the existing `cert-info` / `crl-info` / `check-cert-expiry` subcommands, so an operator can run it from a host that cannot yet start the server at all — ideal for scripting the first deploy of a new tenant. Four new doc comments were added to the `bind`, `cert`, `key`, and `ca` args (previously bare `#[arg(...)]` blocks with no `///` text) so the template now surfaces meaningful help for the four mandatory TLS fields. Seventeen new unit tests pin the contract: template is non-empty and valid UTF-8, every `CONFIG_FILE_FIELDS` entry surfaces as an emitted line, no schema-drift markers appear, TLS required fields are uncommented with `REPLACE_ME`, `bind` is commented-out with its default, section headers appear in order, env vars are documented, boolean and integer defaults render without quotes, optional fields emit the `<unset>` placeholder, `to_kebab_case` conversion preserves underscores-to-hyphens, `wrap_comment` respects the configured column and preserves paragraph breaks, `format_toml_literal` uses type-id dispatch, `tls-min-version` default is quoted (regression guard), the whole template parses as valid TOML with placeholders kept, and the filled template (REPLACE_ME replaced with a real path) round-trips through the `ConfigFile` mirror's `deny_unknown_fields` + kebab-case serde without complaint. (Refs #900)
- **Management REST API — write endpoints for force-disconnect and HTTP-triggered reload (refs #902)** — extends the `rustgate_server::mgmt_api` module with two authenticated POST endpoints that close out the #902 scope opened by the earlier read-only status PR: `POST /api/clients/{cn}/disconnect` signals a specific mTLS session to drain and exit by taking the priority- and normal-sender slots inside its `SessionHandle` (modelled exactly on the `Router::close_all_session_senders` graceful-shutdown path, so writer tasks observe `None` after flushing whatever was queued and no in-flight messages are dropped), and `POST /api/reload` triggers the same `reload_all_configs` pass SIGHUP runs, returning a structured JSON `ReloadReport` rather than requiring the operator to tail the audit log. The disconnect endpoint uses exact CN matching against the router's session map — the key preserved from the cert subject at register time with its original casing, matching `Router::send_to_session` behaviour — and reports `disconnected: false` with `200 OK` when no session is registered under the supplied CN (treating "not connected" as a normal state rather than an error), `400 BAD_REQUEST` for an empty CN segment (`/api/clients//disconnect`), and an audit-preserved `200` with `disconnected: true` on a successful signal; sessions are *not* removed from the routing map by the disconnect call — the session task still runs `unregister` on its own exit path so `session_count` stays accurate while the writer drains and an in-flight `route_inner` lookup cannot race. The reload endpoint is deliberately unified with SIGHUP: it captures the same `cert_reloader`, `acl_reloader_handle`, `--crl` path, OCSP stapler, and federation peer reloader handles the SIGHUP closure captures, drives them through the same `reload_all_configs` function (refactored to return a `ReloadReport` rather than `()`, with every per-component audit event still emitted identically to the SIGHUP path so the audit trail is indistinguishable between the two surfaces), and serializes the result as `{"cert": {...}, "acl": {...}, "crl": {...}, "federation_peers": {...}}` where each component carries `result ∈ {"success", "failure", "skipped"}`, an optional `error` string, an optional `changed` bit (the rotated flag for cert, the swapped flag for ACL and federation peers), and CRL-specific `crl_count`/`crl_max_age_seconds` fields — so a caller can tell the cert rotated but the CRL failed and continued without scraping anything. When the server is started without any reloadable component configured, the reload callback is intentionally left unset and `POST /api/reload` returns `503` with `"reload not available: no reloadable components configured"` rather than fabricating a success response for a no-op — the shape mirrors the "cert reloader not available" contract the read-only `/api/cert/status` endpoint already uses. Both endpoints share the same `Authorization: Bearer` + constant-time comparison + `Zeroizing` token handling as the read-only surface, and `MGMT_PATH_PREFIXES` grew an `/api/clients/` entry (the dispatcher in `metrics.rs` handles the bare `/api/reload` path as an exact-match alongside the prefixes, mirroring how the ACL API's `/api/acl/reload` was handled). The handler type in `rustgate_server::metrics::MgmtApiHandler` changed from a synchronous `Fn(…) -> Option<Response>` into `Fn(…) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = Option<Response>> + Send>>` so the disconnect and reload paths can `.await` on the router's async `RwLock` and the reload future without forcing the handler to `block_on` a nested runtime (which would have been fragile at best and would have deadlocked under `current_thread`); the read-only endpoints pay no observable cost — they simply don't await anywhere inside their arms. A new `ReloadFn` type alias captures the cross-thread callback shape (`Arc<dyn Fn() -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = JsonValue> + Send>> + Send + Sync>`, matching the workspace's `On*` callback convention) and `MgmtApiState` grew a matching `reload: Option<ReloadFn>` field — optional so a server with zero reloadable components can still register the read-only surface without wiring a callback that would panic on invocation. Wiring in `main.rs` relocates the `mgmt_api_slot.set(...)` call to *after* `fed_peer_reloader` is constructed (previously: immediately after the router) so the reload callback can close over every handle the SIGHUP path captures; the `OnceLock` dispatcher in `metrics::serve` reads `mgmt_api_slot.get()` on each request so the late-bind is race-free — a request arriving before the wiring completes simply falls through to the next handler. Seven new unit tests pin the new surface (`disconnect_unknown_cn_returns_ok_with_disconnected_false`, `disconnect_wrong_method_returns_405`, `disconnect_empty_cn_returns_400`, `reload_without_callback_returns_503`, `reload_wrong_method_returns_405`, `reload_callback_is_driven_and_body_is_returned`, plus `mgmt_path_prefixes_cover_all_endpoints` extended to include `/api/clients/alice/disconnect`), and three new `Router::disconnect_client` tests cover the happy path (senders are cleared and the function returns `true`), the unknown-CN path (returns `false`, no side effects), and the case-sensitivity guarantee (a session registered under `Alice` is not disconnected by a `alice` call — defense in depth against a caller that hash-normalises the CN before sending). The three existing `reload_all_configs_*` tests in `main.rs` were updated to assert on the new `ReloadReport` shape (`result == "skipped"` when nothing is configured, `result == "failure"` with a populated `error` for a missing CRL file, `result == "success"` + `changed == Some(true)` for the happy-path ACL reload with a failing CRL) rather than just confirming the function returned without panicking. Closes the #902 epic.
- **Management REST API — read-only status endpoints for cert, CRL, and dedup (refs #902)** — a new `rustgate_server::mgmt_api` module mounts three authenticated GET endpoints alongside the existing `/api/acl/` routes on the metrics HTTP server, gated by the `metrics` feature: `GET /api/cert/status` returns the live server leaf's subject/issuer CN, `notBefore`/`notAfter` in RFC 3339, a `seconds_until_expiry` countdown, an explicit `valid_now`/`expired` pair, and deduplicated/sorted DNS/URI/IP SAN lists (URI SANs cover SPIFFE SVIDs), parsed out of the leaf DER surfaced by `CertReloader::certified_key().end_entity_cert()` rather than a cached copy so the response tracks the actual cert presented on the next TLS handshake; `GET /api/crl/status` re-parses the configured `--crl` path on every request via `TlsConfig::validate_crl_file`, surfacing `count` + `max_age_seconds` on success or a human-readable `error` string on parse/read failure, and distinguishes "not configured" (`{"configured": false}`) from "configured but unreadable right now" (`{"configured": true, "error": "..."}`) so operators can alert on the right signal; `GET /api/dedup/stats` hands back the router's current dedup hits/entries/window, split by `enabled: bool` so a zero-traffic server with dedup enabled is distinguishable from one with dedup disabled entirely — backed by a new `Router::dedup_window_seconds()` accessor that double-derefs the existing `ArcSwap<Option<DedupCache>>` hot-reload field so the mgmt API stays consistent with the live config even across SIGHUP. Every route requires `Authorization: Bearer <token>` against a token loaded from the new `--mgmt-api-token-file` flag (env `RUSTGATE_MGMT_API_TOKEN_FILE`), compared in constant time via `subtle::ConstantTimeEq` with the mandatory `Bearer ` prefix enforced before the comparison so otherwise-valid bare tokens are rejected; the token is wrapped in `Zeroizing<Vec<u8>>` so it is wiped from memory on drop, and the `MgmtApiState` holding it gets a custom `Debug` impl using `finish_non_exhaustive()` that never renders the bytes (a test pins the redaction property). Token length is validated at startup with the same `[32, 256]` byte bounds as the ACL API via the shared `acl_api::validate_bearer_token_length` helper, so misconfigured token files fail fast rather than silently admitting short/long tokens. The handler is deliberately **read-only** — there is no endpoint that mutates router or TLS state — so the token can be issued to narrower scrape/polling jobs than the ACL write token; the companion write-side endpoints (force client disconnect, HTTP-triggered reload) are tracked as a follow-up. Routing uses a known-endpoints match that returns `405 METHOD_NOT_ALLOWED` when an operator hits a valid path with the wrong verb (so "this endpoint exists, just not for POST" is distinguishable from "this endpoint doesn't exist") and `404 NOT_FOUND` on unknown suffixes under the owned prefixes; a recognized prefix with no handler in the `OnceLock` slot falls through to the metrics server's generic 404 so a server started without `--mgmt-api-token-file` looks identical to one that never built the module. All responses are the same `{"data": ...}` / `{"error": "..."}` JSON envelope shape as the ACL API for parseability, with `content-type: application/json` always set. Wiring in `main.rs` creates a `mgmt_api_slot: Arc<OnceLock<MgmtApiHandler>>` at the same point as `acl_api_slot`, registers the handler only when the token file is supplied, and populates it after the router is constructed; `setup.rs::start_metrics` threads the slot through to `metrics::serve`, which dispatches requests under `/api/cert/`, `/api/crl/`, or `/api/dedup/` to the handler before falling through to the legacy generic handler. Thirteen unit tests pin the contract: four on `auth_ok` (missing header, non-Bearer prefix, matching/wrong token), one on path-prefix coverage so a new endpoint cannot silently 404 because its prefix was forgotten, six on routing (unknown prefix returns `None` fall-through, missing auth returns 401, wrong method returns 405, unknown suffix under mgmt prefix returns 404, cert without reloader returns 503, CRL "not configured" returns `configured: false`, CRL with missing file returns `configured: true` + `error` string, dedup disabled returns `enabled: false`), one happy-path `build_cert_status` test that drives the DER parser with a `TestCa`-issued server cert and asserts CN + DNS SANs + validity fields, and one redaction test that formats `MgmtApiState` with `{:?}` and asserts the bearer token does not appear anywhere in the output.
- **HTTP egress batch/bulk delivery (count + byte thresholds, JSON array & NDJSON, closes #906)** — `TargetConfig` in `rustgate-http` gains four opt-in fields (`batch_enabled: Option<bool>`, `batch_max_messages: Option<usize>`, `batch_max_bytes: Option<usize>`, `batch_format: Option<BatchFormat>` where `BatchFormat ∈ {JsonArray, Ndjson}`) that flip a per-target fan-out path from one-HTTP-request-per-message to one-HTTP-request-per-N-messages without changing the route-side `HttpPublisher::publish()` API or adding any new public types on the call site. Defaults are conservative (`100 messages`, `1 MiB`) and batching is off entirely unless the operator writes `batch-enabled = true` in their target config, so existing deployments see zero behavioural change. The new `rustgate_http::batch` module owns a single-owner `Batcher` state machine with synchronous `push(Bytes) -> Option<FlushPayload>` and `drain() -> Option<FlushPayload>` operations, returning a typed `FlushReason ∈ {Count, Bytes, Drain}` so the metric can distinguish "threshold-driven flush" from "shutdown-driven flush" in the series label. The threshold logic checks count first and bytes second so a batch that simultaneously hits both caps is labelled `Count` (the more specific trigger), and a single oversized message — whose serialized body alone crosses `batch_max_bytes` — still flushes rather than parking forever waiting for a companion message. The publisher side wraps the per-target `Batcher` in a `parking_lot::Mutex` (no-poisoning sync mutex, matches the workspace convention) so the hot path holds no `.await` points across a lock, and only bumps the mutex for the push+check under the existing per-target dispatch task; the subsequent HTTP request fires outside the lock so one slow target does not starve siblings. The existing retry loop is refactored out of `dispatch_to_target` into a shared `publish_with_retry(target, body, content_type, batch_size)` helper invoked by both the solo path and the batched path, and every structured log line now carries a `batch_size` field that reads `1` for solo sends and the actual entry count for batched sends — so operators can grep the access log for `batch_size > 1` and see exactly which deliveries were coalesced. A new `drain_batchers(&[TargetState])` helper is wired into `dispatch_worker`'s shutdown arm (after the `rx.close()` receive-drain, before the worker returns) and the channel-closed arm, so a trickle of traffic that never hits a count/byte threshold still produces one final HTTP request per non-empty batcher before the publisher tears down — the "no lost messages on graceful shutdown" contract existing solo-path traffic already enjoys, extended to batched targets. Circuit-breaker interaction is deliberately per-message on admission (each `publish()` still runs the `allow_request()` check before reaching the batcher, so a tripped breaker rejects inbound traffic immediately) and per-request on outcome (each batched HTTP call drives a single `record_success` or `record_failure`), which keeps the breaker's trip math identical to the solo path regardless of whether a target is batching. Config validation rejects four footguns at construction time: `batch_enabled = true` with a non-JSON payload format (raw-xml and protobuf have no portable batch wire format — the error message names both the flag and the format so operators see the conflict immediately), `batch_max_messages < 2` (a one-message "batch" is degenerate and adds envelope overhead for zero coalescence), `batch_max_bytes < 1 KiB` (below the typical single-message JSON envelope a value that small would flush every push and defeat batching), and batching on a target whose `max_payload_bytes` cap would prohibit the combined body (the publisher's existing oversize rejection would then silently drop every batch). The new Prometheus counter `rustgate_http_batches_flushed_total{target,reason}` registers via the existing `OnceLock + init() + accessor` pattern and increments once per outbound batched request, so a steady `reason="drain"` rate against `reason="count"`+`"bytes"` is the operator signal that thresholds are too high relative to arrival rate. The payload layer gains a pure `render_batch(bodies: &[Bytes], format: BatchFormat) -> (Bytes, &'static str)` helper that hands back the framed body and its content type (`application/json` for JSON array, `application/x-ndjson` for NDJSON); both formats treat an empty input gracefully (`[]` and `""` respectively) even though the state machine never flushes an empty batcher, so the function is self-contained and unit-testable independently of the publisher. Empty and binary message bodies are preserved byte-verbatim by the renderer — it never re-parses the JSON bodies produced by `serialize()`, it only concatenates them with the format's framing (`,` for JSON array or `\n` for NDJSON), so a receiver gets the same per-message bytes on the wire regardless of whether the target is batching. Eighteen new tests pin the contract: ten unit tests in `batch::tests` (push below thresholds buffers, count threshold flushes, bytes threshold flushes, simultaneous cap hit labels Count, lone-oversized push still flushes via Bytes, empty drain yields None, non-empty drain labels Drain, flush bodies preserve insertion order, `as_str()` emits the exact metric tokens, `pending_bytes` tracks raw bodies not framing overhead); seven unit tests in `payload::tests` covering single/multi/empty for both formats plus byte-verbatim preservation; and six `tests/publish_integration.rs` end-to-end tests against `wiremock` (count threshold emits one POST with three JSON array entries in insertion order, NDJSON format uses the `application/x-ndjson` content type with terminating newline per RFC 7464, shutdown drain flushes a below-threshold batch exactly once, `batch_enabled = None` retains per-message dispatch unchanged, delivery-id header and body are stable across a batched request's 503→200 retry so downstream deduplication still works, and construction-time rejection of batching + `RawXml` format). Closes #906.
- **Federation JWT: Ed25519 (EdDSA, RFC 8037) signing and verification (refs #952)** — `rustgate_federation::jwt::JwtAuthority` gains two new constructors, `new_ed25519(pkcs8_der, kid, issuer)` and the paired verifier builder `with_ed25519_verifier(kid, public_key_raw)`, sitting alongside the existing HS256 and ES256 entry points with the same asymmetric-crypto security model (private signing key held by the issuing peer, public verifier keys registered per-`kid` by every relying peer, compromised verifier cannot forge tokens). Implementation details: `Algorithm` grew an `EdDsa` variant whose JWT header string is exactly `"EdDSA"` per RFC 8037 §3.1 (**not** `"Ed25519"` — verifiers reject the latter as `UnsupportedAlgorithm`), `SigningKey` grew a boxed `ring::signature::Ed25519KeyPair` variant (boxed for parity with the existing `EcdsaKeyPair` box so `large_enum_variant` stays quiet even on HS256-only authorities that pay no key cost), and `VerificationKey` grew a raw 32-byte `EdDsa` variant that accepts exactly RFC 8032 §5.1.5 raw bytes — no SPKI, no PEM, no JWK wrapping, callers unwrap at the boundary (extract directly from `Ed25519KeyPair::public_key().as_ref()` or the base64url `x` field of a `kty=OKP, crv=Ed25519` JWK). The ring-backed signing path is deterministic (RFC 8032 §5.1.6) so the same `(key, claims)` pair always produces byte-identical tokens — a property pinned by a new `ed25519_signature_is_deterministic` regression and a deliberate choice that eliminates the nonce-reuse footgun that plagues ECDSA, which is the single biggest operational reason to prefer EdDSA over ES256 for new federation deployments. The existing `alg`-confusion defence in `decode()` extends for free: a token header claiming `alg: HS256` with a `kid` that routes to an Ed25519 verifier is rejected with `AlgorithmMismatch { header: Hs256, key: EdDsa }` before any signature check, preventing the "feed the 32-byte Ed25519 public key into HMAC as a shared secret" attack. Key-material validation is defence-in-depth: `new_ed25519` rejects malformed PKCS#8 and — pinned by `new_ed25519_rejects_ecdsa_pkcs8` — also rejects a structurally-valid ECDSA P-256 PKCS#8 blob because ring checks the `AlgorithmIdentifier` inside the DER; `with_ed25519_verifier` rejects any public key that is not exactly 32 bytes so a caller that forgets to strip an SPKI wrapper or that accidentally passes a 33-byte compressed SEC1 point fails at registration time rather than silently producing an always-InvalidSignature verifier. Thirteen new unit tests mirror the ES256 suite: round-trip issue/validate, cross-authority verification via registered public key, header shape (`alg=EdDSA`, `typ=JWT`, `kid=…`), `UnknownKid` routing, no-`kid` rejection on EdDSA authorities (they have `legacy_verifier: None`, same as ES256), `AlgorithmMismatch` against an HS256-forged header, tampered signature (64-zero-byte pad keeps length valid but verification fails), tampered payload, malformed PKCS#8, cross-algorithm PKCS#8, 31-byte and 33-byte public key rejection, `InvalidKid` for empty / oversized / control-char / non-ASCII identifiers, the determinism pin, and a "wrong 32-byte public key registered under the right kid produces InvalidSignature not AlgorithmMismatch" cross-registration test. No behaviour change for existing HS256 or ES256 deployments — the APIs are purely additive, tokens currently-in-flight continue to validate unchanged, and the shared validation pipeline (expiry, issuer, revocation, clock-skew) applies identically. This is part 1 of three for #952; JWKS URL fetching and the `kid` rotation-window state machine ship in follow-up PRs.
- **HTTP egress response body capture for acknowledgement IDs and error details (refs #906)** — `TargetConfig` in `rustgate-http` gains two opt-in fields, `capture_response_body: Option<bool>` (default `false`) and `max_response_body_bytes: Option<usize>` (default `4 KiB`, hard-capped at `1 MiB` by config validation), letting a single target surface the response body of every 2xx HTTP publish on a dedicated `tracing::debug!` line alongside the per-request `delivery_id`. Operators can now grep the access log to recover downstream acknowledgement IDs — Splunk HEC `ackId`, Elastic `_id`, Loki `traceID`, Datadog `id` — without a receiver-side proxy. The capture is *symmetric but asymmetrically gated*: success bodies surface only when the flag is `true` (so existing deployments are not suddenly flooded with receive-side payload logs), but error bodies are *always* captured and embedded in the failure log's `error` field plus the `http_publish_failed` audit event string, because structured 4xx/5xx error details from SIEM collectors are the highest-leverage diagnostic signal and the bytes were going to be drained either way to keep the reqwest connection pool healthy. Rendering goes through `String::from_utf8_lossy` + `rustgate_core::sanitize::sanitize_for_log`, which replaces invalid UTF-8 with U+FFFD and strips CR/LF/control characters — this defends against log-forging attacks where a malicious webhook returns `"real\r\n[audit] fake_event=success"` and tries to inject a counterfeit log line into operator grep results. Memory is defended in depth: the per-target `max_response_body_bytes` is clamped against a crate-wide `MAX_ERROR_RESPONSE_BYTES = 1 MiB` ceiling *and* the helper short-circuits when the server's advertised `Content-Length` exceeds that ceiling, so a malicious target cannot trick the publisher into allocating multi-MB buffers for a body it is about to truncate anyway. A config validator in `rustgate_http::config::HttpConfig::validate` rejects `max-response-body-bytes > 1 MiB` at construction time with `HttpError::Config("target ...: max-response-body-bytes (N) exceeds the 1 MiB cap")`, so an operator mistake fails fast at startup rather than showing up as silent log truncation in production. A new Prometheus counter `rustgate_http_response_bodies_captured_total{target}` registers via the existing `OnceLock` + `init()` + accessor pattern in `rustgate-http/src/metrics.rs` and increments on every captured success body — a flat-lining rate against a climbing `rustgate_http_publishes_total` is the operator signal that the target is returning empty acknowledgement bodies (either the target does not emit them, or the capture was misconfigured). The refactored `send_request` now returns `Result<Option<Bytes>, (Option<u16>, String, Option<Duration>)>` where `Ok(Some(body))` is a 2xx with captured body, `Ok(None)` is either a 2xx-with-capture-off or a 2xx-with-empty-body, and the `Err` tuple carries the numeric status, a formatted error string that always embeds the body snippet when non-empty, and the parsed `Retry-After` header on 429s. The `bytes::Bytes::slice(0..cap)` truncation is zero-copy — a ref-count bump + offset update rather than a `memcpy` — so the captured prefix aliases the reqwest-allocated response body and drops it automatically when the tracing field finishes formatting. Sixteen new tests pin the contract: four unit tests on `format_body_snippet` (preserves UTF-8 JSON, replaces invalid UTF-8 bytes with U+FFFD, sanitises CR/LF log-forging attempts, handles empty bodies), five unit tests on `capture_response_body` (success returns full body, disabled returns None but still drains, empty 204 returns None, oversized body clamps at per-target cap, Content-Length above the ceiling short-circuits before body read), five config-validation unit tests (defaults are conservative, explicit values round-trip through the accessor, above-1-MiB is rejected, 1-MiB boundary is accepted, kebab-case TOML round-trips both fields), and five integration tests in `tests/publish_integration.rs` against `wiremock` (success path completes with capture enabled, capture disabled still drains the body, 5xx body surfaces through the failure path and trips the circuit breaker, oversized 5-KiB body truncates silently at the 1-KiB cap without tripping the circuit, publisher construction rejects a 2-MiB cap with the documented error). The two new metric-schema regression pins in `rustgate-http/src/metrics.rs` extend the existing stability tests to cover the new counter's fully-qualified name `rustgate_http_response_bodies_captured_total`, its single `["target"]` label, and its idempotent `OnceLock` pointer identity. This PR focuses on the response-body half of #906; the batch/bulk endpoint support is tracked in a follow-up.
- **`check-cert-expiry` diagnostic CLI subcommand** — operator-facing pre-flight that inspects one or more PEM files and reports whether any contained X.509 certificate is within a configurable warning window of its `notAfter` time, already expired, or not-yet-valid. Intended to be wired into cron, CI smoke, or `systemd`'s `OnFailure=` hook: the binary's exit code encodes severity on a monotonic ladder — `0` when every cert in every file is valid and outside the warning window, `1` when at least one cert is within `--warn-days` (default 30) and nothing worse was seen, `2` for any harder failure (expired, not-yet-valid, or a file that could not be read/parsed). A single unreadable file alongside an otherwise-OK cert elevates `overall_status` to `expired` so a missing PEM in production never hides behind a passing sibling — the rationale is that an operator running this subcommand from cron cares about "is my TLS material healthy", and a missing file is an operational failure regardless of what else parsed. Every `CERTIFICATE` block in each PEM is inspected independently so chains, bundles, and single-cert files all work transparently; non-CERTIFICATE blocks (keys, DH parameters) are silently skipped, but a file with zero CERTIFICATE blocks is reported as `no_certificate_blocks` so a wrong-file typo surfaces loudly. The stable JSON contract exposes `warn_days`, `overall_status`, `min_days_until_expiry`, and a `files[]` array where each entry carries either an `error` string (mutually exclusive with `certs`) or a `certs[]` list whose per-entry shape (`index`, `subject_cn`, `not_before`, `not_after`, `seconds_until_expiry`, `days_until_expiry`, `status`) is pinned by unit tests — same treatment as the existing `cert-info` and `crl-info` subcommands. `build_report(paths, warn_days, now)` takes `now: OffsetDateTime` as an explicit parameter so tests can pin the clock for deterministic not-yet-valid and expiry-window verdicts without flaking on wall time; `run()` is a thin wrapper that uses real `now_utc()` and returns the computed exit code so the `main.rs` dispatch can `std::process::exit(code)` only on non-zero. The new module `crates/rustgate-server/src/diagnostics/check_cert_expiry.rs` reuses `first_rdn_value` / `asn1_to_rfc3339` patterns from `cert_info.rs` so operators see the same subject-CN and timestamp rendering across the three diagnostics subcommands. Sixteen new unit tests cover the full status ladder (ok / expiring / expired / not-yet-valid), multi-file bundles with mixed statuses, file-level errors escalating the overall verdict, the `--warn-days 0` degenerate case, `min_days_until_expiry` correctness across multiple certs, the `run` empty-paths rejection, the stable JSON top-level keys, the human-render markers, and the monotonic severity ordering invariant. (Refs #900)
- **Per-peer gRPC compression for V2 federation (gzip, zstd)** — `PeerConfig` gains an optional `compression: Option<CompressionKind>` field (default `None`) that opts a single outbound peer into gRPC-level payload compression without affecting any other peer. The new `CompressionKind` enum in `rustgate_federation::config` carries two variants — `Gzip` (RFC 1952, the widely-supported default choice) and `Zstd` (RFC 8478, better ratio at comparable CPU cost but requires tonic 0.10+ on the peer) — and serializes as lowercase `"gzip"` / `"zstd"` tokens matching the existing `RoutingMode` precedent. An unrecognised token (`"snappy"`, `"lz4"`, `"brotli"`, a typo) is rejected by serde rather than silently falling back to `Gzip`, so operator config mistakes surface at parse time instead of showing up as a peer that never sends compressed traffic. `skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none"` keeps pre-#905 config files byte-identical on round-trip: a peer that has not opted in still serializes without any `compression` key. On the client side, `V2ClientConfig` gains a matching `compression` field; when `Some(kind)`, `v2/client.rs::connection_loop` chains `.send_compressed(enc).accept_compressed(enc)` onto the `FederatedChannelClient` before the first RPC, where `enc` comes from a small private `compression_encoding()` helper that maps `CompressionKind → tonic::codec::CompressionEncoding`. On the server side, `v2/server.rs::FederatedChannelServer::new` now unconditionally chains `.accept_compressed(Gzip).accept_compressed(Zstd)` — tonic inspects the incoming `grpc-encoding` header and decodes lazily, so accepting both codecs is zero-cost when no peer sends compressed payloads. This design keeps the fleet mixed-version-safe: a rustgate server on a new build accepts both compressed and uncompressed traffic from any peer regardless of whether that peer has opted in on its own side. The `tonic` workspace features are extended with `gzip` and `zstd` (which pull in `flate2` and `zstd` respectively); both are already transitive through other common tonic consumers so the dependency count is unchanged in the canonical feature set. Eleven new unit tests in `config::tests` pin the serde contract (lowercase token round-trips both ways, unknown-codec rejection, `Copy`/equality bounds on the enum, default-None backward compat, `skip_serializing_if` suppression, full `PeerConfig` round-trips with gzip and zstd), two in `v2::client::tests` pin the `compression_encoding` mapping for both variants, and three integration tests in `tests/v2_integration.rs` drive a compression-aware mTLS server through `send_one_event` with a gzip-compressed client, a zstd-compressed client, and a plain uncompressed client — confirming the server decodes gzip, decodes zstd, and still serves pre-#905 peers unchanged. (Closes #905)
- **WebSocket `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` subprotocol negotiation (RFC 6455 §4.2.2)** — `WsListenerConfig` gains a new `supported_subprotocols: Vec<String>` field (default empty, preserving pre-#884 behaviour) that the listener advertises during the upgrade handshake. The handshake path now uses `accept_hdr_async_with_config` with a new `negotiate_subprotocol()` selector that returns a three-way `NegotiationOutcome { Selected(String), NoProtocolRequired, Unsupported }`: `Selected` echoes the chosen token in the response header and records it on `WsSession::negotiated_subprotocol()` for downstream code; `NoProtocolRequired` omits the response header (server empty OR client silent — RFC-compliant); `Unsupported` short-circuits the handshake with HTTP 400 Bad Request so operators see mismatches surfaced in server logs rather than as cryptic client-side `SubProtocolError` traces. Selection is case-sensitive per RFC 7230 ABNF tokens, honours client preference order (scans client tokens, takes the first that matches any server-advertised token), accepts both multi-header and comma-folded list-valued headers per RFC 7230 §3.2.2, and trims whitespace around comma-separated tokens. Token lookup runs in O(|client| × |server|) over the configured list — fine for the single-digit protocol counts deployments actually ship. New CLI flag `--ws-subprotocols` (env `RUSTGATE_WS_SUBPROTOCOLS`) accepts a comma-separated list in server-preference order; an empty list (the default) leaves subprotocol negotiation disabled for backward compatibility. 14 new unit tests in `subprotocol_selection` pin the selection semantics (client-preference wins, case-sensitivity, multi-header flattening, empty-token trimming, whitespace handling), plus 5 new integration tests in `tests/ws_subprotocol.rs` that drive a real `tokio_tungstenite` client against a real `WsListener` over mTLS+TLS and assert the full response header round-trip, the `WsSession::negotiated_subprotocol()` accessor, the 400-reject behaviour when client and server speak disjoint sets, and the comma-folded header parse path. Closes the subprotocol half of #884; the permessage-deflate compression extension (RFC 7692) is deferred — `tokio-tungstenite` 0.29 has no native support and a manual implementation would roughly double the PR size, so compression is tracked separately for a follow-up.
- **HKDF-SHA256 key derivation for encrypted archives (`KeyFile::key_derivations`)** — optional `BTreeMap<String, Derivation>` sibling to the existing `keys` map in `rustgate_core::encrypted::KeyFile`. Operators holding a single high-entropy root secret (KMS blob, HSM output, another rustgate deployment's master key) can now derive multiple archive subkeys deterministically without re-provisioning raw hex. Each entry takes the shape `{ "kdf": "hkdf-sha256", "ikm": "<hex>", "salt": "<hex>", "info": "<utf8>" }`; the `tag = "kdf"` envelope leaves room for future Argon2id variants for passphrase-derived keys, which is explicitly out-of-scope for this change (HKDF adds no work factor and is unsuitable for low-entropy passphrases). `KeyRing::from_bytes` evaluates derivations after raw entries, inserting the 32-byte result into the same in-memory map so derived keys are indistinguishable from raw keys at use time — they can be the active key, a historical decrypt key, and carry a `key_expirations` entry identically. An id appearing in both `keys` and `key_derivations` is rejected before any decoding or derivation, because silently preferring one entry would hide the operator typo. IKM is floored at 16 bytes (HKDF adds no entropy — a trivially-short IKM produces a trivially-short-security subkey), empty salt follows RFC 5869 § 3.1 (maps to `Hkdf::new(None, ikm)`), and intermediate decoded IKM lives inside `Zeroizing<Vec<u8>>` so it is wiped the moment HKDF's extract stage is done with it. A new `EncryptError::KeyDerivation { id, reason }` variant surfaces per-entry failures without leaking IKM or salt bytes into the error string. Thirteen new tests pin the wiring: RFC 5869 Test Case 3 exact vector (empty salt + empty info, the canonical case where the spec's info octets align with UTF-8), info-separation independence, derived-key end-to-end round-trip through `EncryptedWriter` + `decrypt_file`, mixed raw-and-derived key files, id-overlap rejection, IKM floor, invalid hex IKM, empty-salt acceptance, derived-only configuration, the updated "not found in keys or key_derivations" error message, derivations honoring `key_expirations`, unknown-KDF rejection at parse time (so an older binary reading a newer key file with `argon2id` fails loudly rather than silently ignoring the entry), and the `serde` round-trip with `skip_serializing_if` so pre-KDF key files remain byte-identical. Adds the `hkdf = "0.12"` crate to the workspace (RustCrypto, small, depends on already-present `hmac` + `sha2`). (Refs #883)
- **MQTT post-route egress fan-out to NATS / federation / HTTP sinks** — `rustgate-mqtt` PUBLISH hot path now threads the same three-way egress fan-out the WebSocket transport has carried since #890, so operators who front their deployment with MQTT clients get scale-out via the NATS bridge, server-to-server delivery via the federation forwarder, and webhook delivery via the HTTP publisher without having to bridge through a second transport. The three callback type aliases (`OnNatsPublish`, `OnFederationForward`, `OnHttpForward`) are promoted from `rustgate-websocket::server` (where they originated) to a new `rustgate-core::egress` module so any future session-level transport (WebTransport, QUIC, raw TCP) can reuse the same shapes without depending on a sibling transport crate; `rustgate-websocket` re-exports them through `server` for backward compatibility with existing call sites. A new `MqttForwardingHooks` bundle (`nats_publish`, `federation_forward`, `http_forward`) sits alongside the existing `MqttSessionHooks` on `MqttServerConfig`; both use independent `Option<Arc<dyn Fn>>` slots so each sink can be disabled individually and the `None`-bundle case stays at zero runtime cost. On the session side, `handle_publish_v5` and `handle_publish_v4` now call `router.route_for_egress(msg).await` (the Send-PEP-aware cousin of the old `route()` that returns `None` when the router drops the message via dedup / TTL / Send-authz deny / oversize) and only fire the three callbacks when the router returns `Some(Arc<RoutableMessage>)` — so a dedup'd or denied publish acks the client but does not fan out. A new `fire_forwarding` helper is called *before* the PUBLISH admission observer (`on_publish`) so callbacks see every routable message including those that never make it to the metric; the PUBACK path is lifted into `ack_publish_v5` / `ack_publish_v4` helpers to keep the two versions consistent. The server crate's `start_mqtt` entry point is refactored into a `MqttSetup<'a, P>` struct (mirroring the existing `WebSocketSetup`) so the call site threads `nats_publisher`, `fed_forward`, and `http_forward` by reference, each leg feature-gated behind `#[cfg(feature = "nats|federation|http")]`; the `MqttSetup` struct carries the narrow `#[allow(clippy::too_many_arguments)]` justification the old function did. Six new tests pin the contract: four inline `config::tests` (default-all-None, Debug-None rendering, Debug-Some-each-field rendering, and Arc-strong-count-sharing under Clone — mirroring the existing `MqttSessionHooks` suite) and two new `mqtt_integration.rs` tests (`publish_fires_all_three_forwarding_callbacks_once` — mTLS-authenticated PUBLISH fires all three sinks exactly once with the same post-route payload + the publisher's cert-derived `alpha` group on the federation leg; `publish_with_no_forwarding_hooks_does_not_panic` — `None`-bundle QoS 1 PUBLISH still returns a clean PUBACK). (Closes #903)
- **NATS request/reply pattern (`NatsRequestClient`, `NatsRequestResponder`)** — new `crates/rustgate-nats/src/request.rs` module adds bidirectional query support over the existing NATS connection, separate from the streaming pub/sub bridge. `NatsAdapter::request_client()` wraps `async_nats::Client::send_request` with a 5-second default per-call timeout (override via `with_timeout` or `request_with_timeout`) and maps the `async-nats` error taxonomy into a rustgate-owned `RequestError` enum with four explicit variants: `Timeout { subject, timeout }`, `NoResponders { subject }`, `HandlerError { subject, message }`, and `Client { subject, source }` — so callers can pattern-match the common failure modes without depending on the `async-nats` crate directly. `NatsAdapter::request_responder(handler)` returns `Option<NatsRequestResponder>` — `Some` only when the new `NatsConfig::request_subject: Option<String>` is set, making the responder strictly opt-in. The responder subscribes to the configured subject, dispatches each request to the caller-supplied handler on an independent `spawn_background` task (slow or panicking handlers cannot block the loop), and publishes the handler's result on `msg.reply`; handler errors are relayed via a new `NATS-Rustgate-Error` reply header that the client side decodes into `RequestError::HandlerError` to distinguish "handler rejected the request" from "no responders" or "timeout". The handler signature is `Arc<dyn Fn(Bytes) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = Result<Bytes, String>> + Send>> + Send + Sync>` (aliased as `NatsRequestHandler`) — the same async-callback shape used elsewhere in the workspace (see `rustgate_enrollment::contacts::ContactsProvider`). Nine new config validation tests reject wildcards, control characters, whitespace, empty strings, and non-ASCII in `request_subject`, and confirm the default is `None` (zero behaviour change for existing deployments). Five unit tests in `request.rs` pin the error-display format, the `ERROR_HEADER` constant value, the default timeout, and that the handler alias accepts idiomatic async closures. Five integration tests (all gated on `require_nats!()`) cover the happy-path round trip with an echo handler, `NoResponders` on an unrelated subject when a responder is running elsewhere, `HandlerError` propagation via the reply header, `Timeout` when the handler sleeps past the per-call budget, and the "no `request_subject` → `request_responder` returns `None`" opt-in contract. Closes #907b.
- **NATS consumer-side subject filtering (`NatsConfig::subject_filters`)** — optional `Vec<String>` on the NATS bridge that narrows which subjects the JetStream pull consumer asks for at the wire level, instead of receiving every `{subject_prefix}.>` message and filtering after receipt in `extract_group_from_subject`. Empty (the default) preserves the existing `{prefix}.>` wildcard behavior, a single entry is passed as JetStream's `filter_subject`, and two or more entries go to `filter_subjects` (requires server 2.10+, which is now enabled on the workspace `async-nats` dependency via the zero-cost `server_2_10` feature flag). NATS wildcards (`*` single-token, `>` tail) are accepted inside each filter so operators can subscribe to narrow slices like `points.ALPHA.>` or `points.*.update.v2`. Validation enforces that every entry starts with `{subject_prefix}.` — a filter that escapes the stream's subject space would bind to an always-empty consumer and silently drop all traffic — and rejects empty strings, control chars, whitespace, DEL, and non-ASCII the same way `subject_prefix` itself is guarded. `build_consumer_config` owns the dispatch between the singular and plural wire fields and leaves the unused one at its default (`""` / `vec![]`) because JetStream treats both-populated as a consumer-create-time error. Fifteen new unit tests (ten in `config.rs` covering the round-trip, multi-pattern, wildcard-allowance, out-of-prefix rejection, exact-prefix rejection, empty-entry, control-char, space, DEL, and non-ASCII paths, plus validation-ordering against a bad `subject_prefix`; five in `subscriber.rs` pinning empty-falls-back-to-wildcard, single-entry-uses-singular, multi-entry-uses-plural, insertion-order preservation, and the explicit `{prefix}.>` round-trip). No behavioural change for existing deployments — the field defaults to an empty vec and the wire stays on `{prefix}.>` until an operator opts in. (Refs #907)
- **Circuit breaker `OnStateChange` observer hook + HTTP publisher auto-drain trigger point** — `rustgate-resilience::circuit::CircuitBreaker` gains a lock-free observer callback set once at construction time via the new `.with_on_state_change(cb)` builder. The callback alias `pub type OnStateChange = Arc<dyn Fn(u8, u8) + Send + Sync>` receives `(old_state, new_state)` on every transition using the newly-promoted `pub const STATE_CLOSED / STATE_OPEN / STATE_HALF_OPEN: u8` constants so callers can pattern-match instead of hardcoding 0/1/2. The observer is stored in a `OnceLock` — a second `with_on_state_change` call silently no-ops per OnceLock semantics, and the zero-observer path costs a single atomic pointer check per transition (no extra work on the hot `allow_request` path). Transitions fire the observer inside the existing `prev != STATE_*` guards in `close()` / `trip()` / `try_half_open()`, so redundant same-state writes do not spam subscribers (pinned by `on_state_change_does_not_fire_on_identical_state_writes`). The struct's derived `Debug` is replaced with a manual impl that renders each atomic/counter via `Ordering::Relaxed` loads and prints a boolean `configured` flag for the callback field via `finish_non_exhaustive()` — matching the workspace pattern used by `HttpPublisher`, `SpiffeHooks`, `AuthState`, and `JwtAuthority` (a `dyn Fn` cannot derive `Debug`). Downstream, `rustgate-http::publisher::build_target` now attaches a per-target observer via `build_circuit_observer(&tc.name)` that fires only on `Open → HalfOpen` (the cooldown-elapsed "target probably recovered" moment the DLQ auto-drain needs); the other transitions already emit `http_circuit_tripped` / `http_circuit_recovered` at the `record_failure` / `record_success` call sites in `publish_with_retry` and firing the observer there too would double-log. A new `audit::http_circuit_probing(target)` event labels the probe-window entry for the forensic trail, and the Prometheus `rustgate_http_circuit_state{target}` gauge now reaches value `2` (half-open) during the probe window so dashboards can distinguish "target is being re-tested" from "target is healthy" and from "target is tripped". Seven new breaker-level tests pin the full recovery cycle (Closed→Open→HalfOpen→Closed in order), the set-once silence contract, the None-by-default zero-cost path, and each of the four transition arms individually; four new HTTP publisher tests pin direct-invocation, unrelated-transition no-op, end-to-end gauge behaviour via a real breaker, and the `Send + Sync` bounds on the callback alias. No behavioural change for operators who never configured the observer — the zero-cost path is the default. Refs #881 (DLQ auto-drain on target recovery — the observer wiring is the infrastructure piece; the replay of dead-lettered messages back through the publisher channel is the follow-up now that the probe-window trigger exists).
- **`rustgate cert-info` and `rustgate crl-info` diagnostic subcommands** — two offline inspection tools that parse PEM-encoded X.509 certificates and CRLs without having to start the server, addressing Findings F-178 and F-183 of issue #900. Both live under the new `crates/rustgate-server/src/diagnostics/` module. The `cert-info` command emits `CertReport` with 22 stable fields (subject CN, issuer CN, serial hex, `notBefore` / `notAfter` in RFC 3339, `valid_now` / `expired` booleans, `seconds_until_expiry` signed i64, SHA-256 fingerprint, organization, country, groups, SPIFFE ID, SAN DNS / URI / IP / email, key usage, extended key usage, `is_ca`, signature algorithm). Groups extraction exactly mirrors `rustgate_transport::extract::extract_groups` — splits OU values on `,` with a JSON-array `[...]` fallback — so the diagnostic view stays consistent with what the runtime router sees. The `crl-info` command emits `CrlReport` (issuer CN, `thisUpdate` / `nextUpdate`, `stale` boolean, `seconds_until_next_update`, revoked count, and a `Vec<RevokedEntry>` with serial hex + revocation date + optional RFC 5280 reason). Both subcommands take a PEM file path and an optional `--json` flag; the JSON shape is the public contract, pinned by 20 new unit tests (11 `cert_info` + 9 `crl_info`) that cover happy-path fields, IPv4 / IPv6 / unknown-length IP SAN formatting, expired-cert detection, missing file, garbage input, CRL freshness, multi-entry CRLs, and stable JSON layout. The existing `rustls-pki-types` + `x509-parser` deps are promoted from `optional` to unconditional in `rustgate-server/Cargo.toml` (both are already transitive through `rustgate-transport` so this adds no build cost); `time = { workspace = true }` is added for RFC 3339 rendering. The dispatch in `main.rs` runs before tokio/tracing/config init so the commands are usable in break-glass scenarios on hosts that cannot otherwise launch the server. Human-readable output is deliberately *not* a contract and may evolve.
- **Offline reader for encrypted DLQ files (`rustgate_http::dlq_reader`)** — companion to the writer in `crates/rustgate-http/src/dlq.rs`. Decrypts a `.dlq.enc` artifact with the operator's `KeyRing` and yields typed `OwnedDlqEntry` records for forensic review or replay. Two entry points: `read_dlq_file(path, key_ring) -> Vec<OwnedDlqEntry>` for the common "load it all" case and `for_each_dlq_entry(path, key_ring, cb)` for streaming consumers that want to stop on first callback error (e.g. a future replay driver that halts on the first undeliverable record). Decryption lands in a `tempfile::NamedTempFile` scoped to the function call so plaintext never persists to disk beyond the reader's lifetime. The parser is a `serde_json::Deserializer::into_iter` stream, so concatenated JSON objects with no delimiter (the current writer shape) and any future whitespace-delimited variant both parse correctly. Errors are categorised as `DlqReadError::{Decrypt,Io,Json,PayloadDecode}` so operators can distinguish AEAD integrity failures (wrong key, torn write, tampered chunk, unknown key id) from schema regressions, I/O issues, or malformed base64 payloads. Ten inline tests pin the contract: end-to-end round-trip against the writer (multi-entry, binary payload, empty payload), sealed-but-empty file acceptance, wrong-key rejection, unterminated-file rejection (simulated truncation after writer drop), missing-file error shape, early-abort on callback error, binary-payload base64 round-trip, invalid-base64 rejection, concatenated-JSON parsing without delimiters, and strict-required-field deserialization. (Refs #881)
- **HTTP DLQ per-target total-bytes cap with drop-oldest FIFO eviction** — `crates/rustgate-http/src/dlq.rs` gains an optional `dlq-max-target-bytes` config field that bounds the total on-disk DLQ footprint for a single target across every rotated file. When the sealed-tail footprint exceeds the cap after a rotation, the oldest `.dlq.enc` segments are deleted until the footprint fits; the currently-active segment is always preserved so the live `SharedEncryptedWriter`'s in-memory state cannot be corrupted.
