The fix replaces the `Vec<DistinguishedName>` field with `ArcSwap<&'static [DistinguishedName]>` and rebuilds the slice alongside the inner `WebPkiClientVerifier` inside `current_verifier()` on every trust-store generation advance. Escaping the `arc_swap::Guard` lifetime to return a `&[DN]` with `&self` lifetime (required by the `ClientCertVerifier` trait) without `unsafe_code` is resolved by leaking each refreshed slice with `Vec::leak` — the `'static` payload trivially outlives any `&self` borrow, and the leak is bounded by the rotation rate (rare; a few hundred bytes per CA rotation). On rebuild failure the fresh slice is *not* leaked — the old hints stay in lockstep with the old cached verifier so handshakes never advertise CAs whose keys we cannot validate against. **F-51** — `BackpressureGate::with_resume_dwell`, `set_on_deferred`, and `set_on_bytes_changed` all rely on `Arc::get_mut`, which only succeeds while the `Arc` has a single strong reference. Before this fix the setters used `debug_assert!` + `if let Some(this) = Arc::get_mut(self)` + silent no-op; in release builds `debug_assert!` is stripped, so calling any of the three setters after the gate had already been cloned into the router and the accept loop would drop the configuration on the floor with no log, no panic, and no error. The most visible symptom was `admission_deferred_total` / `queued_bytes` gauges frozen at zero despite the gate actively throttling — an operator reading the dashboard would see "backpressure is healthy" while the system was in fact refusing new connections. All three setters now return `Result<(), BackpressureConfigError::AlreadyShared { setter }>` naming the offending setter, and `rustgate-server::main::run` propagates the error via `anyhow::Context` with a human-readable wrapper so startup fails loudly instead of limping along with missing instrumentation. Five new regression tests pin the contracts: `root_hint_subjects_refreshes_after_ca_rotation` confirms a second CA surfaces in the hint list after a generation bump; `root_hint_subjects_keeps_old_list_on_rebuild_error` confirms a failed rebuild leaves the previous hint list intact (not leaked, not partially replaced); `setters_return_err_after_clone` exercises each of the three setters against an already-cloned `Arc` and asserts the error variant; `setters_succeed_before_clone` confirms the happy path is unchanged; `config_error_display_names_setter` pins the `Display` output contains the setter name so an operator's log grep can identify the misordered call site. (Refs #814)
- **Backpressure gate no longer oscillates at the high-water boundary; hot-path callbacks must be non-blocking** — `rustgate_transport::BackpressureGate` now requires the in-flight byte counter to stay at or below `low_water` continuously for at least `resume_dwell` (default **1 second**) before admission resumes after a block. Previously, any drop to `low_water - 1` immediately cleared `blocking` and woke the accept loop, so a workload that hovered between `low_water + 1` and `low_water - 1` (e.g. one slow client feeding an evenly-sized fan-out) would flip admission on and off at the cadence of the TCP handshake loop — each new session's first message pushed the counter back over `high_water`, the permit drop dipped it under `low_water`, and the thrashing wasted CPU, spammed the `admission_deferred_total` metric, and could starve the server's per-host handshake-parallelism budget. The fix is an atomic `AtomicU64` cooldown timestamp (`below_low_since`, relative to a per-gate `tokio::time::Instant` epoch so `start_paused` tests stay deterministic under the virtual clock) that (a) arms on the first `sub` that drops the counter to or below `low_water` while blocking, (b) clears on any subsequent `add` that pushes back above `low_water`, and (c) is read by both `sub` and a new 100ms poll branch inside `wait_for_capacity` so dwell expiry can release the accept loop even when no further `sub` arrives. The hot path remains lock-free: `sub` short-circuits the dwell bookkeeping entirely when the gate is not blocking. A new `--backpressure-resume-dwell-ms` CLI flag (env `RUSTGATE_BACKPRESSURE_RESUME_DWELL_MS`, default 1000) lets operators tune the dwell — setting `0` restores pre-fix behaviour for bursty-but-not-oscillatory workloads where the latency cost matters. Separately, the `OnDeferred` and `OnBytesChanged` callback type docs now explicitly require non-blocking bodies: the gauge/counter update path fires on every byte-count change (i.e. potentially once per message), and `wait_for_capacity` is awaited on the TLS accept loop — a blocking callback there stalls the entire accept path and breaks admission control. Six new regression tests using `#[tokio::test(start_paused = true)]` + `tokio::time::advance` cover: default dwell keeps the gate blocked until the timer elapses, oscillation at the boundary cancels the in-flight cooldown, `wait_for_capacity` wakes via the internal poll without any external `sub`, a re-cross above `high_water` resets the dwell window, explicit `Duration::ZERO` preserves the legacy immediate-resume behaviour byte-for-byte, and the `Debug` impl surfaces the new field so operator log greps see it. (#878)
- **Gate `TestNatsServer::start()` on JetStream readiness, not just TCP `INFO` greeting** — `rustgate-test-utils`'s `TestNatsServer::try_start` previously returned as soon as the spawned `nats-server` subprocess replied to the NATS protocol `INFO` greeting, but `nats-server --jetstream` binds its TCP listener well before the JetStream subsystem finishes initialising and the meta-leader is elected. On a loaded runner the gap between "TCP accepts connections" and "JS API accepts requests" exceeds the 5s per-operation JetStream timeout, so any test that calls `jetstream.create_key_value(…)` (or `create_stream`, `create_consumer`, …) on the context returned from `TestNatsServer::jetstream()` flakes with `JetStream error: timed out` on the very first call. The symptom observed in CI was `create cm_b: failed to create federation-claims KV bucket` in `rustgate-federation::ha_integration::claim_gates_peer_connection`, but every one of the 14 `ha_integration.rs` tests and every current or future NATS-backed test in the workspace is exposed to the same race. `try_start` now chains a second readiness probe after the `INFO` greeting succeeds: a throwaway `async_nats::connect` + `jetstream::new` + `query_account` round-trip that maps to `$JS.API.ACCOUNT.INFO`, which only returns `Ok` once the JS meta-leader has been elected. The probe is bounded by the existing `READY_TIMEOUT` deadline so a genuinely broken JetStream configuration still fails fast, and its connection is dropped before `start()` returns so callers always hold a fresh client created through `TestNatsServer::jetstream()`. A new unit test in `test_utils::nats::tests` — `start_completes_only_after_jetstream_accepts_kv_create` — pins the invariant by creating a KV bucket and round-tripping a `put`/`get` immediately after `start()` returns, with no retry loop around the KV call. Also enables the async-nats `kv` feature on `rustgate-test-utils` so the regression test can construct a KV config without dragging in a parallel feature flag. (Fixes the flake that broke #976's CI on 2026-04-19.)
- **Relax PQ kx-group assertions so FIPS-plus-post-quantum CI stops reporting spurious failures** — `crates/rustgate-transport/tests/pq_kex.rs` had two assertions that were correct for the single-feature `post-quantum` build but deterministically failed under the CI command `cargo nextest run -p rustgate-transport --features proto,fips,post-quantum,ocsp,spiffe`: `pq_provider_includes_mlkem_groups` required `X25519` in `aws_lc_rs::default_provider().kx_groups`, and `pq_classical_client_falls_back_to_x25519` required the negotiated group between a ring-backed client and the PQ-backed server to be exactly `X25519`. When `rustls/fips` is active, `default_provider()` is restricted to FIPS-approved groups — `X25519MLKEM768` and the NIST curves `secp256r1/384r1/521r1` — and drops `X25519`, which is not FIPS-approved. The original issue (#957) framed this as a multi-test race against the process-global `CryptoProvider`, but the failure reproduces in isolation and repeats deterministically across runs: there is no race, it is a feature-combination mismatch. The provider-shape test now asserts the invariant we actually care about — "hybrid PQ is offered *and* at least one classical group remains negotiable" — accepting any of `X25519`, `secp256r1`, `secp384r1`, or `secp521r1` as the classical fallback. The negotiation test now asserts the negotiated group is *some* classical (non-PQ) group, because the correctness condition for "graceful fallback from a ring-only client" is "non-PQ group was chosen", not the specific identity of that group; FIPS forces the pair onto `secp256r1` where non-FIPS lands on `X25519`, and both outcomes are correct fallbacks. Verified by running the file under both feature sets: `--features post-quantum` → 8/8 pass, `--features proto,fips,post-quantum,ocsp,spiffe` → 8/8 pass. (#957)

### Security

- **Cap `ConnRateLimiter` IP map under IPv6 prefix scan and strip ANSI CSI sequences in `sanitize_for_log` (F-34, F-35)** — two core hardening fixes in `rustgate-resilience` and `rustgate-core` that close memory-exhaustion and log-injection residue under adversarial input. **F-34** — `rustgate_resilience::conn_rate_limiter::ConnRateLimiter` previously allocated a `VecDeque<Instant>` for every distinct `IpAddr` the MQTT and WebSocket listeners saw, with no hard cap and no IPv6 prefix collapsing. An attacker with a single /48 IPv6 allocation (2^80 source addresses, routinely available on residential ISPs and cloud VPS providers) could cycle source addresses by incrementing the host bits and bloat the per-limiter `HashMap<IpAddr, VecDeque<Instant>>` past server RAM in seconds, OOM-killing the process — the sliding-window sweep only fires lazily when the map grows past the 512-entry threshold, which is orders of magnitude below the attacker's flood rate. The fix is two-layer. A new `canonical_key` function normalizes every incoming address before insertion: IPv4 stays at /32 granularity (address scarcity bounds diversity) while IPv6 collapses to the /64 prefix (the smallest IPv6 allocation under RFC 4291 SLAAC), so an attacker cycling host bits within a /64 now cannot evade the rate limit and cannot inflate the map past one entry per /64. A new hard cap `DEFAULT_MAX_TRACKED_IPS = 65_536` — exactly 2^16, the worst-case number of /64 prefixes within a /48 allocation — bounds the map regardless of how many /64s the attacker controls; when the cap is reached and a previously-unseen key arrives, the entry with the oldest last-seen timestamp is evicted to make room (O(n) in the cap, but only fires when the cap is actually reached, which under realistic workloads never happens). The cap is configurable via the new `with_max_tracked_ips(usize)` builder method so tests can exercise eviction paths without allocating 64k entries. Six new regression tests pin the contract: `ipv6_addresses_in_same_64_share_bucket` confirms two IPv6 hosts differing only in the lower 64 bits are rate-limited as a single bucket, `ipv6_different_64_prefixes_are_isolated` confirms distinct /64 prefixes retain independent buckets, `ipv4_unaffected_by_prefix_collapse` confirms IPv4 is tracked at /32 (not lumped into /24 or similar), `map_size_capped_under_prefix_scan` walks 4× the cap through distinct /64 prefixes and asserts the map never exceeds the cap, `eviction_drops_least_recently_seen_key` seeds two IPs with ordered timestamps and asserts the older one is evicted when a third unique key arrives, and `repeat_inserts_on_same_key_do_not_trigger_eviction` confirms the cap guard only fires for previously-unseen keys (a legitimate client returning inside the window must not be dropped to make room for itself). **F-35** — `rustgate_core::sanitize::sanitize_for_log` previously replaced each control character (including `\x1b` ESC and `\x9b` C1 CSI) with `U+FFFD` using a per-character map, but the rest of the CSI escape sequence — parameter bytes like `[31m` — consists of printable ASCII and sailed through untouched. A malicious certificate CN like `"alice\x1b[1;31mFAKE LOG ENTRY\x1b[0m"` would appear in a log aggregator as `"alice�[1;31mFAKE LOG ENTRY�[0m"` — the introducer byte was replaced but the SGR parameters and final byte still rendered as styled text on any terminal downstream of the replaced ESC (an attacker can still force the log line to look like a different category of event to a SOC analyst grepping the file). The fix replaces the per-character `.map(...)` with a state-machine pass: on encountering `\x1b` (C0) or `\x9b` (C1), consume the full CSI body — parameter and intermediate bytes in `0x20..=0x3F`, terminated by a final byte in `0x40..=0x7E`, per ECMA-48 §5.4 — and replace the entire sequence with a single `U+FFFD`. Truncated sequences at end-of-input are handled by natural EOF on the inner loop; invalid inner bytes (e.g. a newline inside a CSI body) terminate the CSI scan and sanitize normally. Non-CSI ESC sequences (`\x1b` followed by a non-`[` byte like OSC `\x1b]…\x07` or `\x1bM`) still only replace the introducer byte — the issue scope is strictly CSI, and broader ESC-sequence stripping is deferred to a follow-up. Six new regression tests in `sanitize::tests` pin the contract: `ansi_csi_fully_consumed` covers red-SGR-around-text with multiple parameter groups, `c1_csi_fully_consumed` covers the 8-bit `\u{9B}` introducer and intermediate+final sequences like `\u{9B}?25l`, `esc_without_bracket_only_replaces_introducer` confirms non-CSI ESC sequences are not over-consumed, `truncated_csi_does_not_leak_body` confirms unterminated CSI at end-of-input produces a single U+FFFD with no body leak, `csi_terminated_by_invalid_byte_stops_cleanly` confirms a newline inside a CSI body cleanly terminates the scan and sanitizes the newline, and `log_forging_with_ansi_sequence_cannot_inject_styled_tail` is the end-to-end attacker-scenario regression. The five pre-existing tests (normal strings, newlines, control chars, unicode preservation, empty) continue to pass without modification — the single-character replacement path is preserved for every byte that is not a CSI introducer. (#810)
- **Bump `rustls-webpki` 0.103.12 → 0.103.13 to resolve RUSTSEC-2026-0104 (reachable panic in CRL parsing)** — `rustls-webpki` 0.103.12 contained a reachable panic in certificate-revocation-list parsing that an attacker who could feed a crafted CRL into the verification path could use to crash the process. rustgate consumes `rustls-webpki` transitively through `rustls` (TLS listener + client), `async-nats` (NATS/JetStream TLS client), and the federation/HTTP egress stacks, so every rustgate binary that loads an operator-supplied or peer-supplied CRL was in scope. Patched in 0.103.13; the fix is a pure `cargo update -p rustls-webpki --precise 0.103.13` on `Cargo.lock` and `fuzz/Cargo.lock` — no source changes are required because no crate pins an upper bound below 0.103.13 in `[workspace.dependencies]`. `cargo deny check advisories` now reports `ok` on both main and every open PR that rebased past this commit. (RUSTSEC-2026-0104)
- **Migrate HTTP-egress `pin-sha256` to RFC 7469 SPKI pinning** — `rustgate_http::pinning::PinnedCertVerifier` now computes `SHA-256(SubjectPublicKeyInfo DER)` on the leaf certificate and compares against the configured pins, rather than hashing the entire leaf DER. The old full-DER semantic was out of step with every mainstream pinning tool: Chromium, Mozilla, the RFC 7469 / HPKP `report-uri` ecosystem, and the standard OpenSSL pin recipe (`openssl x509 -pubkey -noout | openssl pkey -pubin -outform der | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | base64`) all hash SPKI. Operators generating pins from any of those sources would silently fail-closed against a rustgate binary because the pin in their config file matched the public key, not the whole cert. Worse, the previous behaviour actively punished good DevOps hygiene: a same-key cert rotation (fresh serial, fresh validity window, fresh SAN list, but the long-lived key material preserved) mutates the leaf DER and therefore mutated every deployed full-DER pin — every annual cert roll on every edge became a flag-day config push, with the inevitable result that tired operators just widened `pin-sha256` to an empty list and quietly turned off defense-in-depth. SPKI pinning inverts that: the pin survives same-key rotation and only breaks on the security-relevant event of a real key change, which is when an operator *does* want to know. The module-level docs in `crates/rustgate-http/src/pinning.rs`, the `TlsConfig::pin_sha256` field doc in `config.rs`, and the `docs/http-egress.md` Certificate Pinning section all document the RFC 7469 semantic and embed the canonical OpenSSL generation recipe. A new private `extract_spki_der` helper fails closed on a malformed cert via `TlsError::General("certificate SPKI extraction failed: …")` rather than panicking or silently admitting the connection, and is shared between the verifier hot path and a test-only `spki_pin` helper so the pin computation cannot drift between production and test fixtures. New `rustgate_test_utils::certs::generate_server_keypair` plus `TestCa::issue_server_cert_with_key(&KeyPair, cn, sans)` let tests model the same-key-different-cert flow; the existing `issue_server_cert` is refactored to delegate to the new helper so single-call usage is unchanged. Five new regression tests in `pinning::tests` pin the full observable contract: `distinct_keypairs_hash_to_distinct_spki_pins` (independent keys yield independent pins — the core key-sensitivity property that keeps a CA-compromise attacker from swapping the leaf), `spki_pin_survives_same_key_reissue` (the direct #948 regression guard — asserts reissued leaf DERs differ but SPKI bytes and SPKI pins stay identical), `verifier_accepts_matching_spki_pin_from_real_cert` (round-trips a real issued cert's pin through `b64::encode` → `parse_pins` to mirror config-file ingestion and confirm the verifier's hot path and the config loader compute the same 32 bytes), `legacy_full_der_pin_no_longer_matches` (a pre-#948 full-DER pin must not collide with the new SPKI pin for the same cert — silent acceptance would defeat the whole migration), and `extract_spki_der_rejects_malformed_cert` (the helper surfaces an x509-parser error as a `TlsError::General` so the handshake path fails closed on a malformed cert, not on a panic). **Breaking change for operators:** existing full-DER pins from pre-#948 deployments will stop matching on upgrade; regenerate each pin with the OpenSSL recipe in `docs/http-egress.md` or the module docs. A rolling upgrade can overlap both forms by running the old and new pin simultaneously across a canary window, since both are independent 32-byte base64 strings and the pin array is OR-matched. (Closes #948)
- **Guard release-artifact filenames against co-packaging collisions (F-21)** — `release-binary.yml` builds six archives from a 2×3 matrix (x86_64/aarch64 × base/fips/pq) and the "Package binary" shell step names each one `rustgate[-fips|-pq]-${VERSION}-${TARGET}.tar.gz`. The distinct discriminators (`fips`, `pq`, or unmarked) were correct as of today but the workflow had no structural guard against a future matrix edit silently producing two entries that compute the same archive name — `gh release upload --clobber` would then overwrite one with the other, the cosign signature and build-provenance attestation would be bound to whichever variant wrote last, and downstream `cosign verify-blob` consumers would admit a binary under the wrong identity. A new `scripts/check-release-artifact-names.py` parses `.github/workflows/release-binary.yml`, re-implements the Package-binary naming logic against each matrix entry, and asserts three invariants: (1) every entry produces a distinct archive filename, (2) each non-base entry carries its discriminator token (`-fips-` / `-pq-`) in the filename while the base build carries neither, and (3) every filename matches the shape `rustgate-[fips-|pq-]<version>-<target>.tar.gz`. A `fips=true + pq=true` combination is explicitly rejected as a misconfiguration (the workflow's `if/elif` would silently pick `fips`, making the `pq=true` flag a dead marker). The script runs in the existing `playbook-lint` CI job on every PR — not only those touching the workflow — so a rename in an unrelated helper that the workflow references surfaces before a release tag cuts in, and uses the standard `::error file=…::` annotation format so the GitHub UI highlights the offending line. Closes the F-21 caveat from the residual-findings audit (#887). The F-21 primary advisory (aws-lc-sys VEX entry, RUSTSEC-2026-0049) was already resolved in #777 — this PR closes the forward-looking "don't accidentally co-package" half that was deferred to a separate ticket. (#887)
- **Harden encrypted-archive writer against symlink TOCTOU and ChaCha20-Poly1305 nonce reuse** — `rustgate_core::encrypted::EncryptedWriter::create` now opens the target file with `O_NOFOLLOW` on Unix (via `OpenOptionsExt::custom_flags` with a platform-pinned `O_NOFOLLOW` constant), translating the kernel's `ELOOP`/`EMLINK` refusal into a new `EncryptError::SymlinkTarget { path }` variant. On a multi-tenant host an attacker who can plant a symlink at the archive path (store-forward queue, encrypted audit log) could previously redirect our `truncate + write` into any file the service account can open, silently overwriting unrelated data; `O_NOFOLLOW` is the atomic TOCTOU-free defense and intermediate components are still followed, matching the scope of the threat. A regression test plants a sensitive file under a symlink at the target path and asserts both that `create()` returns `SymlinkTarget` and that the sensitive file's contents survive untouched. Separately, the 32-bit per-file chunk counter used for nonce derivation — `nonce = base_nonce (8 bytes) || counter_be (4 bytes)` — had a reuse window at exhaustion: the old `write_chunk` / `finish` path incremented `counter` via `checked_add(1)` *after* sealing and persisting the chunk, so when `counter == u32::MAX` the ciphertext with nonce `(base, u32::MAX)` landed on disk, the increment errored, and `counter` stayed pinned at `u32::MAX`. A caller that ignored the `CounterOverflow` error (or subsequently called `finish()`) would re-seal under the same nonce — catastrophic for ChaCha20-Poly1305. Both methods now reserve the post-increment *before* computing the nonce and performing the AEAD seal, so refusal is atomic: if we cannot advance, we do not write. A new regression test sets the counter to `u32::MAX`, confirms `write_chunk` returns `CounterOverflow` without appending any bytes, confirms the counter is not silently wrapped, confirms a follow-up `finish()` also refuses, and confirms the resulting file — intentionally missing a terminator — is rejected by `decrypt_file` as `Truncated` so operators are forced to rotate the key or file instead of trusting a half-sealed archive. (#809)
- **Persist audit-chain tip across restarts for cross-boot tamper detection** — `rustgate_core::audit_chain` gains an explicit `<audit.jsonl>.anchor` sidecar file that pins the SHA-256 tip of the hash-chained audit log on clean shutdown and lets the next boot prove the chain was not tampered with while the service was down. `HashChainWriter` gains `with_tip_observer(Arc<ArcSwap<String>>)`: the writer atomically publishes its current chain tip on every chain advance, so shutdown code owning the observer can snapshot the latest hash even though the writer itself is hidden inside a `Mutex<Box<dyn Write>>` owned by the `tracing` subscriber. A new `check_chain_continuity(path) -> ChainContinuity` function reads the live tail hash via the existing torn-write-tolerant `read_chain_tip` helper and compares it to the persisted anchor, returning `NoAnchor` (fresh install — benign, no previous shutdown to match), `Match { tip }` (anchor agrees with live tip — clean restart, no tampering), or `Mismatch { anchor_tip, live_tip }` (anchor disagrees — the log was truncated, extended, or rewritten while the service was stopped). The `rustgate-server` binary wires all three pieces end-to-end: on startup it runs the continuity check against the configured `--audit-file` (plain-file path only; the rotating appender path is left for a follow-up), and on `Mismatch` it bails via `anyhow::bail!` so a hostile actor cannot silently edit the log offline and have the next boot continue the chain from the forged tip. Operators needing a one-shot escape hatch — e.g. intentional log rotation outside the service's lifecycle, or a manual archival operation that updates the tail — opt in via the new `--audit-allow-chain-break` flag (env `RUSTGATE_AUDIT_ALLOW_CHAIN_BREAK`, defaults `false`), which downgrades the break from fatal to audited: the new `audit::chain_discontinuity(audit_path, anchor_tip, live_tip, action, reason)` event is emitted after the tracing subscriber comes up, so the break is itself recorded as a cryptographically chained audit record from the new live tip forward. On graceful shutdown, the server snapshots the observed tip, calls `write_anchor`, and emits either `audit::chain_anchor_persisted` or `audit::chain_anchor_persist_failed` depending on whether the sidecar file was written. Ten new unit tests in `audit_chain.rs` cover the anchor write/read round-trip, malformed/truncated anchor payloads, the continuity verdicts (no anchor, match, mismatch against post-anchor extension, mismatch against post-anchor truncation), observer updates on chain advance, and a full end-to-end lifecycle test that models the production path: writer → observer snapshot → anchor write → next-boot continuity check returns `Match`. Two new CLI tests pin the default-false posture of `--audit-allow-chain-break` and its opt-in behaviour. (#718)
- **Tenant-isolated cross-path dedup cache** — `rustgate_transport::DedupCache` now folds the sender's tenant (derived from the client cert's X.509 Organization field, exposed via `Identity.tenant`) into the SHA-256 key preimage alongside the existing `uid || 0x00 || time_le || 0x00 || payload` slots. Previously a message sent by tenant `A` could suppress a byte-identical message sent by tenant `B`, opening a timing side-channel where a malicious tenant could probe for the existence of specific messages in another tenant by submitting candidate `(uid, time, payload)` triples and observing whether delivery succeeded (= the other tenant did not send this) or was silently deduplicated (= the other tenant sent exactly this). The router hot path at `route_inner` now passes `msg.source.tenant.as_deref().unwrap_or("")` into `check_payload`; the fallback to an empty string preserves pre-tenant behaviour for clients whose certificate has no Organization field (they share one tenancy slot by convention). Single-tenant deployments, or multi-tenant deployments where cross-tenant duplicate suppression is explicitly desired, can opt back into the pre-#722 behaviour via the new `--dedup-cross-tenant` CLI flag (env `RUSTGATE_DEDUP_CROSS_TENANT`, default `false`) and the corresponding `dedup-cross-tenant` TOML key. The flag is wired through `DedupCache::with_cross_tenant(bool)` — a stance-setter, fixed at construction time, not a runtime toggle — and the server logs a `WARN` on startup when cross-tenant mode is active so the trade-off is visible in the operational audit trail. Five new regression tests in `dedup.rs` (`different_tenants_same_payload_pass_independently`, `same_tenant_same_payload_still_deduped`, `cross_tenant_mode_suppresses_across_tenants`, `missing_tenant_treated_as_empty`, `tenant_affects_check_payload_too`) pin both the default and the opt-in behaviour. The protocol reference in `docs/protocol.md` §4.3 documents the new key format, the threat model, and the unsafe-opt-in caveat. (#722)
- **Refuse plaintext enrollment and fail-closed on rate-limiter mutex poison** — `rustgate_enrollment::EnrollmentServer::run` now rejects an empty/whitespace `cert_pem` or `key_pem` up front with an explicit `EnrollmentError::Config` that names the refusal — "enrollment server requires TLS … refusing to start". The downstream TLS builder would also reject empty inputs via `parse_certs`/`parse_key`, but its generic "failed to parse server certs" error hides the security rationale: PKCS#12 enrollment responses embed **unencrypted** certificate bags integrity-protected only by the standardized publicly-known `"atakatak"` password, so the TLS channel is the only real confidentiality boundary on that endpoint. EST (RFC 7030) endpoints (`/.well-known/est/*`) share the same listener, so the precondition check implicitly refuses plaintext EST as well — if the TLS config is rejected, nothing starts. Separately, `rustgate_enrollment::ratelimit::RateLimiter::check` now fails closed on state-mutex poison (issue #767 / F-41): the previous `Err(e) => e.into_inner()` path trusted potentially corrupted map state on the security-critical CSR-signing hot path and could bypass the per-IP rate limit if a prior panic had left the sweep counters in an inconsistent state. The new posture returns `false` (handler translates to HTTP 503), fires the optional `PoisonCallback`, and emits a WARN-level `tracing` record; poison is sticky with no in-process recovery. A new `--features metrics` counter `rustgate_enrollment_rate_limit_poison_total` exposes poison events as a distinct metric from rate-limit rejections (both surface as 503 otherwise), so an alert on any non-zero sample catches the degraded state quickly. Pinned by three new regression tests: `poisoned_mutex_fails_closed_and_fires_callback` and `poisoned_mutex_without_callback_still_fails_closed` in `ratelimit.rs`, and `run_rejects_empty_cert_pem_to_prevent_plaintext` / `run_rejects_empty_key_pem_to_prevent_plaintext` in `server_integration.rs`. (#767)
- **Persist the CRL `crlNumber` counter across enrollment-server restarts** — `rustgate_enrollment::RevocationStore` previously held the CRL serial in a `static AtomicU64` initialised to `1` at process start, so every restart re-issued a CRL with `crlNumber = 1`. RFC 5280 §5.2.3 requires the `crlNumber` extension to increase monotonically for each CRL issued by a given CA, and x509 verifiers that enforce this (OpenSSL's `X509_CRL_get_ext_d2i(…, NID_crl_number)` path among them) will reject a restarted-CA's CRL as a replay of a prior one — locking clients into stale revocation state until their cached CRL expires, or hard-failing verification depending on verifier posture. The counter now lives on the store instance (`RevocationStore::crl_serial: AtomicU64`) and is persisted to the revocation JSON under a new versioned wrapper (`StoredDb { format_version, last_crl_number, entries }`); the legacy pre-#765 flat-map layout still loads via a serde `untagged` fallback, so existing deployments upgrade transparently on the first persist. When no prior counter is on disk (fresh install, lost state file, or a legacy document), the in-memory counter seeds from `wall_clock_fallback_serial` (UNIX milliseconds) so the next `crlNumber` exceeds any plausible small-integer serial an older build would have issued — preserving monotonicity even across state loss. A hand-crafted or corrupted `last_crl_number = 0` is treated identically to "no stored value" (filtered out before the fallback) so defence-in-depth survives a truncated-but-valid-looking file. The `revoke` hot path now regenerates the CRL **before** `persist`, capturing the bumped serial atomically with the new revoked entry; the initial CRL issued in `RevocationStore::new` is followed by an explicit `persist` so a crash between startup and the first revocation cannot re-issue the same `crlNumber`. Pinned by four new tests in `revocation.rs`: `crl_serial_seeds_from_wall_clock_when_db_missing`, `crl_serial_persists_and_grows_across_reload` (the direct #765 regression guard), `crl_serial_increments_per_revocation`, and `crl_serial_accepts_legacy_flat_db_and_applies_fallback` (upgrade path), plus `crl_serial_zero_is_treated_as_missing` for the hand-crafted-file corner case. (#765)
- **Zero the CA private key's serialized DER on enrollment-server teardown** — `rustgate-enrollment`'s `CsrSigner` and `RevocationStore` previously held the CA key in a bare `rcgen::KeyPair`, which does not implement `Zeroize`. rcgen internally keeps two copies of the private key material: a ring-backed parsed form in `KeyPair::kind` and a plain `Vec<u8>` copy of the PKCS#8 DER retained for re-serialization via `KeyPair::serialize_der`. On `EnrollmentServer` shutdown both copies were released to the allocator without wiping, so the PKCS#8 DER sat in freed heap until overwritten — reachable to any adversary with post-process memory access (e.g. core-dump capture, swap residue, or a co-located attacker exploiting a later allocator reuse). The workspace now enables the `zeroize` cargo feature on rcgen 0.14.7 (unlocks `impl Zeroize for KeyPair` that wipes `serialized_der`), and a new `rustgate_enrollment::keypair::ZeroizingKeyPair` newtype forces that `zeroize()` call from its `Drop` impl. `CsrSigner::issuer` and `RevocationStore::issuer` are retyped to `Issuer<'static, ZeroizingKeyPair>`; the wrapper delegates `SigningKey` and `PublicKeyData` by reference so rcgen's certificate and CRL signing paths see no behavioural change. The ring-level parsed key in `KeyPair::kind` is a known residual — ring does not expose a `Zeroize` bound on its `EcdsaKeyPair` / `Ed25519KeyPair` / `RsaKeyPair` types, and the workspace-wide `unsafe_code = "forbid"` lint rules out pointer-cast workarounds; the wrapper documents the residue explicitly instead of concealing it. A dedicated unit test calls `zeroize()` on a populated rcgen `KeyPair` and verifies `serialize_der()` subsequently returns all-zero bytes, pinning the upstream contract so a future rcgen bump that regresses `impl Zeroize` fails CI instead of silently widening the residue window. `Debug` redaction is asserted alongside so the wrapper's secret-hygiene property cannot be quietly weakened by a downstream trait-impl change. (#766)
- **Cap audit-chain rewind budget and enforce minimum archive rotation cadence** — closes both halves of #811. **F-32**: `rustgate_core::audit_chain::read_chain_tip` previously read the entire audit log into memory via `file.read_to_end(&mut bytes)?` at every startup and, on any torn-line recovery, recursed by re-opening and re-reading the whole file from scratch — a hostile or accidentally-enormous log (e.g. 10 GiB of garbage) could stall the tip-recovery phase for minutes and, with each corrupt trailing record, walk the whole file again, compounding the delay into an effective startup DoS. The function is now refactored to seek to `file_len.saturating_sub(REWIND_BUDGET)` (16 MiB) and read only the trailing window, drops any partial leading record that straddles the budget boundary, and walks torn/corrupt trailing records in a bounded iterative loop (not recursive) whose worst-case work is `O(REWIND_BUDGET)` regardless of file size. If the entire rewound tail contains no valid record — i.e. the tip is genuinely unrecoverable — the function returns `io::ErrorKind::InvalidData` instead of silently re-genesising the chain, so the operator must verify/repair the log out-of-band; a tamper-detection posture rather than a tamper-hiding one. Three new regression tests pin the contract: `read_chain_tip_refuses_when_tail_has_no_records` crafts a file larger than `REWIND_BUDGET` whose last 16 MiB contain no newline and asserts the error path is taken (never incidentally finding the valid prefix record), `read_chain_tip_recovers_from_large_prefix` builds a ~20 MiB filler prefix followed by a single real chain record at the tail and confirms the tip resolves correctly without reading the prefix, and `read_chain_tip_recovers_torn_write_after_large_prefix` adds a torn partial trailing record on top of the large prefix and asserts the previous good tip is returned after bounded truncation. **F-69**: `rustgate_server::cli::Cli::validate` now enforces `MIN_ROTATION_INTERVAL_SECS = 60` as a hard lower bound and emits a startup warning below `RECOMMENDED_MIN_ROTATION_INTERVAL_SECS = 300` on `--archive-rotate-interval` when CoT archive rotation is enabled. Aggressive cadences (e.g. 1 second) open/close archive files and rewrite the chain-tip anchor constantly, widening the torn-write window and stressing disk I/O for no operator benefit. The guard is scoped — if neither `--archive-max-size` nor `--archive-max-age` is set, the rotation task never spawns and the interval is irrelevant, so the check is skipped. The legacy `.max(1)` defensive clamp on the interval is removed from `main.rs` since it is dead code after the validation gate. Four new CLI tests cover the new error path at 30s, the boundary-accept at 60s, the above-recommended-accept at 600s, and the skip-check-when-rotation-disabled case. (#811)
- **Pin defense-in-depth guarantee for authz obligations on federated ingress** — the V2 federation wire protocol does not carry `Obligation` metadata: upstream data-plane obligations (`MaskPoint`, `MaskPayload`) are baked into the payload before forwarding, audit-shaped obligations (`TagClassified`, `AuditExtended`) are not serialized at all, and the receiver has no way to distinguish "upstream honoured policy" from "upstream ignored policy". Following the intent of Option A in issue #719, this makes the existing behaviour an explicit contract: every federated message is handed to `router.route()` which re-runs the full PEP chain (Send-PEP with the peer CN as subject, then per-recipient Receive-PEP with each recipient's CN as subject), and local Receive-PEP obligations are always applied to a per-recipient copy of the envelope. A new **Cross-origin authz obligations** subsection in `docs/federation.md` spells out the trust model and the multicast caveat (federated messages only arrive as `Destination::Broadcast`, never `Destination::Multicast`, so the existing top-level Send-PEP skip for multicast does not apply); a Security-note comment block on the `on_inbound` closure in `rustgate-server::setup` cross-references the docs so the guarantee is visible at the construction site. Three new integration tests in `crates/rustgate-transport/tests/authz_routing.rs` (`federated_broadcast_applies_local_mask_point_receive`, `federated_broadcast_applies_local_mask_payload_receive`, `federated_broadcast_respects_per_recipient_receive_deny`) pin the behaviour against a future refactor that would otherwise silently bypass the per-recipient Receive-PEP on federation-origin traffic. Closes the defense-in-depth half of the authz/federation epic; the wire-level obligation propagation variant (Option B/C) remains deferred pending a cryptographic binding between the obligation list and the payload. (#719)
- **Fail-closed on unknown authz `Obligation` variant in the data plane** — `rustgate_transport::obligations::apply_obligations` and `RoutedMessage::with_obligations` now take an explicit `UnknownObligationPolicy` parameter and return `Result<_, ObligationError>` rather than silently delivering the unmodified payload when the authz engine returns a variant the transport build does not recognise. The `Obligation` enum is `#[non_exhaustive]`; a newer authz deployment running against an older transport binary could previously hand the PEP a future variant (say a hypothetical `TransformPayload`) and the stale transport would skip it, emit a DEBUG log, and deliver the original bytes — directly defeating the policy author's intent, exactly the fail-open pattern XACML §7.2 calls out. The new default `UnknownObligationPolicy::FailClosed` drops the outbound copy and emits both the existing `authz.obligation_unknown` audit record and a new WARN-level operational log tagged with the variant Debug repr and the hashed source CN. Every data-plane call site is migrated: Send-PEP in `route_inner` aborts the whole dispatch (no local sessions, no egress), `filter_offline_messages` drops the drained record, `replay_positions` skips the cached position for the current recipient, and the four per-recipient fan-out paths (`send_to_session`, `send_to_group`, `send_to_all`, `send_to_group_excluding`) drop that recipient only. Operators needing to tolerate deliberate version skew during a rolling upgrade opt into the legacy behaviour with the new CLI flag `--authz-allow-unknown-obligations` (env `RUSTGATE_AUTHZ_ALLOW_UNKNOWN_OBLIGATIONS`, defaults `false`), which selects `UnknownObligationPolicy::SkipAndContinue` on the router via `Router::with_allow_unknown_obligations(true)`. Under that policy every known obligation still runs, each unknown variant produces its audit record and a DEBUG log, and delivery proceeds. The fuzz target `obligation_apply` is updated to thread the new policy argument; a new regression test asserts the default enum discriminant is `FailClosed` so a future refactor cannot silently flip the posture. (#728)
- **Reject unverified `federate_groups` claims from federation peers by default** — `FederatedEvent.federate_groups` is advisory wire metadata that the sending peer populates based on its own local identity store; there is no cryptographic link between the claimed groups and the origin CN the peer names. A Byzantine or compromised federation peer holding a valid mTLS certificate could previously assert arbitrary group memberships for any origin CN (e.g. claim `federate_groups = ["Admin", "Secret"]` for an arbitrary CN) and a naïve downstream consumer of `federated_event_to_routable` would stamp those groups onto `Identity.groups` where an ACL or authz policy matching `groups.contains("Admin")` would then admit the forged event. The conversion function now takes an explicit `trust_peer_groups: bool` argument and, by default (`false`), drops the wire `federate_groups` vector and produces an empty `BTreeSet<GroupId>` on the synthesised `Identity`; when non-empty claims are dropped a new `audit::federation_group_claim_rejected(peer_cn, origin_cn, claimed_groups)` record is emitted with the rejected list so SIEM rules can surface forgery attempts. A new `FederationConfig::trust_peer_groups` field (plumbed through `--federation-trust-peer-groups` / `RUSTGATE_FEDERATION_TRUST_PEER_GROUPS` and the TOML `federation-trust-peer-groups` key) lets single-operator deployments where every peer is an equally-privileged node of the same fleet opt back in with eyes open; the flag docs and new **Threat Model** section in `docs/federation.md` spell out that opting in delegates group-authority to every federation peer and is only safe when the peer set is administratively coequal. The production XML-forwarding path (`federated_event_to_xml` → `on_inbound` → transport) was already safe by accident (the XML bytes do not embed `federate_groups` and the inbound callback rebuilds a fresh `Identity` from the peer cert CN with `BTreeSet::new()` for groups), but the defence is now explicit at the sole `RoutableMessage` construction site, configurable, and pinned by a full-stack mTLS integration test that sends a forged `federate_groups` list over the real gRPC wire and asserts the resulting `Identity.groups` is empty. (#720)
- **MAVLink codec defaults to v2+signature required** — `rustgate_mavlink::MavlinkFrameCodec` now rejects MAVLink v1 frames and unsigned v2 frames at the framing layer by default, returning the new `MavlinkError::V1FrameRejected` and `MavlinkError::UnsignedFrameRejected` variants respectively. v1 has no signature field at all, and v2 with `INCOMPAT & SIGNED = 0` bypasses the v2 signing trust boundary — accepting either silently on a link that runs signed traffic hands an attacker a trivial downgrade path. Operators running mixed fleets opt back in via the new `MavlinkFrameCodec::with_allow_v1(true)` and `MavlinkFrameCodec::with_require_signing(false)` builder methods; both are stance-setters rather than combined into a single mode so the choice is explicit at wiring time. Rejection consumes only the offending magic byte, so a following valid signed-v2 frame still decodes — an attacker cannot stall the codec by prefixing an unsigned or v1 header. New `rustgate_core::audit::mavlink_unsigned_rejected` and `rustgate_core::audit::mavlink_v1_rejected` helpers let the session layer (arriving with the UDP/TCP listeners in a follow-up PR) emit distinct SIEM-grade records for the two failure modes. (#752)
- **Reserve `__*__` sentinel group ids in operator-authored ACL policies** — the transport layer synthesises group ids with the shape `__name__` for populations that never present an mTLS identity (`__plaintext__` for anonymous plaintext TCP/UDP sessions per `rustgate_core::constants::PLAINTEXT_GROUP`, `__ANON__` for anonymous federation ingress, `__default__` as the tenant-quota fallback). Those ids were previously indistinguishable from user-defined group ids at the ACL PEP, so an operator policy keyed by `"__plaintext__": {"send": ["anyone"]}` — whether authored by mistake or by a compromised config-authoring path — would be applied to every anonymous plaintext session the server accepted, broadcasting to a population the operator never enumerated, and shadowing the synthetic group's transport-layer meaning. A new shape-based check `rustgate_core::constants::is_reserved_group_id(&str)` (matches `name.len() >= 4 && starts_with("__") && ends_with("__")`) is now enforced at every operator-facing policy surface: the startup loader (`rustgate_server::setup::load_group_acl`), the hot-reload path (`rustgate_server::acl_reloader::AclReloader::reload`), and the REST ACL API (`rustgate_server::acl_api::valid_group_id`). The hot-reload path is fail-closed — on rejection the stored content hash is **not** advanced, so the next poll tick re-parses the bad file and re-emits the same `acl.reload_failed` audit record rather than silently treating the rejected state as "already loaded"; a regression test overwrites the file with a different valid policy after the rejection and asserts the next reload swaps, proving the reloader did not mistakenly fingerprint the bad input. The shape check is deliberately byte-shape based rather than a hard-coded allow list so a future transport-internal sentinel (e.g. `__federation__`) does not create a silent ACL-namespace collision the moment it lands. 13 new tests across `rustgate-core::constants`, `rustgate-server::acl_config`, `rustgate-server::acl_api`, and `rustgate-server::acl_reloader` pin the shape, the startup loader, the REST PUT/DELETE surface, and the reload fail-closed posture. (#749)

### Changed

- **Thread `BackpressurePermit` through every egress publisher so slow downstream targets pressure the global admission gate** — `BackpressureGate` now lives in `rustgate-resilience::backpressure` (ingress-side `rustgate-transport::backpressure` re-exports the types for source compatibility) and is plumbed as an optional `Arc<BackpressureGate>` field on every egress publisher: `HttpPublisher`, `NatsPublisher`, federation `V1Client`, and federation `V2Client`. Each publisher wraps its internal `mpsc::Sender` payload in a private `QueuedMessage` / `V1Queued` / `V2Queued` envelope that carries an `Option<Arc<BackpressurePermit>>`; the permit is acquired on `publish`/`send` and released by RAII when the dispatch worker (or replay / shutdown drain) drops the envelope, so the gate's in-flight byte counter reflects the aggregate sitting in every publisher's bounded channel rather than only the router's ingress admission work. With the gate wired, a stalled HTTP webhook target, a disconnected NATS cluster, or a federation peer whose gRPC `ServerEventStream` has stopped draining will pressure the gate past its high-water mark and flip `is_admitting()` to `false` — exactly the observable signal the TLS accept loop uses to back off new connections. HTTP's `publish` short-circuits to the dead-letter queue under a new `reason = "backpressure"` tag when `is_admitting()` is false so in-flight events are never silently dropped; NATS fire-and-forget publishes and federation outbound sends continue to acquire permits so the gate observes their byte reservation regardless of the fail-fast decision. Each publisher exposes a new `with_backpressure(gate: Arc<BackpressureGate>)` builder so wiring is opt-in and backward-compatible — existing callers that do not attach a gate see zero behavioural change. A new cross-crate integration test in `crates/rustgate-http/tests/publish_integration.rs::slow_egress_target_pressures_global_backpressure_gate` wires a `wiremock` responder with a 2 s response delay to a publisher bound to a shared gate with a 1 KiB high-water mark, fires enough 900-byte payloads to exceed it, asserts `is_admitting()` flips to `false` within 500 ms of the burst, and — after shutdown drains in-flight permits — asserts the gate recovers to admitting within the dwell window, proving the RAII accounting round-trips cleanly. Two new inline unit tests in `rustgate-http::publisher` (`backpressure_over_high_water_drops_to_dlq`, `backpressure_permit_releases_on_worker_drain`) pin the DLQ short-circuit and the permit release invariants at the publisher's own seam. (Closes #956)
- **Require justification comments on every production `#[allow(...)]` (F-156)** — `scripts/check-allow-justified.py` now scans every `.rs` file under `crates/*/src/` and fails CI when a production `#[allow(...)]` attribute is not preceded by a `// justification:` comment. The rule catches the silent-suppression pattern where a contributor reaches for `#[allow]` to hush a clippy lint instead of either fixing the underlying issue or recording why it cannot be fixed — over time those un-annotated allows accrete into an unreviewable wall of exceptions and the workspace-wide `-Dwarnings` posture quietly becomes advisory. The script is deliberately scope-narrow: `rustgate-test-utils` is exempt whole-crate (test support only), files under `crates/*/tests/` are skipped, and items under `#[cfg(test)]` or inside a `mod tests { … }` block are ignored — tests legitimately exercise code paths clippy cannot model from production configuration alone. Findings surface as GitHub `::error file=…,line=…` annotations so reviewers see them inline on the PR diff rather than buried in job logs. 32 existing production `#[allow]` sites across 14 crates (`rustgate-core`, `rustgate-cot`, `rustgate-enrollment`, `rustgate-federation`, `rustgate-http`, `rustgate-mqtt`, `rustgate-resilience`, `rustgate-server`, `rustgate-transport`, `rustgate-websocket`) are retrofitted with inline justifications that cover the four justification families the new rule recognises: (a) generated code we cannot patch upstream (prost/tonic modules in `federation/v2/proto.rs`), (b) feature-conditional types where the allowed spelling is the only one that compiles across every feature combination (every `.clone()` on the `nats_publisher` that is `()` when `nats` is off and `Option<NatsPublisher>` when it is on), (c) `too_many_arguments` on dispatch entrypoints called from exactly one site where bundling into a struct would move the fan-in upstream with no call-site reduction (the MQTT `handle_subscribe_v5/v4` and `handle_unsubscribe_v5/v4` family, the WebSocket `handle_ws_session` and `ws_read_loop`, the CoT `handle_open` quick-xml dispatch, the enrollment `handle_request` HTTP router), and (d) `dead_code` accessors or fields that are read by an outside-the-crate consumer the compiler's dead-code heuristic cannot see (the federation admin-API gauges, the OCSP cache counters, the `MetricsIdentity` Tier-2 flag). A new **Allow annotations (F-156)** subsection in `CONTRIBUTING.md` under *Code Quality → Workspace lint policy* documents the rule, the exemption scope, the four accepted justification families, and what does not count (bare "clippy false positive", unscoped "fix later", "obvious"). Wired into the `playbook-lint` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` alongside the F-21 release-artifact-name check and the F-154 shared-infrastructure-drift check. (Closes #821)
- **Migrate coverage job from `cargo tarpaulin` to `cargo llvm-cov --nextest`** — the `coverage` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is the longest-running PR job after Phase A landed (~9m16s on self-hosted with warm sccache, versus ~4-5 min for `test` on the same runner), and the gap is structural rather than cache-warmth: `cargo tarpaulin` runs each test binary serially under `ptrace` so the `--jobs` parallelism in `test` does not transfer. The migration swaps in `cargo-llvm-cov` — which wraps `cargo nextest run` with `RUSTC_WRAPPER`/`-Cinstrument-coverage` and therefore inherits nextest's native parallel test-binary execution — while keeping every downstream-visible artifact identical: the job still uploads `coverage/cobertura.xml` as the `coverage-report` artifact from the same path, so the `upload-artifact` step and any consumer that pulls the artifact by name is unchanged. Five concrete edits land in the coverage job: (1) the `dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable` step now installs the `llvm-tools-preview` component alongside the default profile so `llvm-profdata` and `llvm-cov` are available for the source-based coverage instrumentation — this is the same component tarpaulin's `--engine llvm` path required internally, so the coverage model is unchanged; (2) a new `Install cargo-nextest` step guarded with `command -v cargo-nextest` mirrors the guard pattern used in the `test` job so the tool is installed once on GitHub-hosted and skipped on the pre-baked self-hosted image; (3) the `taiki-e/install-action@v2` step swaps `tool: cargo-tarpaulin` for `tool: cargo-llvm-cov` so the installer resolves to the prebuilt `cargo-llvm-cov` binary rather than downloading and linking tarpaulin; (4) the run command changes from `cargo tarpaulin --engine llvm --workspace --features … --out Xml --output-dir coverage --locked` to `mkdir -p coverage && cargo llvm-cov --locked --workspace --features nats,enrollment,est,proto,full-detail,metrics,federation,federation-ha,websocket,mqtt,otel,http --cobertura --output-path coverage/cobertura.xml nextest` — cargo-llvm-cov's flag-ordering contract requires top-level options (`--locked`, `--workspace`, `--features`, `--cobertura`, `--output-path`) to precede the `nextest` subcommand, and unlike tarpaulin's `--output-dir` the `--output-path` argument does not auto-create the parent directory so an explicit `mkdir -p coverage` is needed ahead of the run; (5) the inline comment block documents both the model-equivalence (both tools ultimately emit LLVM source-based coverage) and the flag-ordering gotcha so a future maintainer editing the invocation does not silently break it. The `CONTRIBUTING.md` §CI Pipeline table is updated to name the new tool so operators reading the repo-level docs see `cargo llvm-cov --nextest` rather than `cargo tarpaulin`. Expected wall-clock impact: coverage drops from ~9m16s toward ~5-7 min on the same self-hosted runner, and the speed-up is proportional to the CPU count — `test` already scales with `$(nproc)`, so the coverage job inherits the same linear speed-up once llvm-cov drives nextest. No production code paths are touched, the artifact contract (`coverage/cobertura.xml`) is preserved, and the `RUNNER_POOL` ternary on `runs-on` is untouched so the job still falls back to `ubuntu-latest` when the variable is flipped.
- **Speed up CI on self-hosted runners: wire mold linker, prune redundant installers, split check-features depth by event** — the CI pipeline is now shaped around the `RUNNER_POOL == 'self-hosted'` repo-variable path where the `github-runner:v2` container image bakes in Rust 1.94, sccache, mold, cargo-nextest, protobuf-compiler, cmake, golang, musl-tools, and the aarch64 cross-compiler. Four changes land in `ci.yml` plus the installer guards in `nightly.yml` and `weekly-fuzz.yml`. (1) Top-level `RUSTFLAGS` becomes a conditional expression — `${{ vars.RUNNER_POOL == 'self-hosted' && '-Dwarnings -C link-arg=-fuse-ld=mold' || '-Dwarnings' }}` — so self-hosted jobs link through `mold` (3-10x faster than the GNU linker on Rust workspaces of this size) while the GitHub-hosted fallback keeps the default linker since `ubuntu-latest` does not ship mold. (2) Every `Swatinem/rust-cache@v2` step (5 call sites across `lint`, `clippy`, `check-features`, `test`, `coverage`) is guarded with `if: vars.RUNNER_POOL != 'self-hosted'` — on self-hosted the shared sccache volume at `/home/rlchiofalo/ci-shared/sccache` (40 GB, 96%+ hit rate once warm) is the only cache we need, and layering Swatinem on top would waste 30-90 s per job on cache upload/download against a GitHub Actions cache that is itself capped at 5 GB per repo. (3) Redundant installer steps are guarded with `command -v X` checks rather than `RUNNER_POOL` conditionals so they are robust against misconfiguration — if the variable is unset or set to an unexpected value on a self-hosted image where the tool is already present, the check still skips the install; if the container image loses the tool, the install still fires and CI does not flake. Guards cover `protoc` (3 sites), `cargo-nextest` (3 sites), the `fips` multi-tool bundle (`protoc`, `cmake`, `go`, `musl-gcc`), the `aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc` cross-compiler, the `post-quantum` bundle (`protoc`, `cmake`, `go`), and the `cargo-fuzz` nightly binary on the nightly/weekly-fuzz workflows. On self-hosted this collapses ~5-8 minutes of per-job apt-get/curl time into near-zero; on GitHub-hosted the behaviour is unchanged. (4) The `check-features` job's `cargo hack check --feature-powerset` now runs at `--depth 1` on pull-request events and `--depth 2` on push-to-main — most feature regressions are per-feature rather than combinatorial, and depth 2 was burning ~32 wall-clock minutes per PR for rare pair-breakage. Branch protection on `main` ensures depth-2 runs before any release is cut from a protected branch, so the combinatorial surface is still exercised before a release tag; PRs get a ~8-12 minute check-features job instead. Net effect on a cache-warm self-hosted PR run: PR wall-time drops from ~114 minutes (documented baseline) toward ~48 minutes, a ~60 % reduction. The fallback to `ubuntu-latest` via the `RUNNER_POOL` ternary is preserved unchanged, so flipping the repo variable reverts every job to the previous behaviour without a merge. No production code paths are touched.
- **Replace `FramedCodec` disabled-feature `unreachable!()` with fallible `try_from_strategy`** — `rustgate_transport::FramedCodec::from_strategy` is replaced by `try_from_strategy(&FramingStrategy) -> Result<Self, FramedCodecError>`. The two pre-existing `unreachable!()` branches in the `#[cfg(not(feature = "proto"))]` / `#[cfg(not(feature = "mavlink"))]` arms would have aborted the process under the workspace-wide `panic = "abort"` release profile if a SIGHUP-reloaded listener config ever pointed at a codec whose cargo feature was not built in — taking down every in-flight TLS connection for a misconfiguration that should have produced a structured rejection. The new `FramedCodecError::FeatureNotEnabled { feature: &'static str }` variant names the offending cargo feature (`"proto"` or `"mavlink"`) in its `thiserror`-derived `Display`, and a `From<FramedCodecError> for io::Error` impl maps onto `io::ErrorKind::InvalidInput` so existing session pipelines propagate the failure via `?` without changing the error-kind surface. The three server-side call sites in `rustgate_server::session` migrate to `try_from_strategy(...)?`. The `rustgate-client` call site uses `.expect(...)` with a rationale ("Codec enum only exposes always-available strategies") since the public `Codec` enum intentionally exposes only unconditional variants (`LengthPrefixed1/2/4`, `XmlStream`, `LineDelimited`) — the fallible signature documents the contract at the crate boundary while provably never firing from that caller. Aligns with the workspace `clippy::panic = "deny"` rule. Pinned by four new regression tests in `crates/rustgate-transport/src/codec.rs`: always-available variants round-trip, both `#[cfg(not(...))]` branches return `FeatureNotEnabled` with the correct feature name, and the `From<FramedCodecError> for io::Error` conversion yields `InvalidInput` with the feature name in the rendered message. (#750)
- **Consolidate `base64` engine usage into `rustgate_core::b64`** — new `rustgate_core::b64` module provides workspace-wide `encode`, `decode`, `encode_url_safe`, and `decode_url_safe` helpers wrapping the two `base64` engines the workspace actually uses (`STANDARD` per RFC 4648 §4 and `URL_SAFE_NO_PAD` per RFC 4648 §5). Previously 17 files across five crates reached for `base64` directly in three inconsistent styles — `base64::engine::general_purpose::STANDARD.encode(…)`, `base64::Engine::encode(&STANDARD, …)`, and `use base64::Engine as _; STANDARD.encode(…)` — making it easy to paste the wrong call shape or mismatch the engine to the spec (the JWT code in `rustgate-federation` correctly used §5 while every other caller used §4). `rustgate-http`, `rustgate-federation`, `rustgate-transport`, and `rustgate-enrollment` drop their direct `base64` dependency and import via `rustgate_core::b64` instead; the raw engines are re-exported under the same module for the handful of callers that still need the `Engine` trait directly. No behavioural change — the underlying `STANDARD` / `URL_SAFE_NO_PAD` semantics are preserved byte-for-byte. (#830)
- **Expand SA affiliation coverage to full MITRE Appendix A set** — `rustgate_cot::SaAffiliation` now recognizes all 11 affiliation codes defined in MITRE CoT Message Router User's Guide (MP090284) Appendix A / Figure 2-3, aligned with MIL-STD-2525 standard identity: `Pending` (`a-p-*`), `AssumedFriend` (`a-a-*`), `Friend` (`a-f-*`, renamed from `Friendly`), `Neutral` (`a-n-*`), `Suspect` (`a-s-*`), `Hostile` (`a-h-*`), `Joker` (`a-j-*`), `Faker` (`a-k-*`), `Unknown` (`a-u-*`), `NoneSpecified` (`a-o-*`), `Other` (`a-x-*`). Previously only `f/h/n/u` were recognized, so `a-s-…` (suspect), `a-j-…` (joker), and `a-k-…` (faker) events were misclassified as non-atoms by `is_sa_event` / `sa_affiliation`. (#932)

### Security

- **Cap authz policy rule count at 10,000 before compile** — `rustgate_server::authz_reloader` gains a `MAX_POLICY_RULES = 10_000` cap enforced in both `load_once` (startup) and `AuthzReloader::reload` (hot-reload) paths. The existing 4 MiB raw-file cap (`MAX_POLICY_FILE_BYTES`) bounds the pre-parse read, but a 4 MiB JSON document can still compile into tens of millions of minimal rules — enough to starve a pod's RAM during `NativeEngine::new()` or degrade every subsequent decision eval to a linear scan through the compiled bucket table. A new private `check_rule_count` helper rejects oversized policies between parse and compile, emitting `audit::authz_reload_failed` with stage `"validate"` so operators can distinguish a size-rejected policy from a malformed one in the audit trail. Real-world policies live in the low hundreds of rules; 10,000 is ~100x headroom over any plausible hand-authored deployment. Closes the F-37 half of #812. The F-36 half (sharded decision cache against adversarial CN rotation) was already in place — `rustgate_authz::cache::DecisionCache` shards (default 16) are keyed by a mix of both 64-bit halves of `SubjectHash` plus the resource hash so adversarial collisions on any single component cannot funnel traffic into one shard, and `rustgate_authz_cache_hits_total` / `rustgate_authz_cache_misses_total` counters are already emitted every 10 s from `main.rs` for hit-ratio derivation in PromQL. (#812)
- **Apply `step-security/harden-runner` to every PR CI job and deduplicate the pinned `nats-server` release descriptor** — the runner-hardening action previously shielded only the `audit` job, leaving the remaining eleven jobs (commit-lint, playbook-lint, lint, clippy, check-features, test, coverage, fips, post-quantum, helm, docker) running with default egress and no telemetry into outbound connections from third-party actions. Every job now starts with `step-security/harden-runner@v2.18.0` in `egress-policy: audit` mode — matching the workspace-wide pattern already used in `audit` and `release-binary.yml` — so every outbound connection is observable in the step-security dashboard; this is the prerequisite for a later tightening to `egress-policy: block` with a curated allowlist once real traffic data has been collected. Separately, the pinned `nats-server` v2.10.24 tarball SHA-256 was hardcoded in four places (cache key + sha256sum check, repeated across the `test` and `coverage` jobs) — a bump now only requires editing the two new workflow-level env vars `NATS_SERVER_VERSION` and `NATS_SERVER_SHA256`, eliminating the silent-mismatch class of bug where the cache key advertises one hash while the integrity check validates another. (#781)
- **Helm chart RBAC / ServiceAccount posture is now CI-enforced** — the `helm` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` previously ran only `helm lint` and a bare `helm template … > /dev/null`, so a future chart change adding a `Role`, `ClusterRole`, `RoleBinding`, `ClusterRoleBinding`, or `ServiceAccount` with wildcard verbs, over-privileged rules, or a default-SA binding would land on `main` with a green check. The job now renders the production values (`helm template rustgate helm/ -f helm/values-production.yaml`) and scans every document with a purpose-built Python validator that fails the build on: wildcard `verbs` / `resources` / `apiGroups` / `resourceNames` inside any `Role` or `ClusterRole`; `ClusterRole` rules that list `secrets` cluster-wide; rules granting mutating verbs on `nodes`; rules that create/delete/patch/update `customresourcedefinitions`; `RoleBinding` / `ClusterRoleBinding` subjects targeting the `default` ServiceAccount; `ServiceAccount` objects that do not explicitly set `automountServiceAccountToken: false`; and workload `PodSpec`s (Pod, Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, CronJob, ReplicaSet) that omit `automountServiceAccountToken: false` without naming a non-default ServiceAccount. The scanner is a pure-Python script — deliberately chosen over kubeaudit (planned-for-deprecation upstream since October 2024) and polaris (pulls in broader pod-security hardening that is out of scope for this PR). A prerequisite chart fix (`helm/templates/tests/test-connection.yaml`) adds `automountServiceAccountToken: false` to the Helm test Pod so the existing chart passes the scan on a clean baseline. (#782)
- **Release pipeline: attest private-repo builds and sign SBOMs** — closes the remaining two gaps from the release-pipeline hardening epic (#778). **F-79**: both `attest-build-provenance` invocations (`release.yml` for the container image, `release-binary.yml` for each cross-compiled binary archive) previously ran under `if: github.repository_visibility == 'public'`, which silently skipped SLSA build-provenance attestation on private forks and internal mirrors — a build that passes CI on an internal repo shipped without the in-toto statement that downstream `gh attestation verify` or Sigstore policy controllers expect. The guard is removed; both actions use the Sigstore public good instance for public and private repos alike per upstream docs, and the transparency-log entries contain only subject digests and build metadata (no private source material), so unconditional attestation is both safe and required for SLSA L3 on every build. **F-84**: the SPDX SBOMs produced by the release pipeline were previously uploaded as raw release assets with no cryptographic binding to the build that produced them. The container-image SBOM is now bound to the image digest via `cosign attest --type spdxjson`, verifiable downstream with `cosign verify-attestation --type spdxjson`. The source SBOM is signed as a detached `.sigstore.json` bundle via `cosign sign-blob` (since release-asset files are not registry-addressable, `sign-blob` rather than `attest` is the correct primitive) and additionally receives a build-provenance attestation via `actions/attest-build-provenance`, verifiable downstream with `gh attestation verify`. The container-image attestation is gated behind `continue-on-error: true` on the post-sign best-effort block in `release.yml` so an SBOM generation or attestation hiccup does not un-ship an already-signed image; consumers who require attested SBOMs gate admission on the attestation's presence, not on the release job's exit code. F-78 (Trivy scan gates cosign sign) was already addressed in #777; this PR closes the remaining two sub-items in the same triple. (#778)
- **Reject federation RPC when mTLS client-cert CN is unavailable** — the V2 gRPC `FederationService` previously fell back to the remote IP address when `request.peer_certs()` returned no cert or when `x509_parser` failed to extract a CN, logging only a `warn!` and proceeding. A peer presenting an expired, malformed, or missing cert would then be identified by IP and could silently match an IP-keyed `peer_groups` allow-list entry previously populated by a legitimate peer on the same address — a `send_one_event`, `health_check`, or streaming RPC would be processed under that stolen identity, reaching the authorization and hop-count checks. `peer_id_from_request` now returns `Result<String, Status>`; on any extraction failure it emits the new `audit::federation_peer_rejected(remote_addr, reason)` event and short-circuits every RPC handler (`send_one_event`, `health_check`, `server_event_stream`, `binary_message_stream`, `server_rol_stream`, `client_federate_groups_stream`) with `Status::unauthenticated` before any group or hop-count evaluation runs. The `reason` tag distinguishes `peer_cert_missing` (non-mTLS connection) from `peer_cert_unparseable_or_empty_cn` (cert present but subject CN absent after DER parse and control-char stripping) so operators can triage deployment misconfigurations separately from malformed-cert probes. Non-mTLS testing paths that relied on the previous IP fallback must now supply a real client certificate; the `v2_integration` test harness is migrated to TestCa-backed mTLS to match the production invariant. (#759)
- **Sanitize peer-controlled fields and hash client CNs in structured logs** — the federation gRPC server in `rustgate_federation::v2::server` emits a `warn!` with the offending group name when a peer claims a group it is not authorized for. `group` was logged raw, so a malicious peer could register a group name containing `\r\n[audit] forged=true\r\n` and forge an entire fake audit record in text-mode log output (the JSON layer is not vulnerable, but the default `tracing_subscriber::fmt` text formatter is, and operators often run mixed pipelines). `group` is now routed through `rustgate_core::sanitize::sanitize_for_log` on both call sites — the single-event `validate_event_groups` path and the streaming `send_event_stream` path that logs the full `federate_groups` vector. A regression test attaches a capturing `MakeWriter` to the `rustgate_federation::v2::server` target, pushes an event with an attacker-crafted group name, and asserts no raw `\r\n` survives into the captured bytes and no line in the output begins with the forged marker. Separately, `rustgate_websocket` and `rustgate_mqtt` session handlers replaced 24 raw `cn = %identity.cn` / `cn = %cn` tracing-field emissions (session start/end, CONNECT/DISCONNECT, subscribe/unsubscribe, client-ID collisions, rate-limit drops, replay drops, tenant-quota rejections, keep-alive timeouts) with `cn = %hash_cn(&…)` so production logs carry a 48-bit PII-safe correlation token per MEMORY.md / shared-infrastructure.md convention, matching the existing pattern in `rustgate_transport::router`. Audit events that genuinely need the raw CN for compliance retain it via `rustgate_core::audit::*` functions. (F-153, #802)
- **Fail closed on stale store-forward queue without persistent HMAC key** — `rustgate_transport::ClientQueue::open` (and `open_with_hmac_key(.., None)`) previously generated a fresh random HMAC key on every invocation. When the on-disk queue already contained entries from a previous run, the new key could not verify the old tags, so every stored message was silently discarded on the next drain — a direct violation of the store-forward contract. `ClientQueue::open` now returns a new `StoreForwardError::StaleQueueWithoutKey` error when rebuilt-index depth is non-zero and no persistent key was supplied. The server binary gains two new flags to disambiguate operator intent: `--client-queue-key-file <path>` (env `RUSTGATE_CLIENT_QUEUE_KEY_FILE`) loads a 32-byte hex-encoded HMAC key subject to the same owner + 0600/0400 permission gate as the HTTP-egress secret files; `--client-queue-wipe-on-start` (env `RUSTGATE_CLIENT_QUEUE_WIPE_ON_START`, mutually exclusive with `--client-queue-key-file`) calls the new `ClientQueue::open_with_wipe` which clears the on-disk tables and emits a `store_forward.key_rotated` audit event (with `reason=explicit_wipe_on_start` and the pre-wipe depth) so the deliberate data loss is visible in the compliance audit trail. Operators who restart the server without either flag on a directory that contains stored entries will now see the server refuse to start instead of silently losing queued messages. (#740)
- **Owner check on HTTP egress secret files** — `rustgate_http::auth::read_secret_file` now verifies that the secret file's owning UID matches the running process's effective UID on Unix, in addition to the existing `mode & 0o077 == 0` permission-bit gate. Catches the misconfiguration where a secret is dropped by `root` with correct 0600 permissions but the service runs as a different user — the read would previously succeed silently, leaving operators unaware that the file is outside the service account's lifecycle. (#829)
- **Harden authz obligation actuation** — closes nine gaps surfaced by a post-merge security audit of the obligation data-plane feature (#717): (1) `MaskPoint` bypass via case variation, namespace prefix, or attribute-budget trip — the matcher in `rustgate_cot::mask` now strips optional `ns:` prefixes, does ASCII-case-insensitive comparison, and propagates attribute-budget errors so the caller fails closed instead of leaking coordinates; (2) `apply_mask_point` ignored `strip_coordinates` errors — now splits on payload intent (non-XML passes through with `recovery = "forwarded_unmasked"`, XML-intent parse failure erases the payload with `recovery = "dropped"`) and emits a new `authz.obligation_failed` audit record on every recovery path; (3) `send_to_session` persisted the *post-Receive* form of the payload to the store-forward queue, causing `TagClassified` audit records to fire for messages that never went over the wire and double-actuating Receive-side obligations on drain — now persists the pre-Receive form so `filter_offline_messages` re-evaluates the Receive PEP against the current policy snapshot; (4) unknown `Obligation` variants (the enum is `#[non_exhaustive]`) now emit an `authz.obligation_unknown` audit record so operators running a stale transport against a newer authz engine detect the skew via the audit trail. Both new audit events carry `destination_kind` (direct/group/broadcast/multicast) so SIEM rules can distinguish unicast from fan-out failures. (#734)
- **Advisory scan now gates the build** — removed `continue-on-error: true` from both the `cargo deny check` and `cargo audit` steps in the PR CI workflow. These guards were originally added to tolerate an upstream advisory-DB parse failure (RUSTSEC-2025-0138 malformed TOML), but once the underlying DB was fixed the guards stayed in place and silently masked every subsequent real advisory — a new CVE in a production dependency would have produced a yellow check mark instead of a failing build. The `--ignore` list for individually-reviewed advisories (RUSTSEC-2025-0134 unmaintained-no-replacement, RUSTSEC-2026-0049 mitigated-at-transport-layer) is preserved, each with a dated reviewer note; new suppressions require an explicit ignore entry and a rationale. A prerequisite `rustls-webpki` bump from 0.103.11 → 0.103.12 was required to land this change (fixes RUSTSEC-2026-0098 URI name-constraint bypass and RUSTSEC-2026-0099 wildcard name-constraint bypass). (#777)
- **Release signature gated on Trivy pass** — the `Release Docker Image` workflow previously ran the Trivy container scan *after* `cosign sign` with `continue-on-error: true`, meaning a CRITICAL or HIGH vulnerability in the shipped image did not fail the release: the image was pushed, signed, and announced regardless. Trivy now runs *before* `cosign sign` with `exit-code: '1'` and no `continue-on-error`, so a CRITICAL/HIGH finding short-circuits the job and leaves the image unsigned — consumers who require a cosign signature for admission control will correctly refuse to pull it. The SARIF upload step still runs after sign with `!cancelled()` so findings appear in the GitHub Security tab whether the release succeeded or failed, aiding triage. To ship an image despite a known finding, add a dated entry to `.trivyignore` with reviewer rationale rather than relaxing `exit-code` or re-introducing `continue-on-error`. (#777)

### Fixed

- **Deflake `sign_client_valid_csr` and sibling enrollment integration tests against server-startup race** — `rustgate_enrollment` integration tests spawn `EnrollmentServer::run` in a detached tokio task via `spawn_server_with`, which returns immediately before the server has bound its TCP listener. The `send_request` helper then called `TcpStream::connect(self.addr).await.expect("TCP connect")` with no retry, producing an intermittent `ConnectionRefused` on loaded CI runners — observed in issue-triage trails and reproduced in PR #977's test job. A new `connect_with_retry(addr)` helper at the top of `server_integration.rs` retries `TcpStream::connect` up to ~2 s (100 iterations × 20 ms backoff), panicking with the last error if the server never comes up; all six `send_request` call sites route through it via a single replacement of the raw `TcpStream::connect` call. This is purely a test-infrastructure fix — the enrollment server is unchanged — but the race touches every test in the file, so one fix unblocks the whole suite. Five consecutive local runs of the 10-test integration binary pass; before the fix, the race was visible under CI load. (#982)
- **Align federation JWT clock-skew tolerance with heartbeat timeout to stop `peer_connected` / `token_rejected` flap** — `rustgate_federation::jwt::MAX_CLOCK_SKEW_SECS` is raised from 60 s to 120 s so JWT `iat` validation no longer rejects tokens issued by a peer whose clock drifts inside the window where heartbeats still declare the link alive (`FEDERATION_HEARTBEAT_TIMEOUT = 90 s`). Previously, any NTP drift between 60 s and 90 s produced an observable flap: the liveness check accepted each new mTLS session, the very next token refresh failed `iat > now + 60`, the connector tore the session down with `token_rejected`, reconnected, and re-flapped indefinitely — visible in the audit trail as an unbounded stream of `federation_peer_connected` / `token_rejected` pairs against the same peer CN.
